What's the difference between Android's Qi2 And Qi2.2 wireless charging?
There are some key distinctions that make a big difference.
We live in a wireless world, so understanding the different standards at play can help you to maximize the performance of your gadgets and your chargers. For most devices, the wireless charging standard you'll be using is Qi2.
The latest iteration of this is Qi2 25W, also commonly called Qi2.2. It was announced last summer that the new speed would be supported by both iPhones and select Android smartphones. Although Google was slow to adopt Qi2, we're now starting to see Qi2 25W listed as a feature for the next generation of Android phones, including the Pixel 11 lineup announced recently.
So does it matter which version your device supports? There are a couple key distinctions that make Qi2.2 a worthwhile upgrade.
More power, more speed
The difference between Qi2 and Qi2.2 charging comes down to power. Qi2 25W offers 25 watts of power delivery when it's charging a compatible device. Qi2 is capped at 15 watts, so the new standard offers a substantial boost to power.
In practice, that means your device will charge faster if it's using Qi2 25W. With Qi2, your gadgets could take between 50 and 80 minutes to reach 50 percent battery from zero. Qi2 25W, on the other hand, will get you to half battery in about half an hour. Considering wireless charging has traditionally been less efficient than wired, that's a welcome improvement.
An additional benefit to Qi2.2 is improved thermal protection. So if you've ever noticed your phone getting pretty toasty while it's on a wireless pad, the upgrade will be a good one. Even if you can't feel the difference, it might subtly help to extend your phone's lifespan, because the lower peak temperature while charging can help your battery last longer.
All told, Qi2 25W offers a solid improvement over its predecessor, so reap the rewards if your hardware supports this latest power option.

I won’t lie to you: I hated the first digital wall calendar I tried.
I tested it last year and was left unimpressed. It was expensive and massive, and my calendar details were slow to appear (if they appeared at all). The device felt more like clutter than a useful addition to my home. So, I wrote off the idea of using a digital wall calendar, but to my surprise, they have only picked up in popularity and options since then. After trying a few new models myself this year, I can now see why.
These gadgets work by taking your online calendar—whether your Google Calendar, the calendar app on your iPhone, or your corporate Microsoft calendar account—and putting it on a digital screen that you can mount on the wall or prop up on a countertop or table. They’re often more than just calendars, also functioning as chore charts, meal planners, and sometimes even digital photo frames. I usually have smart displays all over my home, especially in my kitchen and living area, but for the past two weeks, I’ve replaced them all with digital wall calendars. And you know what? I don't miss talking to those annoying AI-powered assistants.
Instead, as someone who already lives and breathes by her Google Calendar, I love being able to see it on a large display in the middle of the kitchen, without needing my phone—especially when it’s on a digital wall device that immediately reflects my most up-to-date calendar. My husband and I have also been using the extra features more often, particularly to guide my 4-year-old through his evening bedtime routine with the help of his own companion device. Here's everything you need to know about the best digital wall calendars and whether they're right for you.
Updated August 2026: I've added the Skylight Buddy as a kid-friendly tool that includes some features of these digital calendar devices. I’ve also ensured accuracy and up-to-date information throughout.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
My Favorite Digital Calendars
What’s a Digital Wall Calendar?
You might have heard these gadgets called by various names. Maybe “digital wall calendar” or “smart calendar device.” Maybe you've just heard the name Skylight Calendar, which is a notably popular model right now. No matter what you call them, these devices all do the same thing: replace a paper calendar with a digitized one that connects to the calendar tools you're already using, like Google Calendar or Apple Calendar. The devices let you see your entire family’s schedule in one view, with the ability to update or add to it without needing a phone or a separate account. It also erases issues like unreadable handwriting and forgetting to write down an event you've already scheduled digitally, and its color-coding system makes it easy to see who's on the hook for which activities.
While these are often called wall calendars, you can usually choose to place them on a tabletop. I preferred the models that included a tabletop stand, but I was still able to prop up the ones that only came with wall-mounting hardware during my testing.
What Else Can a Digital Wall Calendar Do?
These devices aren't just calendars; they’re also designed for larger family management. You'll find features to help you plan meals, track to-do lists for multiple people, and earn rewards on a digital chore chart. The Skylight Calendar 2 is a favorite of mine because it includes a photo screensaver, but you'll need to be a Plus subscriber to get that and some of the other bonus features. Basically, you can use these calendars to manage your family's full schedule, chores, meals, and more in a single device.
Is a Digital Wall Calendar Worth It?
I didn't expect to feel this way, but having a physical version of my hyper-detailed Google Calendar in the center of my home has been a delight. My husband and I both check our calendar at a glance while we're chatting in the kitchen, and at the start of the week, we'll camp out in front of it for a few minutes to plan the week's dinners and grocery needs. My top pick, Skylight Calendar 2, actually prompts us to add items to our grocery list based on what meals we picked (if it's a stored recipe, that is).
My husband and I have found it so useful in part because we're both good about adding events to our individual calendars, so now this device can reflect that work. It lets us skip pulling out our phones when discussing plans for the next day or the upcoming weekend.
The Best Digital Calendars
Skylight's calendar is the most popular for a reason. The brand is known for its digital photo frames, and now you can use the same Skylight app to operate any of its three digital calendars: The older 10-inch Calendar ($170), the newer Calendar 2 ($320), and the Calendar Max ($630). The main difference between these is size, but Calendar 2 is the newest model, with improved performance and interchangeable Snap Frames ($30 to $50) you can purchase to change the device's look.
What makes Skylight great is its software. It's easy to use, and it quickly imported my Google Calendar and the wide variety of calendars shared to it, so I could immediately add all of my family's schedules to the device. The left-side menu bar shows all the pages you can toggle between. Calendar, Lists, Tasks, Rewards, Meals, and Recipes are the main areas you'll use; you can also access the Photos, Sleep, and Settings pages from the same menu.
The app and device interface are clean and intuitive compared with other models, many of which feel like Android tablets with a fancy calendar mode added. I was able to easily assign calendars I created on the device to family members. For example, I assigned my husband's calendar to him without needing him to log in or import it, and I could have assigned any calendar I created to my son as well. I also liked that shared events only appear once on the Skylight, but with both of our designated colors added to show the event in question applied to both of us.
Lists and Tasks sound similar, but Tasks are meant to function as a chore chart, connecting back to the Rewards page to build habits and earn the reward you set after hitting a certain goal. The main audience for this is children who are old enough to check the calendar. Lists are for things like your groceries. If you add recipes to the Recipe tab and then add those to your meal plan for that week, Skylight will offer to put the corresponding ingredients on your shopping list.
The downside of Skylight is the paywall. To access some of the best features—meal planning, rewards, photo screensaver, and the in-app AI assistant tool Sidekick—you'll need to be a Plus subscriber for either $79 a year or $8 a month. Having this device double as a digital photo frame makes it worth the cost to me. I love getting to have my two favorite things nearby: photos of my family and instant access to our shared calendars.
The Everblog HomeCal has an operating system that feels pleasantly similar to the Skylight. It has a bit of an Android undertone to it, but it doesn't feel like a giant tablet as much as the Apolosign or Cozyla calendars (both below). Setup was pretty seamless, but there was a delay for the device to update with my calendar invites. It would also take a while for the Everblog to reflect changes I made to my Google Calendar on another device. While it worked well for the most part during testing, I occasionally noticed events missing from my Everblog. It also turned each calendar email account I connected to the device into a separate profile, which was annoying. I could toggle off the extra emails when I was on pages outside of the calendar, though, so I didn't have three profiles for myself on my Chores page, for example.
The menu on the left-hand side is very similar to Skylight's, with options like Calendar, Chores, and Meal Plan. There isn't a recipe section, which I miss, but there is a Fridge section, which lets you track the groceries you already have. Part of why this exists is because Everblog also has a smaller, battery-powered version of this calendar that's designed to attach to your fridge, aptly named the FridgeCal ($249). Still, I prefer the Recipe tab on the Skylight. The Everblog also has a Chores tab, but no additional tab for tracking regular chores or other to-dos separately.
There's a free photo option, but the uploader tool in the app only lets you add one photo at a time. Painful, but I'm sure many would feel it's worth the free price tag. To use the feature, you'll need to go into the settings on the physical device to turn on photo slideshow as your screensaver. The Everblog defaults to pinging loudly at the start of any calendar event, which you can only change on the device, not in the app.
There's a button on the bottom right-hand corner of the screen that will take you to a homepage with an overview of the calendar and chores, and access to other applications like Spotify and Netflix, if you set up your accounts on this device for streaming content. It comes enabled for wall mounting, but you can purchase the Calendar Stand ($39) if you want to situate it on a tabletop, and there's a wooden frame ($99) you can buy to snap on to give it a nicer look.
Apolosign's digital calendar has three sizes: 15.7, 21.5, and 27 inches. It runs Google's Android OS, so it operates very similarly to an Android tablet and to Google's Pixel Tablet, if you've used either as a smart display, as I have. The Apolosign has two modes: Calendar and Android. Calendar mode worked similarly to Skylight. I seamlessly connected it to my Google Calendar, imported over most of my various shared calendars, and color-coded them.
The Calendar mode has a left-side menu bar (you'll have to tap to make it appear), with sections for Home, Calendar, Routines, To-Dos, Rewards, and Meals. The Home page has a two-column design, showing you the calendar on one side and your Routines and To-Dos on the other. You can then tap into any of these sections or check off items directly from the Home page. Apolosign also has baked-in notifications that chime to remind you about calendar events and to-dos, plus phone notifications to let you know how many items are on your calendar that day.
WIRED Reviewer Kat Merck also tested Apolosign, but used Android mode instead of Calendar mode. Android mode allows you to customize widgets and layout, so she opted for a monthly view. This mode also lets you use photos from Google Photos as a background and screensaver. She says it's nice to be able to customize the layout in this mode, but it struggles to sync with other programs, including Apolosign's own app.
I don't like the Apolosign experience quite as much as the Skylight or Everblog, and Kat agreed that this device is not very intuitive and takes a lot of patience to set up. But having no paywall is a huge plus, and many people will feel it's worth getting used to the more Android-style experience to not pay a monthly or yearly fee. But since it's essentially a large Android tablet, iPhone users have flagged on Reddit that they can't two-way sync between it and their iPhone devices. The Apolosign is often on sale for the same price, if not cheaper, than the Skylight.
If you want a version made for kids, Skylight has something along those lines called the Skylight Buddy (8/10, WIRED Recommends). It's not a digital calendar but rather a chore-and-routine display that helps kids visualize and check off their daily to-dos without needing to navigate an entire family calendar.
My 4-year-old loves his 7-inch Buddy, and it really does help get him to brush his teeth and put on his PJs in a timely (well, more timely) fashion now that it's in his room. It also has a night-light and sound machine, but the sounds are limited, and the night-light is pretty dim. So for those capabilities, I'm sticking to the Hatch Baby my son is used to and loves.
Ultimately, this is most useful if you already have and use a Skylight Calendar. That’s because the Buddy can sync to and show designated tasks already on the Skylight Calendar. But even if you don't have the Calendar and just want more of a routine tool or chore-tracker for your child, this is a really good option. There are subscription options to get more features—Buddy Plus is $39 a year, and Skylight Plus is $79 a year. Skylight Plus is what you should get if you have the Calendar, as it unlocks paywalled features for both devices. But I haven't needed any subscription-only capabilities to keep my son excited about and engaged in his bedtime routine.
Others I’ve Tested
Cozyla Calendar Plus 2 (15.6 Inches) for $350: This calendar is similar to Apolosign with an Android-based operating system, but it didn't import my shared calendars, meaning it took more work to set up. It was overall frustrating to navigate and didn't guide me through its tools as effectively as Skylight or Apolosign. While Cozyla doesn't have any subscription fees, its 15.6-inch size is more expensive than both Skylight's and Apolosign's.
Hearth Display for $699: This is another digital calendar and family tool that has a paywall with an affordable Family Membership ($6 a month) but a much higher initial price point. It's only available in a large, 27-inch size, and I found it was slow to load my calendar and also bulky compared to more affordable options.
FAQs
How Do Digital Wall Calendars Work?
Digital wall calendars sync with your existing digital calendar app of choice, like Google Calendar, and display it on the physical screen. There are usually additional tools for recipes, to-do lists, and chores, but each digital wall calendar varies in how you import the information. You may have to manually import it or type the details into the device, but once you get used to the process, the function can be helpful for the whole family.
Will Changes to My Calendar Appear Instantly?
Changes you make on your native calendar app, like Google Calendar and Apple's Calendar, should reflect quickly onto the digital wall calendar device. But changes you make on the device aren't always backward compatible with the native calendar. It depends on the calendar's settings and how the information was shared; I can edit my primary personal calendar on the Skylight Calendar 2, for example, but I can’t edit my work calendar that I shared to the Skylight through my personal. There are also some syncing issues you may run into with the Apolosign, which doesn't two-way sync with an iPhone since the digital calendar runs on an Android operating system.
How Is a Digital Calendar Different From a Smart Display?
Many smart displays look similar to these devices but have an entirely different operating system. Sure, the Google Pixel Tablet has some overlap with the Apolosign and Cozyla, since they all run an Android operating system. But unlike smart displays, digital calendar devices are designed with specific tools to run your family and none of the clutter. You'll lose out on smart-home support, though Apolosign claims you can use Google Assistant on it (that hasn't worked for me so far). On most devices, you'll also compromise on extras like video streaming (you can, however, stream on Everblog). But as someone who uses a smart display regularly, I really didn’t miss it once I switched over to the digital calendar device. I do wish there were a weather-report page, as most digital wall calendars just show the current weather.
Does It Have to Go on the Wall?
No—in fact, most of these devices come with a table-stand option. I only tested in table-stand mode since I had multiple of these devices in my house at one time, but the wall-mounting option is nice, allowing you to keep your tabletops clear. The 15-inch models are great for tabletops, and you may want to consider larger sizes for the wall-mounting route.

Drills cut by Trump are central to the US-South Korea alliance
The United States and South Korea have regularly conducted military drills to prepare for potential conflicts with North Korea
SEOUL, South Korea -- For decades, the United States and South Korea have regularly staged military drills to prepare their soldiers to work together smoothly in the event of a crisis or conflict with North Korea.
But this year's Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, one of the two main drills conducted by the allies annually, could be disrupted after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered his Pentagon chief to “substantially” scale it back just before its start Monday.
He cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and South Korea’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran. It was unclear what parts of the 11-day exercise were being cut and to what extent, but many experts say Trump's move threatens to hurt combined U.S.-South Korean readiness and eventually weaken their decades-long alliance.
The Ulchi Freedom Shield, or UFS, is a computer-simulated tabletop exercise meant to hone the allies' ability to deal with potential regional security threats like North Korean aggression. The two countries usually hold field training exercises during the tabletop exercise period.
South Korea's military had earlier said this year's exercise would be similar in scale to previous years, with the participation of about 18,000 South Korean soldiers. The U.S. military said it would incorporate lessons from recent conflicts such as North Korea’s battlefield experiences on the Russia-Ukraine front. Local media reported South Korea and the U.S. had planned 14 field training exercises.
The UFS, along with a similar joint war game in the spring, is a central pillar of the U.S. -South Korea alliance, which dates back to the 1950-53 Korean War. But it's also a long-running source of tensions with North Korea, which has denounced the exercises as a rehearsal for war and responded with provocative missile tests.
Last Friday, North Korea's Foreign Ministry accused the U.S. and South Korea of plotting more provocative drills this year and vowed to respond with “a new level of a deterrent.” The U.S. and South Korea have said their regular drills are defensive in nature.
In a social media post, Trump called the exercise costly, "with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America.” During his first term, Trump complained about the cost of drills with South Korea, suspending joint exercises in 2018 to advance now-stalled nuclear negotiations with North Korea.
Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of about 28,500 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea, visited South Korean Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back on Tuesday for talks likely focusing on the adjustment of this year’s drills, according to media reports. South Korea’s Defense Ministry said it couldn’t confirm the report.
Yang Uk, an analyst at Seoul’s Asan Institute for Policy Studies, said the U.S. will likely participate in the tabletop exercise but cancel “some costly field training that requires large-scale movements of troops."
Yang said that a downsizing or suspension of military drills matters because commanders of the allies change periodically. He said a one-year suspension of drills would see commanders unfamiliar with procedures of those drills taking part when they resume.
Jung Chang Wook, head of the Korea Defense Study Forum think tank in Seoul, said Trump’s step could result in the U.S. downsizing other regular drills with South Korea, posing “a big, crippling blow” to their joint operation posture.
Lee Illwoo, an expert with the Korea Defense Network, said downsizing the exercise will likely delay the planned transfer to a system in which wartime operational control would be exercised by a binational command led by a South Korean general.
Under the current system, the U.S. military would command joint forces in the event of war.
The South Korean and U.S. militaries had earlier said the exercise would be an opportunity to support preparations for the transfer. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Tuesday stressed the need to complete the transition during his term that ends in 2030.
Many South Koreans view the transition to South Korean leadership of the combined forces in wartime to be a matter of national sovereignty, but others worry that could weaken the alliance.

Srinagar, Aug 19: Two Mumbai doctors who belonged to Parsi community will reportedly receive Pakistan’s highest civilian award posthumously for “faithfully guarding the secret” of the country’s founder, Muhammad Ali Jinnah’s illness.
The doctors – physician Dr Jal Ratanji Patel and radiologist Dr Jal Dhaybho-Koo – have been nominated by Islamabad for the Nishan-e-Imtiaz award, which will be conferred on them at a ceremony in March, 2027. The announcement was made on social media platform X by Ahsan Iqbal, federal minister for planning, development and special initiatives and head of the Awards Committee, Hindustan Times reported.
It said that both doctors had examined Jinnah's X-ray in 1946, and had diagnosed him with an advanced stage of tuberculosis, concluding that he had only a year or two to live, according to Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre's book, ‘Freedom at Midnight’.
In his post, the Pakistan minister said both doctors had “faithfully guarded the secret” of Jinnah's terminal illness. “I feel honoured to have had the privilege, as Chairman of the Awards Committee, of nominating for the Nishan-e-Imtiaz two remarkable doctors, a physician and a radiologist, both members of Bombay's Parsi community, who faithfully guarded the secret of Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah's terminal illness,” Iqbal said on X.
He said the doctors have maintained “absolute professional confidentiality” at what he said was a “critical moment”, adding that they had “performed a quiet but extraordinary service.”
“Their fidelity to their professional oath inadvertently became a significant contribution to the circumstances that made the creation of Pakistan possible,” Iqbal said.
Keeping the diagnosis secret was significant to the creation of Pakistan, as has been highlighted by Louis Mountbatten, the last viceroy under the British regime who planned and enacted the partition in 1947.
“Lord Mountbatten later acknowledged that, had he known how seriously ill Jinnah was, he might have delayed partition—potentially altering the course of history and perhaps even jeopardising the creation of Pakistan,” Pakistan minister Iqbal said in his post.
According to the account in ‘Freedom at Midnight’, a book by Larry Collins and Dominique Lapierre, the knowledge of Jinnah's illness could have possibly altered the course of events leading up to the partition.
“If I had known all this at the time, history would have taken a different course. I would have delayed the decision to grant Independence by several months. Pakistan would not have come into existence,” Mountbatten told the reporters later.
Historian Akbar Ahmed, in his book ‘Jinnah, Pakistan and Islamic Identity: The Search for Saladin’, noted that Jinnah had been suffering from tuberculosis since 1930s, when the disease had no effective antibiotic treatment.
“Since 1938 he had been constantly complaining of 'tremendous strain' on his nerves and physical strength. After that, he began to fall ill regularly, although his illness was kept secret,” Ahmed wrote in the book. However, this secret was known by a very tight group of people, including Jinnah's sister Fatima and the two doctors.

In mid-August 2026, social media users circulated a claim that U.S. President Donald Trump ordered sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln to sign nondisclosure agreements before they were allowed to leave the aircraft carrier.
One Facebook post spreading the rumor was captioned, "Trump is making USS Lincoln sailors sign an NDA before they can get off the ship. #navy #ussabrahamlincoln #military #nda #fascism."
(Facebook user Politics Girl Official)
Variations of the claim also spread on social media platforms, including Threads, X and Instagram. We also received emails from readers asking whether the claim was true.
In short, it was not. We found no evidence Trump ordered sailors to sign NDAs before coming ashore, and the rumor originated from a Facebook post with a "satire" label.
The earliest version of the claim we found came from a Facebook post by Karl E. Rominger. Its headline read "TRUMP ORDERS USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN SAILORS TO SIGN NDAs BEFORE COMING ASHORE."
The post's text stated:
Donald Trump announced today that sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln will not be permitted to leave the ship until they sign legally binding nondisclosure agreements promising never to say anything "negative, nasty or insufficiently beautiful" about their deployment.
Especially off-limits: the mysterious laundry-room fire. Sailors are specifically forbidden from suggesting the fire was anything other than a completely ordinary laundry-room fire that absolutely, positively had nothing whatsoever to do with Iran. They are also forbidden from wondering aloud whether the carrier remained at sea while repairs were completed so nobody standing on a dock with a cellphone could photograph whatever definitely did not happen.
"Nothing happened," Trump explained. "And anybody saying something happened will spend the remainder of their natural life at Fort Leavenworth for talking about the thing that never happened."
Pete Hegseth, Marco Rubio and J.D. Vance immediately described requiring thousands of returning sailors to sign secrecy agreements on the gangway as "totally normal military procedure." Hegseth added that anyone asking why such an agreement would be necessary if nothing happened clearly hates the troops. 
Trump initially claimed the NDA was his idea before explaining that Susie Wiles developed it, Hegseth approved it, Rubio translated it into diplomatic language, and Vance volunteered to explain on television why Americans should never believe anything sailors tell their own families.
Because nothing says nothing happened quite like threatening everybody who was there if they talk about it.
 
(Facebook user Karl E. Rominger)
The post explicitly labeled its content as satirical. It ended: "Follow Karl E. Rominger for more news, satire and uncomfortable questions. #KarlTalks #Satire #USSAbrahamLincoln #Trump #Politics."
Moreover, the Facebook profile page describes its content as "Political parody, sharp commentary" and it features numerous other fictional stories written in a similar style.
Story inspired by real-life fire on another carrier?
There was a real laundry-room fire aboard a U.S. aircraft carrier during the Iran conflict. It happened on the USS Gerald R. Ford, when a fire broke out in the ship's laundry room on March 12, 2026, which U.S. Central Command said was not related to combat.
The Ford later stopped in Greece for repairs, and more than 200 sailors were treated for smoke inhalation.
The satirical Facebook post may have been referencing this incident when mentioning a "mysterious laundry-room fire," but we found no evidence confirming that. In any case, the fire happened on a different carrier months before August 2026.
Abraham Lincoln deployment context
The rumor spread while the USS Abraham Lincoln already was drawing attention over its unusually long deployment. As of this writing, the aircraft carrier had spent about nine months at sea, and reports described food and supply shortages and low morale among its crew. Other claims about conditions aboard the carrier also circulated online. For instance, in August 2026, we investigated reports that sailors tried to go overboard during the extended deployment.
All in all, certain concerns about the USS Abraham Lincoln's extended deployment and its conditions in August 2026 were well-documented. However, the allegation that Trump ordered its sailors to sign NDAs before being allowed ashore originated from an account that labels its content as satire.
For further reading, we have previously investigated other fabricated posts from the same account. For instance, in June 2026, we fact-checked a fabricated screenshot claiming Trump said he walked out of an NBC "Meet the Press" interview because reporter Kristen Welker kept staring at his ear.
Because the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Alan Dershowitz Won’t Forget What Larry David Did to Him
He has new friends on Martha’s Vineyard. But his tales of cancellation have not subsided.
Here it is, August on Martha’s Vineyard, and Alan Dershowitz has barely been heard from.
Well, that’s not exactly true. He has been heard from on many topics—because Dershowitz is who he is, and pretty much anyone can join Substack, and TV bookers can be hard to resist. Still, he has said little publicly about the maddening injustice he’s faced in recent years: his annual summer shunning at the hands of the island’s liberal social gentry. Has this perennial comedy of ill manners—the Vineyard cancellation of Alan Dershowitz—finally run its course?
The story has become a familiar seasonal menace; as pernicious as ticks, and as hard to kill. Its particulars are known. Dershowitz, the inexhaustible Harvard Law professor who represented a gallery of notorious clients over several decades, was once a kibitzing dynamo here. But that was before the blacklists and the badgering.
In his telling (and retelling), Dershowitz became socially radioactive during Donald Trump’s first term, when he began speaking out on the president’s behalf, and then joined his first impeachment defense team. Although he did not personally support Trump—he’d been a lifelong Democrat who’d voted for Hillary Clinton in 2016 and would support Joe Biden in 2020—his stock explanation was that everyone is entitled to legal representation. It was the same basic principle he had applied when representing the likes of Mike Tyson, O. J. Simpson, Claus von Bülow, and, more recently, Jeffrey Epstein. It was no different, in fact, than the occasion of Dershowitz’s first-ever visit to Martha’s Vineyard, in 1969, when he was enlisted to help in the defense of Ted Kennedy after his late-night accident at Chappaquiddick.
Yet defending Trump was apparently too noxious for Dershowitz’s reputation. “I never thought I would see McCarthyism come to Martha’s Vineyard,” he lamented in a column in The Hill in 2018. According to Dershowitz, locals have urged his exclusion from various Vineyard businesses and institutions. Every summer, it seems, has brought a new episode in ostracism, cold shoulders in the hot sun.
There was the Great Pierogi Incident last year at the West Tisbury farmers’ market, in which a vendor refused to sell half a dozen dumplings to Dershowitz, citing his representation of “several sexual predators and abusers, including Jeffrey Epstein.” Dershowitz claimed that he was being discriminated against over his vocal support for Israel and initiated a follow-up spectacle a week later in which the vendor, Krem Miskevich, refused to accept a signed copy of one of Dershowitz’s books (The Ten Big Anti-Israel Lies) as a peace offering.
In 2022, Dershowitz said he’d received a fan email from a reader who alleged that he’d been beaten up at the beach (he did not specify where) just for carrying a copy of a book written by Dershowitz. “Without warning, I was slugged and punched in the face,” the man wrote to Dershowitz, who reprinted the unverified email on Substack in a post titled “Email From a Man Who Got Beaten Up for Reading My Book.”
And then there was the infamous clash at the Chilmark General Store with Dershowitz’s now very-much-ex-friend Larry David. In the annals of Dershowitz’s social spiral on the Vineyard, this conflagration has taken on almost-mythic dimensions, like his own personal Stalingrad. Dershowitz was sitting on the porch of the store with another friend, “who happened to be a very kind of radical woke lefty from New York, but very tolerant,” he told me. David was not very tolerant, at least of Dershowitz. He walked onto the porch, refused to shake Dershowitz’s hand, called him “disgusting,” and stormed off. Dershowitz said at the time that David was so irate, Dershowitz worried that the comedian might suffer a stroke.
That unpleasantness on the porch, memorialized on Page Six, took place five summers ago. But Dershowitz talks about it as if it were yesterday.
On a recent Saturday, I ventured north from Washington for a little hardship duty in Chilmark, the preciously pastoral town on the western side of the island where Dershowitz has owned a home since 1991. I approached him first by email, telling Dershowitz that I was curious about his current social standing on the Vineyard and how things were going for him this summer. The subject matter could be freshly topical, I figured, because his two most prominent clients—Trump and Epstein—are more toxic than ever. To my surprise, Dershowitz agreed to speak with me.
Actually, I was not surprised.
“We can meet on the porch for a slice,” he proposed.
Dershowitz, who turns 88 next month, has been presiding from the rocking chairs of the Chilmark General Store for decades, juggling pizza and discourse. When I arrived, I found him wearing a bright-red T-shirt with the words Proud American over an Israeli flag and an American one, each in the shape of a heart. He told me that he’d asked his wife, Carolyn Cohen, to join us but she had no interest. “She said, ‘I’m so sick and tired of this subject,’” he told me. Dershowitz conceded that he, too, is weary of it. “But, you know, it’s important that people get the whole context,” he said.
The whole context, in 2026, is basically this: Dershowitz says he has started a new life on the Vineyard. But just because his persecution tale has become an island eye-roll does not mean that it has subsided. Especially, according to Dershowitz, in his own, bucolic neighborhood. “Here in Chilmark, it’s 90 percent negative,” Dershowitz reported to me. That reception contrasts with what he gets in Miami Beach, where he spends his winters and where, he said, he is treated “wonderfully.” He is “treated very well” even in the more heavily trafficked Vineyard towns on the other side of the island. “In Edgartown and even Oak Bluffs, the African American community, I’m treated very well,” he said. “It’s all Chilmark. And it’s all Jewish, anti-Zionist.”
I noted that he can at least still hold court at the Chilmark General Store. But he argued with my choice of the term holding court.
“I used to—not anymore,” he said.
“You don’t hold court anymore?” I asked, as he arguably held court. “What is this?”
“You’re interviewing me,” he said. In the past, it would have been a high-end conclave. “Normally, we would have this whole area,” he said, motioning to a group of rocking chairs on one side of the porch. “I would have Larry David here,” he said. “Ted Danson was here sometimes,” he added. “The guy who did Ghostbusters—he died a few years ago—he was here.” (This was Harold Ramis, who died in 2014.)
“The whole crew of Chilmark friends, I would say, 20 or so, no longer talk to me,” Dershowitz said.
He pointed next door to the Chilmark Tavern, one of his favorite restaurants on the Vineyard, where he claims that some of his vacation nemeses are trying to get him banned. “A bunch of people went to the Chilmark Tavern and said If you continue to serve Dershowitz, we’re not coming here,” he insisted.
I was skeptical of this. “Ask her; you can check with her,” he said. “Jenny.” When I contacted Jenna Petersiel, the proprietor of the Chilmark Tavern, she told me that she’d assumed that The Atlantic wanted to speak with her about the challenges of running a restaurant, or ticks. “A discussion of Alan Dershowitz had not crossed my mind,” she said, declining to comment otherwise. Dershowitz also told me of an event he had attended on the Chilmark Tavern deck not long ago. A woman got out of her car, he claimed, “saw I was up there, turned around, and went back to her car.”
He appears to have a limitless supply of such stories, in part because it seems as if Dershowitz initiates a fair number of confrontations himself. The week before our conversation, he had returned to the hallowed cultural battleground of the Pierogi Wars, the West Tisbury farmers’ market. He was wearing his U.S.-Israel shirt (or “my Zionist T-shirt,” of which he has two—one red, one blue) and saw a guy wearing a Free Palestine shirt. “I walked up to him. I said, ‘Can we take a picture together?’” The man refused. “He said, ‘No, no, no Israel,’ and he walked away.”
Dershowitz believes that many of his old Vineyard friends revile him for calling out the “anti-Zionist” and “radical” bent of the progressive left. He showed me his phone and cued up what he calls “my daily love note.” This one was an unsolicited email he’d just received, with “GENOCIDAL ZIONIST ISRAEL!” in the subject line; he kindly forwarded the note to me. “They always combine Zionism with pedophilia,” Dershowitz observed of his correspondents.
A few times during our conversation, I questioned Dershowitz about whether people really reject him because of his Zionist views or whether it might involve something more comprehensive: him being Alan Dershowitz. His position on the Middle East seems farther down the list of reasons that people might not like him than his affiliations with Trump and Epstein and his overall reputation, accrued over decades.
But Dershowitz claims, for instance, that he’s no longer asked to speak at the Martha’s Vineyard Book Festival because “they censor anybody they disagree with.” (A spokesperson for the book festival told me in an email that Dershowitz’s claim is “completely false” and that “the festival line up over the past two decades hardly reflects a narrow or excluding agenda.”)
“I personify what the woke hates,” Dershowitz said. Before I could ask him what, exactly, “the woke” is, he explained that he is now seen as a “traitor” to the Democratic Party. The enmity is mutual. In September, he has a new book coming out called Why I Quit the Dems: And So Should You! The subtitle is Confessions of a Reluctant Republican.
I asked Dershowitz directly whether he had voted for Trump in 2024.
“You’re allowed to ask it,” he said. “And my wife does not allow me to answer it.”
“Okay, so you’re going to hide behind your wife,” I said.
“I’m going to hide behind my wife,” he confirmed.
For the record, Dershowitz added that he always votes, and said that he had not voted for Kamala Harris. Also, his new book includes a blurb from President Trump (who obviously read every word).
Despite all of this, Dershowitz has arrived at a nuanced take on his snubbing. “I think it’s selective cancellation,” he told me. “We decided, basically, to change our life on the Vineyard.”
He said that he keeps busy by writing and doing regular paid appearances on Newsmax, occasional hits on Fox News, Piers Morgan’s show on YouTube, and other outlets. (He used to be on CNN all the time, but no more—“CNN has canceled me.”) He said that he does not lack social options. He has become very active in a Vineyard Chabad that he helped start. He told me at one point about all of the new friends he’s made. “Most of them are more supportive of Israel than the other group was,” he said. “And I often ask myself, How did I allow myself to become part of that other group?”
When I asked Dershowitz who his new friends are, we wound up talking about someone who is definitely in the “other group”: Larry David.
They used to speak all the time, Dershowitz told me. They would have dinner, share jokes. “I allowed him to use my gym to work out,” Dershowitz said. “I helped him on a number of occasions.”
“Larry David doesn’t talk to me anymore,” Dershowitz said at another point. “He screams and yells at me when he sees me.” He told me that he used to be a fan of Curb Your Enthusiasm but can no longer bring himself to watch it. When discussing David, Dershowitz often spoke in the present tense, describing their breach as if it were an active feud and a still-fresh wound.
Predictably, David had minimal enthusiasm for discussing any of this when I reached out to him.
“I don’t know why he’s still thinking and talking about me,” he told me by email.
As for the five-year-old confrontation at the Chilmark store, David added this: “I have lots of confrontations on my show but rarely in life,” he said. “And then only if I think I can take them in a fight. Hence the Dershowitz dust-up.”
While Dershowitz and I spoke on the porch, a woman sitting in a rocking chair next to him kept leaning in, almost certainly eavesdropping. She confirmed this about half an hour into our conversation.
“I’m sorry to interrupt,” the woman said to Dershowitz. “I was just sitting here. And I just wanted to say, you sound super fascinating. And I hope nobody’s ever mean to you. Ever.”
Dershowitz kvelled.
“Did you plant her there or something?” I joked (sort of).
“I only paid her 10 dollars,” he joked (I think).
During our conversation, Dershowitz told me about a less cordial episode that had taken place last month in front of the Chilmark store, just a few feet from where we were sitting. The incident was not covered in the media, but Dershowitz had filmed a portion of it on his phone and shared the video with me. A guy in a Yankees cap had spotted Dershowitz at the store and promptly launched a barrage of Bronx cheers his way from the parking lot.
The man showed exemplary message discipline.
“Do you defend pedophiles? Do you defend pedophiles?” he repeated. “Yes, he does.”
Dershowitz demanded that his tormentor identify himself.
“My name is Jeffrey Epstein Jr., great friend to Alan Dershowitz,” the man replied.
Dershowitz kept demanding that the man state his name.
“What are you going to do?” the man asked.
“I’m going to sue you if you give your name,” Dershowitz said. (Surprisingly, the man continued to withhold his name.)
“Why? What are you going to sue me for?” he asked.
“For defamation.”
The heckler also mocked Dershowitz for, among other things, claiming to a TV reporter that, although he’d once received a massage from an adult woman at Epstein’s house, he’d kept his underwear on during the experience.
“He was on the plane, and he kept his underwear on,” the man taunted, while retreating across the street. There was some more hollering back and forth.
“You’re still a schmuck,” Dershowitz shouted.
In the pantheon of rogues and sleazeballs that Dershowitz has represented, Epstein stands out. Dershowitz helped orchestrate the late sex offender’s controversial plea deal in 2008; Epstein was allowed to plead guilty to state prostitution crimes in Florida, but he avoided federal trafficking charges and wound up serving just 13 months in jail. (At the time of his death, in 2019, he was awaiting trial on federal charges of child sex trafficking, by which point Dershowitz had fallen out with him and was no longer representing him.) Earlier in their relationship, they were frequent companions. Dershowitz was a visitor to Epstein’s homes in Palm Beach and New York, and went once with his wife and daughter to Epstein’s infamous island. (“No young women there,” Dershowitz wrote to me by email. “No one there except staff and ghislaine Maxwell.”)
I asked Dershowitz whether he’d ever been a passenger on Epstein’s plane.
“Oh, 20 times,” he said. As Epstein’s attorney, he explained, when he had to travel to Florida, his client would fly him down. However, the heckler’s claim that Dershowitz had received a massage on the plane was incorrect. That had taken place at Epstein’s home in Palm Beach. “This was a shoulder-and-neck massage, from an older woman,” Dershowitz told me. He said that this was “the only massage I’ve ever had in Epstein’s situation.”
“I’ve never in my life had an erotic massage. Not even from my wife,” he added, excruciatingly.
Dershowitz has said repeatedly that he never witnessed or participated in any unlawful sexual impropriety related to Epstein. In 2014, the Epstein survivor Virginia Giuffre alleged in court documents that the financier had trafficked her to multiple men while she was a minor. This included Dershowitz, who vehemently denied the charges. Giuffre sued Dershowitz for defamation, and Dershowitz countersued, claiming that she had made up the accusations. Giuffre withdrew her suit against Dershowitz in 2022, acknowledging that she might have made a mistake in identifying him. She died by suicide last year.
“I wish I never met him,” Dershowitz told me, speaking of Epstein. “But I don’t regret my representation of him.” This struck me as a classic bit of Dershowitz hairsplitting, and I was not quite sure what to make of it. Regardless, Dershowitz conveyed far more remorse over representing Epstein than I heard him express about any of his other clients. And he told me that he is resigned to Epstein being a lasting stain on his reputation and legacy.
“I’ve been already told I will have a bad obituary in The New York Times,” he volunteered.
“Who told you that?” I asked. “Do they work at The New York Times?”
“No,” Dershowitz said. He claimed to have heard it “from a guy who does obituaries for another newspaper.” (Apparently, all obit writers swap notes.) He added that an obituary writer for the Times did call him.
“With his deep obituary voice,” he noted, affecting a stentorian baritone. “I have to tell you that your obituary will include the allegations against you from Jeffrey Epstein,” the Times reporter said, according to the deep-voiced Dershowitz. He said that he’d urged the obit guy to “put it in perspective.” (Danielle Rhoades Ha, a New York Times spokesperson, declined to comment on any specific obituaries but told me by email, “We don’t write ‘negative’ or ‘positive’ obituaries, but strive for fair, comprehensive and accurate accounts of a person’s full life.”)
Dershowitz wanted to make clear to me how unfair he believes the Epstein-related allegations against him are. He and his wife have been married for 40 years, he said: “I have never cheated. I have never hugged—I don’t hug people. I don’t like hugging.” He also told me that he is “not a big massage person.”
“And by the way, nobody on the Vineyard believed this, even the people who hated me,” Dershowitz added. “Because they all see me with my wife.”
He went further. “In fact, the lawyer for Virginia Giuffre, he came over to me one day”—it was during a deposition—“and said, ‘Alan, I’ve seen you with your wife. I can’t believe you would ever have done anything.’”
I said I was dubious that the opposing lawyer would say something like this.
“I’ll give you his name—his name is Chuck Cooper.”
Reached by phone for comment, Charles Cooper, Giuffre’s lawyer, told me the exchange that Dershowitz had described had never taken place.
“This event that he’s reporting and this comment that he’s attributing to me are both categorically untrue,” Cooper said. He added that he remembers seeing Dershowitz with his wife on only one occasion, and that it was enough for him to make only a “fleeting observation.” Either way, “I did not say and I would never have said what he’s attributed to me,” Cooper said. “Give me a break.”
In the course of my discussion with Dershowitz, I learned of another fundamental change to his life, one that filled me with something I did not expect to feel: pathos.
Last year, Dershowitz’s son Elon died at 64, after suffering a stroke. He had been diagnosed with a malignant brain tumor when he was 10 and had been told that he’d be lucky to make it to his bar mitzvah. “We took extraordinary steps,” Dershowitz said, “all over the world.”
Elon had been his father’s sidekick. A film producer, he was the prime mover behind Reversal of Fortune, the 1990 legal thriller based on Dershowitz’s book about his successful defense of the British socialite Claus von Bülow in his trial for the attempted murder of his wife. The film solidified the status of Dershowitz (played by Ron Silver) as one of the “super lawyers” of his generation. “We went to the Oscars together,” Dershowitz said of him and Elon. Jeremy Irons won Best Actor for his portrayal of von Bülow. They went to an after-party. “I sat next to Gregory Peck, and it was a great moment,” Dershowitz said.
When Dershowitz spoke about Elon, I detected a note of anguish in his voice. On the Vineyard, they’d been pretty much inseparable. Dershowitz’s son used to join him at the Chilmark store, when he still held court. “He would come to the porch with me every day,” Dershowitz said. If anyone came up and started giving him trouble, Elon would get after them. “He was my guy.”
Everybody on the Vineyard liked Elon, Dershowitz said: “Even when they turned against me, they generally didn’t turn against Elon.”
“Although Larry David did.”
“Even when my son died—and Larry knew him very well—he never sent me a card,” Dershowitz said. “Never called me, never did anything to acknowledge it.”
After I returned from the Vineyard, I spoke with Dershowitz by phone. Since my visit, he’d suffered a fractured rib. When I asked how it had happened, he lamented that the cause was nothing dramatic. “I mean, I’d love to have a great story,” he said. “Passionate lovemaking, you know?” (Although definitely not an erotic massage.)
Alas. “I sneezed too hard,” he said. “My doctor told me at my age, a sneeze or a hard cough can fracture a rib.”
Despite being in pain, Dershowitz said that he was planning to go that night to a Chabad event at the home of the billionaire hedge-fund manager Paul Singer, a big Republican donor and supporter of Israel. In a few days, Dershowitz was scheduled to be honored at the Chabad to mark the 75th anniversary of his bar mitzvah. We briefly revisited the Pierogi Incident; he sent me a link to a Facebook post from someone marking “the anniversary of Pierogigate” and vowing to “have a potato pierogi later today in honor of Dershowitz.”
When I mentioned Larry David’s name again, Dershowitz sounded freshly pained—as if I’d elbowed him in his bad rib. They had been really good friends, he reiterated. I asked whether he’d had any interaction with David since the Chilmark-store episode in 2021. Not really, Dershowitz said, except for one chance meeting at a restaurant, in which David had again blown him off. Later, Dershowitz wanted to know whether I’d spoken with David for this story.
After our initial email exchange, I finally did speak with David by phone late last week. He was on vacation on Martha’s Vineyard, and I expected him to be cantankerous and annoyed—which he was at first. When I brought up the matter of Elon’s death, however, David’s tone shifted. “He’s 100 percent right,” David told me, referring to Dershowitz. “I should have reached out, and I certainly regret not doing so. As I said on Curb once, ‘I think of nice things. I just don’t act on them.’”
David, who turned 79 last month, said that he has been “softening” and might be open to some kind of rapprochement with Dershowitz, if only to extinguish their one-way feud once and for all. “I’m starting to feel a little sorry for him, actually,” David told me. “Certainly because of his son.”
It was a touching moment, and seemed sincere. But something also felt off, as if the network had enlisted focus groups and then ordered up a feel-good ending.
Then David sent me an email the next morning.
“I’m loath to say anything mean because he’s been so ostracized,” he wrote of Dershowitz. A reversion to sarcasm! “But he only has himself to blame. He made a deal with the devil. Literally. And I’d bet the devil hasn’t said a word to him since the impeachment.”

President Trump is expected to nominate Heidi Overton, deputy director of domestic policy for the White House, to serve as the next commissioner of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, STAT writes. Overton, who has been a powerful health policy voice in Trump’s second term and, at times, frustrated leaders of the Make America Healthy Again movement, will have to face scrutiny from a U.S. Senate panel before getting the job, should Trump choose her. Overton joined the White House at the start of Trump’s term and has led health policy ever since, working closely with the U.S. Health and Human Services Department.
A personalized mRNA cancer vaccine, added to an existing treatment, slowed the return of melanoma and its spread to other parts of the body in a late-stage clinical trial, results that could herald a new, powerful approach in oncology, STAT writes. Merck and Moderna did not immediately release detailed data, but if the results hold up, they could deliver new hope and potentially longer lives for patients. They could also be a further testament to the power of mRNA as a platform to develop both traditional vaccines and therapeutics. Approval of the treatment would also be a boon for Moderna’s mRNA platform, which has become a political lightning rod.

Thai schools hold active shooter drills after deadly attack
The drills follow a directive requiring schools to draw up security plans and rehearse emergency response procedures
Schools in Thailand conducted active shooter drills on Wednesday, as authorities moved to strengthen security measures two weeks after a 14-year-old opened fire at a school and killed at least eight people.
At the Surasamontree School in Bangkok, students took part in a “run, hide, fight” exercise, with a police officer dressed in black and acting as a mock attacker, armed with a handgun and an assault rifle firing blanks.
Students ran from the gunman and hid under tables and behind locked doors, while others used furniture to block entrances. In one scenario, students tackled and pinned down the attacker after he entered the classroom.
The drills follow a directive signed on August 10 by Education Minister Prasert Jantararuangtong requiring schools to draw up security plans and rehearse emergency response procedures.
“Every school is responding because this is a new-age threat that can happen anywhere,” said Visitsak Vipattanamongkol, superintendent of the Explosive Ordnance Disposal unit at the Patrol and Special Operations Division of the police.

Arsenal agree £50m-plus deal to sign Villa's Konsa
- Published
Arsenal have agreed a deal worth more than £50m to sign Aston Villa defender Ezri Konsa.
The England international is set to have a medical before completing his move to Emirates Stadium.
BBC Sport revealed last week that Arsenal had reopened talks with Villa over a deal for Konsa but still fell short of reaching an agreement.
The Gunners then appeared to pivot to Bayer Leverkusen's Jarell Quansah.
However, Arsenal refocused their efforts on Konsa and have now struck a deal for the player with Villa.
The 28-year-old, who joined the Villans in July 2019, has made 286 appearances over the past seven seasons.
Konsa featured 48 times last term in all competitions, scoring two goals and contributing one assist, as Unai Emery's side lifted the Europa League and finished fourth in the Premier League to secure Champions League football for 2026-27.
Konsa has not featured at all during Aston Villa's pre‑season, including the 2‑1 defeat to Paris St‑Germain in the Uefa Super Cup, after Emery gave him four weeks off following the World Cup.
He played in every game of England's World Cup run as the Three Lions finished third.
Speaking after the final warm‑up match against Borussia Monchengladbach, Emery explained the absence of Konsa, Emiliano Martinez and Ollie Watkins, saying: "They are joining us after this match."
Analysis: Changes were expected but Villa's squad could be transformed
Usually, winning the Europa League and qualifying for the Champions League would leave a club in a position of strength.
However, Villa have been picked apart this summer to become a victim of the system they have been vocal against.
Ensuring they comply with Uefa and the Premier League's financial rules led them to sell Morgan Rogers to Chelsea for a record £117m.
Even then, Youri Tielemans - who like Rogers scored in May's Europa League win over Freiburg - was also sold to Manchester United.
Villa wanted to alter their left-back profile so Lucas Digne was allowed to join Paris St-Germain, with Atletico Madrid's Matteo Ruggeri replacing him.
Now, though, there is still huge uncertainty over Villa's squad just four days before they start the season at Brighton.
Villa face the prospect of losing the core of their squad by the end of the month with goalkeeper Martinez also set to leave.
Changes were expected, with an anticipation the squad would start to break up this summer - but Villa could undergo a transformation which would normally happen over two or three windows.
Skipper John McGinn was defiant last week when asked about changes, saying they still have the same structures and values which made them a success, and Villa still played well despite losing to PSG in the Super Cup.
But doubts over the squad remain.
Boss Emery squeezed everything he could out of them over the past two years and now Villa face a crucial two weeks before the end of the transfer window.

Satish Ghadge alias Satish Maratha, a 34-year-old history-sheeter, was murdered in Surat’s Bhestan area on 5 August 2026. He was attacked by a group of assailants while travelling in a car. Police suspect the killing was linked to an old gang rivalry. Four adults and four juveniles have been detained or arrested in connection with the case, and police are investigating the alleged conspiracy behind the murder (here, here, and here).
In this context, a post featuring a screenshot from a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that Satish Maratha was murdered by Muslim youths in Surat. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: Satish Maratha was murdered by Muslim youths in Surat.
Fact: None of the accused in the case are Muslims. S.B. Desai, in-charge of Surat’s Bhestan Police Station, told Factly that all the accused are Hindus and that the murder of Satish Ghadge alias Satish Maratha was the result of a personal rivalry. Police arrested nine accused, including four minors, in connection with the case. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A Google Lens search for the viral screenshot led us to multiple media reports (here, here, and here) published in August 2026 that featured the same visuals. According to these reports, 39-year-old Satish Maratha was brutally murdered on the afternoon of 5 August 2026 in the Bhestan area of Surat. Satish was travelling in his Swift car with a young woman when bike-borne assailants broke the car window. When he stepped out, the attackers surrounded him and assaulted him with swords and knives, reportedly inflicting more than 39 injuries. Police arrested nine accused in connection with the case, including four minors.
The reports also stated that Satish had a long-standing dispute with Rahul Mandal over a liquor stand and dominance in the area. Around a month and a half before the murder, Satish was reportedly attacked with chilli powder under the Godhra Bridge but survived. However, none of the reports mentions any involvement of Muslims in the incident.
To verify whether there was any communal angle to the incident, we contacted S.B. Desai, the in-charge of Surat’s Bhestan Police Station. He told Factly that all the accused in the Satish Maratha murder case are Hindus. He also stated that the murder was the result of a personal rivalry and confirmed that the three minors involved in the incident are also Hindus.
To sum up, none of the accused in the Satish Maratha murder case in Surat are Muslims.

On 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release, Kazakhstan became the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.
Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.
“Today, we became witnesses of a truly historic event,” declared Yerlan Nysanbayev, Kazakhstan’s environment minister, after the release. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken.”
The caspian tiger was considered extinct in the 1970s after decades of fur hunting, habitat destruction and eradication campaigns. Its range once spanned from eastern Turkey to north-west China, including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and swathes of central Asia, mostly in forest highlands and along the edges of lakes and rivers, particularly in Tugai forests that were widely destroyed for agriculture.
It was officially declared extinct in 2003, but a scientific breakthrough just six years later laid the foundation for the recent release. DNA analysis of the tiger’s genetic history revealed that the caspian tiger and the amur tiger found in eastern Siberia were almost identical, with populations probably intermingling until the early 1900s before they were isolated by hunting. What became known as the caspian tiger spread west from Siberia and were separated from the amur tiger by a single letter of genetic code.
“For all intents and purposes, this is the return of the caspian tiger, only this time they flew instead of walking,” said Dale Miquelle, an authority on Siberian tigers who formerly headed the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Russia programme. “The idea of bringing back a subspecies of tigers that has disappeared is very exciting. This is as close as we’re going to get to that process.”
Today, it would be practically impossible for the caspian tiger to re-establish its former range. A 2017 feasibility study identified two places in the region with enough suitable habitat to re-establish populations, both in Kazakhstan. The most promising was thought to be Ile-Balkhash, where Umit was released, which the Kazakh government made a nature reserve in 2018.
While this summer’s release is the first example of a cross-border tiger translocation, there have been several successful releases in the Russian far east as part of efforts to restore the amur tiger’s former range. One scheme involved rescuing orphaned cubs whose mothers had been shot by hunters in Siberia, and then releasing them into former ranges when they were strong enough. The project, which Miquelle worked on, was a huge success – especially because there was no human contact with the young big cats.
“The success rate was pretty close to 100% after the release. These animals adapt amazingly quickly. One young female killed a Himalayan black bear within 24 hours of being released and others have learned to hunt on their own in the wild really quickly,” he says.
But it is not all good news. Wild tigers have suffered a catastrophic century, with numbers falling from about 100,000 at the beginning of the 20th century to about 5,500 today. In many parts of Asia, they are still declining – and facing new threats from climate breakdown and disease. In recent years in Russia, African swine fever wiped out enormous numbers of wild boar, a tiger’s favourite prey, causing many to target human settlements. Ensuring there is enough food for the returning caspian tigers is key to their survival, says Miquelle.
“I am very hopeful this can work. In Russia, a number of translocations resulted in the recolonisation of tiger habitat. So there’s a blueprint that suggests that this can work as long as there is suitable habitat and sufficient prey,” he says.

35 Bihar students hospitalised after detergent allegedly mistaken for salt in mid-day meal
Bihar rural development minister Shravan Kumar visited the hospital and met the affected students, promising a detailed inquiry.
At least 35 students fell ill after consuming a mid-day meal at a government school in Bihar's Nalanda district, following which they were hospitalised, officials said on Wednesday.
The incident took place at Middle School in Parasi in the Noorsarai police station area, and the affected students were hospitalised at the Bihar Sharif Sadar Hospital, Dr Jayaprakash Singh, civil surgeon, Nalanda, told ANI news agency. Meanwhile, some others were receiving treatment at Chandi and Andarsarai, Dr Singh said.
The civil surgeon visited the hospital and took stock of the situation, according to PTI news agency. He said that all students receiving treatment at Sadar Hospital, Chandi and Andarsari were out of danger.
Deep Dive
Bihar rural development minister Shravan Kumar visited the hospital and met the affected students. He also spoke to the doctors regarding the students' condition. The minister said a detailed inquiry would be conducted to identify the lapse in the preparation.
Detergent allegedly mistaken for salt
Dr Singh said the students had complained of stomach pain after consuming their meal, adding that detergent was allegedly added to their food instead of salt. Some students also felt dizzy and began vomiting.
“All the children were suffering from stomach pain and vomiting. Consequently, they were transferred here, and a medical team immediately began their treatment. It is reported that detergent was added instead of salt to the food...” he told ANI. The principal of the school, Shailendra Kumar Singh, said the mid-day meal, comprising soybean rice, had been served to the students by an NGO as per the prescribed menu.
Dr Singh added that samples of the meal served had been collected, but there is no confirmation on the cause yet. He said the matter will be examined by the food inspector.
Some students had already eaten the food when others said the food lacked salt, according to the PTI report. The containers of both salt and detergent powder had reportedly been kept at the same place in the kitchen, owing to which the cook allegedly mistook the detergent for salt and added it to the food, PTI cited locals as saying.

Iran threatens to attack US targets in Europe if Trump escalates war, says report
Data shows that traffic through the shipping route remains at a standstill despite Trump saying it is open for business
Iran is considering launching attacks on US military targets in Europe if President Donald Trump escalates the conflict, according to a report.
Sources close to Iran’s government told the Financial Times that potential targets included a British air base in Cyprus that was targeted by a drone in March.
Other countries in southeastern Europe such as Bulgaria, which approved US access to its Bezmer air base for refuelling last month, were also weighed up as a potential target for strikes.
It follows warnings that Tehran is considering switching to a “fully offensive” strategy, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Monday.
A deal between the US and Iran appears further away than ever as Trump declared the Strait of Hormuz as American territory on Tuesday.
Sharing a bizarre map of the region with a large blue circle around the waterway, he declared the vital shipping route “NEW US territory” on Truth Social.
Shortly after sharing the image, the US leader announced that there are “no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled with the Islamic Republic of Iran”.
“The Naval Blockade remains in full force and effect,” he continued on the platform. “The Hormuz Strait is open and operating. All water mines have been removed or detonated.”
However, data shared by Kpler with The Independent shows that only ten vessels passed through on Monday, compared to 130 to 140 before the outbreak of war. Six commodity vessels crossed the strait on Tuesday, according to Kpler data seen by Reuters.
Iran had earlier said the shipping route is to remain closed until the US meet the conditions agreed in an interim deal, according to Iran’s top negotiator Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf in comments shared by state media.
Conditions include lifting a marine blockade and sanctions as well as releasing Iran’s frozen assets.
Saudi Arabia’s Aramco resumed oil loading from inside the Strait last week with more waiting to load, according to shipping data and trade sources who spoke to Reuters.
Tehran says it has reached an agreement with Oman over a plan for ships to transit the Strait and that they are now working to finalise details for a joint statement.
Muscat has been working on a resolution to reopen shipping through the waterway, which passes through both countries.
On Monday, the US leader threatened to launch an attack on Oman as a 60-day period to negotiate a ceasefire deal expired.
“If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the s**t out of them,” Trump said in an interview with Fox News, after reports Oman and Iran are working out their own solution to control the strategic waterway.
He was later asked if he was out of patience with Oman and told reporters: "No, I don't think they behaved very well, but we'd handle them very easily, just like we do other things."
A deal appeared to be in sight after Iran and the US agreed to a 14-point memorandum of understanding brokered by Pakistan over two months ago.
But the agreement collapsed last month over different understandings surrounding a clause on the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran attacked three commercial vessels passing through the Omani corridor of the waterway. The US almost immediately revoked sanctions relief on Iranian oil sales and US Central Command launched a wave of strikes on more than 80 military targets in response.
Both sides accused the other of violating the ceasefire agreement.
The fifth clause of the MOU states that the Islamic Republic of Iran will “make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels, with no charge for 60 days only, from the Persian Gulf to the Sea of Oman, and vice versa.”
It adds: “The traffic of commercial vessels will immediately start, and considering the need for removing the technical and military obstacles, and de-mining by the Islamic Republic of Iran, will be instated within 30 days.”
The confusion arises over the next section, stating that both sides “will conduct dialogue with the Sultanate of Oman, to define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz, in discussions with other Persian Gulf Littoral States, in line with applicable international law and the sovereign rights of coastal states of the Strait of Hormuz.”
Iran says that this means that the governance of the strait remains under Iranian control and that passage without approval constitutes a violation but the US says that attacks on vessels are a violation of Tehran’s promise to allow commercial vessels unfettered access.
