French civil servant drugged us to make us urinate on ourselves, say accusers
- Published
"I was really weak. I couldn't really feel my legs any more," says Anaïs de Vos. "I was scared. I didn't know what was happening."
It was July 2011 and Anaïs, who was then 27, was being interviewed for a job at France's Ministry of Culture in Paris.
She didn't usually drink coffee but when the interviewer, a senior civil servant called Christian Nègre, offered her one, she agreed out of politeness.
He made it himself, she tells BBC Global Women, but "it tasted bad… so I drank about half".
The meeting had started in the office, but after a few minutes Nègre suggested they go outside.
As they strolled through Paris's streets, Anaïs began to feel an inexplicable and uncontrollable need to urinate.
She says she told him she needed to find a toilet urgently.
"He looked me right in the eye and said, 'Oh, do you need a wee?'
"I felt like a child. I thought it was really weird the way he looked at me, almost gleeful."
She says he directed her to the door of a storage cupboard under a bridge on the River Seine and said: "You can do it here."
Now, Anaïs is one of nearly 250 women who believe Nègre drugged them in alleged incidents between 2009 and 2018, subjecting them to what is known as chemical submission, where drugs are used to gain control over someone.
The concept of chemical submission came to prominence in France in 2024 when Gisele Pelicot's husband was found guilty of sedating her and inviting strangers to rape her while she was unconscious.
"I started to panic," Anaïs continues. "I had visions of him pushing me into the room and closing the door behind me."
Feeling it was "too strange", she insisted they move on.
They walked to the Louvre to use the toilets there, but they cost one euro and she had left her purse at the ministry's offices. Nègre told her he didn't have any cash either.
Desperate and in pain from trying not to urinate, Anaïs found a cafe that let her use their toilet.
By then, "I felt really weak physically", she says. As she approached the bathroom, she lost control and wet herself.
Accused: France's mass drugging case
Women who accuse a civil servant of drugging them at job interviews share their stories
Thinking back to 2011, Anaïs gets some comfort from the fact that when she did urinate, it was out of Nègre's sight. "At least he didn't see me," she says.
"I was so grateful I was only wearing a dress," she adds, explaining it made it easier to disguise what had happened.
After three hours with Nègre, she says she "felt dizzy and drained".
She didn't get the job and had suspicions about him, but could never work out exactly what it was that had made her feel so uncomfortable.
Anaïs felt the incident damaged her self-confidence and in the years that followed, she ended up on a less ambitious career path.
Then in 2019, she received a letter from the police. When she met them, she learned they suspected she was one of almost 200 women Nègre was accused of drugging during job interviews, purportedly for roles at the ministry.
"I was shocked," she says. "But I was happy to know I wasn't crazy. Something had happened that day."
Dozens more alleged victims have since emerged.
Police believed Nègre had used diuretics, which are used to manage a number of medical conditions, including high blood pressure, and cause the body to produce excess urine.
Anaïs had had a fleeting thought the day she had met Nègre, that maybe he had slipped something into her drink, but put it aside telling herself: "It's the Ministry of Culture. It's not possible."
'Experiments P'
Anaïs says police told her they found a spreadsheet of the alleged victims on Nègre's computer, entitled Experiments P, which was how they found her.
The document, she says, noted the time the women arrived for their interviews, when the diuretic was administered, how long it took before they urinated, and what underwear they were wearing.
Looking back, Anaïs is now convinced the strange taste in the coffee Nègre made her was the diuretic.
The investigation into Nègre began in June 2018, when he was caught by a colleague taking a photograph of a woman from beneath a table, the prosecutor's office said in a statement released in February this year.
He was initially suspended from his job as regional director of cultural affairs before being sacked by the Ministry of Culture in 2019.
Prosecutors said that in 2018 he told investigators he had "imposed humiliating situations on women" during job interviews.
Many of the women say the first time they realised they may have been victims was when police contacted them.
Some came forward when they saw Anaïs and other accusers in media reports.
Nègre, who is in his 60s, is now under formal investigation on charges that include drugging, invasion of privacy and sexual assault. He is awaiting trial.
The BBC put the allegations contained in this article to Nègre through his lawyer, but he declined to comment.
Another person named in Nègre's notes was Marie-Hélène Brice. He interviewed her for a job at the Ministry of Culture in 2016 in Strasbourg, where he was then working.
She says he told her she looked stressed and suggested they take a walk outside to "calm her nerves".
But as they strolled along the canal, Marie-Hélène, like Anaïs, felt an uncontrollable need to urinate, which began to cause her pain.
She says Nègre told her that he knew of a public toilet nearby, but when they arrived at the location there was no toilet.
"I was really starting to suffer… pains to the point that I was white, pale, I had tears streaming down," she says.
Marie-Hélène says she had no choice but to urinate in public. She says Nègre offered to shield her with his jacket.
"I was terribly embarrassed," she says. "He didn't take his eyes off me."
Marie-Hélène says that for years she felt ashamed.
Like Anaïs, she was also contacted by police who told her she was among Nègre's alleged victims. "It was a very big shock," she adds.
Chemical submission
Marie-Hélène says that as well as psychological distress, she has also been left with urinary problems.
She explains that while the events might not fit the pattern of what people usually think of in cases of sexual assault, she has no doubts about what happened to her: "I have been attacked, I have been intoxicated, I have been poisoned, but for me it is a sexual assault, clearly."
The issue of chemical submission has been picked up by French MP Sandrine Josso. She became a leading campaigner after French senator Joel Guerriau was found guilty this year of spiking her drink with ecstasy in order to sexually assault her.
Josso argues that for too long France has not done enough to support women who have been drugged and prosecute offenders.
She was behind the introduction this year of a pilot programme where women who suspect they have been drugged can take samples of blood, urine or hair to a lab for testing, without having to file a formal complaint with police.
"People are mobilising, victims are reporting more, filing more complaints, and that's important," Josso tells BBC Global Women.
But there are limitations. Anaïs, Marie-Hélène and many other alleged victims of Nègre did not suspect they had been drugged - and unless testing takes place very soon after drugging, substances won't show up in blood and urine samples.
Drugs may be detectable for longer in hair, but as time passes it becomes harder to pinpoint when they were administered.
The use of diuretics in this way is "very unusual" according to Prof Jean-Claude Alvarez, who runs the pilot at the Raymond-Poincaré AP-HP Hospital. He says he has never seen anything like it in 26 years as a toxicologist.
The lab routinely tests for 400 substances and "now, in France, we are looking for diuretics", he adds.
It is now 15 years since Anaïs's encounter with Nègre and seven years since she first spoke to police.
Like many of the other accusers, she is frustrated at the length of time it is taking for Nègre's case to come to court.
Meanwhile, the alleged perpetrator has continued to work in human resources, according to Fondation des Femmes, a women's rights group that is supporting about 30 of the women affected.
"Everything is unsettling and I am angry at how we are treated," says Anaïs, who is now 42 years old.
She says she first spoke to police in 2019, but then heard nothing about the case until 2023, despite emailing them many times.
"For four years, I was alone with the knowledge that I was a victim. I didn't know what to do," she says. "I am very angry with the justice system."
Marie-Hélène describes this waiting as "secondary victimisation".
"As a victim, I have to prove the impact, go to a psychiatrist, write specific notes," she says.
The delays to the case have made what happened harder to bear.
"We do not necessarily feel [we are] completely taken seriously," Marie-Hélène says.
Kalliopi Mingeirou from UN Women told the BBC that governments, police and justice systems needed to do more to tackle drug-facilitated sexual assault, and that authorities were facing "very serious challenges" and delays in cases of alleged abuse are "destroying women's lives".
The BBC asked the French police, judiciary and government to respond to the criticisms of their handling of the case, but they did not respond.
For a long time, Marie-Hélène was silent until she stopped feeling shame.
"I don't have to hide myself - I am a victim," she says.
"It is important for me to speak publicly because it allowed some victims to recognise themselves, to discover they were a victim and to file a complaint in turn.
"Speaking out is necessary in the world in which we live, it is important to talk about sexist and sexual violence."
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

I love the idea of robots taking over menial tasks, so I was excited to try the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni. This premium window-cleaning robot is highly rated online. I have a robot vacuum and a robot mower, and I would never go back to doing these chores myself. Sadly, I had such a traumatically awful experience with the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni that I’m left wondering why anyone would want a window-cleaning robot at all.
Before I embark on this tale of woe, I should point out that most of my issues are with the whole category, not the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni specifically. There are circumstances where I can imagine it working well. I briefly tested another window-cleaning robot, the much cheaper Mova N1 ($199), for comparison, and can attest that the Ecovacs has a much smarter design and cleans more efficiently. It might even be the best window-cleaning robot you can get; I just don’t think a robot for cleaning windows is worthwhile for most homes.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
The Good
The Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni has a smart design and comes in a charging case that includes its own battery. The case has slots and compartments for cables, spare pads, cleaning solution, and the bot itself, attached with a retractable, braided, 18-foot cable. It looks like a little cooler with a folding handle and weighs around 15 pounds. A full charge gives you 110 minutes of cleaning.
The Winbot is 10 by 10 by 2.5 inches and weighs around 4 pounds. You attach a cleaning pad to the Velcro sections and fill it with the cleaning solution. It has a leatherlike strap for picking it out of the case and sticking it to the window. Press the button on the front to start it up. It takes a few seconds to ramp up the suction, then tells you when it’s firmly in place, so you can let go. This is a nerve-racking moment the first few times, but the suction is plenty powerful.
You can press a button on the case to cycle through the four modes. There are Deep and Thorough modes, recommended for exterior windows, Fast mode for interior windows, and an Edge Cleaning mode. I was surprised by how quick and easy it was to set up, and I started with the biggest window in our house, a recently installed, ground-level, modern window at the back, roughly 7 by 10 feet.
The Winbot navigated to the top using its tank-style tracks and then cleaned in horizontal lines. It has wee bumpers that detect the edges, and it deploys an occasional spurt of cleaning fluid onto the glass ahead of it. The cleaning pads are microfiber pads. The Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni did a decent job on this first window. If you have a lot of large windows like this, it might be worth looking at. My only complaints were that it left a dirty residue in the corners and smearing in places.
I had it clean my back door next, which is a large pane of glass, but it struggled with the handle. I was surprised to find that, after cleaning the inside and outside of the first window and door, it asked me to change the pad and refill the cleaning solution. It comes with one spare pad, and you can flip them over, though you will quickly end up with muck in the Velcro if you do.
My Victorian house has tall bay windows, and I was excited to try the Winbot there next. I struggle to reach the top of these windows. I have tried a ladder and an extending cleaning pole, but neither is ideal. I figured the Winbot might just be the solution. I was wrong.
The Bad
I have a traditional sash-and-case bay window, recently replaced at great expense. I tried the Ecovacs Winbot W2S Omni on the largest, top-central pane first. It mostly cleaned the inside but got stuck on the metal loop fittings for opening the window and had to give up. I tried it on the outside. It was slow, but it eventually cleaned most of the window, except for a clag of muck in the corners and dirty stripes down the edges. Unfortunately, when it got to the bottom, it did a weird stuttering maneuver, managing to damage the astragal by ripping off paintwork.
OK, so window-cleaning robots cannot deal with traditional windows. I know textured glass interferes with the suction and, predictably, handles and fixtures interfere with the movement, but it also struggles with astragals that aren’t thick or solid enough. I wouldn’t risk using it with any that aren’t finished in hard plastic or something else durable.
I figured I’d give it one last chance on the upstairs bay window, as it’s a PVC replacement that was put in before we moved in, so it has thicker astragals finished in hard plastic. Using it one story up gave me serious anxiety. After an alarming five minutes or so of watching it loudly and squeakily navigate the window, it began to sound an alarm and flash a red light, with a stern voice informing me it was stuck and I should check the app for solutions. Where was it stuck? You guessed it, right at the top of the window where I had no hope of reaching it.
I’m not ashamed to say I panicked. I worried that if it suddenly fell, it would potentially smash into the window downstairs. The charging case does act as a counterweight; other window-cleaning bots have tethers to attach to furniture. There’s also a button to retract the cord and cut the slack, but there’s still potential for damage if it falls. I tried to lean out of my window, while it loudly alerted, to see if I could reach the release button. No joy.
By this time, a couple of passersby had stopped to watch. I tried to pull it in using the cable, but it wouldn't budge. Eventually, I figured out I could lower the top pane just enough to reach it. But pressing and holding the button to power down the suction, while hanging out my window and holding the strap, felt downright dangerous. My heart was pounding in my ears by the time it finally released. I got it inside and back into its case, where it will remain until I return it.
The Ugly
Reflecting on this sorry saga, I can't help feeling, even without my mishaps, which may be partly down to user stupidity and bad luck, that window-cleaning robots are just a massive waste of time.
They're way too much work to use. Time-wise, I could clean the windows far faster and do a better job with less stress. By the time you’ve set up a window-cleaning robot and stuck it on the window, you could have cleaned it yourself. You have to babysit the damn thing and then detach it and move it to the next window. Even if you get to a point of trusting it, you’ll have to return every five to 10 minutes. It can’t deal with window handles, fittings, or certain astragals, and windows must be at least 12 by 16 inches, but realistically larger, for it to be worth using. It always leaves dirt in the corners and cannot remove stubborn stains like bird droppings.
Using it on upstairs windows is harrowing. Leaning outside to retrieve it feels dangerous. It also goes through cleaning solution and dirties up the pads very quickly. I’d probably need eight pads if I wanted to clean all my windows in one go, and the 230-milliliter bottle of solution provided would maybe last me three full washes. Of course, both the extra pads and the solution are overpriced ($30 for 1 liter of cleaner and $20 for two pads), and the manual warns you not to use anything else.
It’s also loud. I measured 68 decibels when cleaning. When I used it on my front windows, several people heard it and stopped to stare. The universal reaction from family, friends, and strangers was bemusement. No one seemed to think a window-washing robot was a good idea.
Now, if you live high up in an apartment with large, modern windows and there’s no window-cleaning service, it could be great, though attaching and detaching it will be scary. I also wondered if it might be handy for folks with mobility issues, but it’s actually quite a lot of work to use. There are scenarios where I can see potential value, but for the average home, I don’t think it’s worth it. As for me, I’m done with window-cleaning robots forever.

How does someone feel lonely while being deeply loved? How does someone feel unsupported while living in a joint family? Despite partners, families and friends, many adults feel nobody truly knows them. As loneliness draws growing global concern, this paradox deserves attention. While technology, urbanisation and changing social structures all play a role, growing evidence suggests that its roots may begin much earlier — in childhood.
The World Health Organization estimates that one in six people worldwide experience loneliness, with significant consequences for health and well-being. The report highlighted that loneliness is linked to around 100 deaths every hour globally.
One of the largest studies ever conducted on loneliness, led by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues, and published in Perspectives on Psychological Science in 2015, analysed data from more than 3.4 million participants and found that loneliness was associated with a 26% higher risk of premature mortality. Loneliness has also been linked to heart disease, depression, weakened immunity, disturbed sleep and cognitive decline. These findings tell us why loneliness matters. But they do not explain why two people living in similar circumstances experience relationships so differently.
The India story
In India, we often assume that close-knit families protect against loneliness. However, many adults still feel emotionally isolated despite living with family and appearing socially connected. Young adults are moving away for education and work, traditional neighbourhood networks are weakening, and older adults are increasingly living alone. These changes undoubtedly contribute to loneliness. But they do not explain why many people feel emotionally alone even while surrounded by loved ones. Emotional loneliness often starts within families when people never feel safe enough to reveal who they truly are.
While researching Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) and their long-term consequences, one observation repeatedly stood out. Many adults described a quiet, persistent loneliness that had little to do with the number of people in their lives. Childhood adversity is often imagined as dramatic — abuse, violence. Yet much of it leaves no visible mark.
A child who grows up feeling emotionally unseen, criticised rather than comforted, or accepted only when meeting expectations, gradually learns to become invisible, adapting to cope. Some adapt by creating an external persona that appears outgoing and entertaining. These adaptations may help children survive difficult environments, but they can later become barriers to intimacy, trust and genuine connection.
Among ACEs, interpersonal experiences such as emotional neglect and peer isolation may be where adult loneliness begins. Long before adulthood, they shape a child’s expectations of relationships. Children learn to protect themselves by hiding vulnerability. Adults may continue using the same strategy long after the threat has passed.
Our recently published study among Indian adults found that ACEs were strongly linked to lasting difficulties in managing emotions, self-worth and relationships — the kind of struggles often seen in people carrying deep, unresolved trauma. Childhood experiences accounted for nearly half of the variation in these difficulties. This suggests that loneliness is not always a matter of limited social contact; it may also reflect deeper disruptions in the capacity to trust, feel safe and experience belonging. Our findings suggest loneliness extends beyond health, affecting well-being, relationships and quality of life.
This distinction is important to understand since it shapes how we respond. Public health initiatives often encourage people to socialise more, join community groups or spend less time online. These are worthwhile. However, for someone whose nervous system has learnt that closeness feels unpredictable or unsafe, simply increasing social contact may not reduce loneliness.
What emotional safety looks like
By contrast, children who grow up feeling emotionally safe, accepted and supported are more likely to develop a lasting sense of trust and belonging that protects against loneliness later in life. Recovery often begins with relationships in which people no longer feel they must hide who they are.
This is not about blaming parents. Most caregivers do their best with the emotional resources they received. Understanding these patterns is not about assigning guilt. It is about recognising how emotional experiences pass from one generation to the next, and how they can be transformed.
Loneliness affects health, productivity, relationships and healthy ageing. In a country with a large working population under 35, investing in children’s emotional well-being is not only a mental health priority, but also a long-term social and economic investment. As India strengthens its commitment to mental health, recognising the role of early emotional experiences offers an opportunity to invest in prevention, not only treatment. Instead of asking only “Why am I lonely?”, we might also ask, “When did I first learn that I had to face my feelings alone?” For many people, that offers a more compassionate understanding of why connection can feel so difficult.
When a child grows up around adults who stay calm amidst chaos, and who accept and help them navigate difficult emotions, the child feels accepted and confident. For this, adults need to work on their own trauma.
If India is serious about addressing its growing loneliness crisis, the conversation must extend beyond technology and changing lifestyles. To tackle loneliness, we must begin where connection begins: childhood.
The writers are co-authors of What Happened to Me? vs What’s Wrong with Me?: Indian Perspectives on Childhood Trauma and Recovery (Penguin Random House India).

More than one in three older adults surveyed in a Hyderabad-based study showed signs of mild cognitive impairment, with researchers finding a strong association between cognitive decline and deficiencies in several key vitamins.
Micronutrients deficiencies in older adults with mild cognitive impairment
The findings by scientists at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) suggest that better nutritional status may play an important role in preserving brain health as people age. Older adults with mild cognitive impairment were more likely to have deficiencies in several micronutrients, particularly vitamins D, B2 and B9, highlighting the potential role of nutrition in maintaining brain health during ageing.
Published in the international journal ‘Nutrients’, the study - Neuronal Biomarkers and Micronutrient Status in Adults with Mild Cognitive Impairment, also identified significant associations between blood levels of essential vitamins, neuronal biomarkers and cognitive performance. The findings underscore the importance of early nutritional assessment and intervention among older adults at risk of cognitive decline.
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is considered an intermediate stage between normal ageing and dementia, in which individuals experience measurable changes in memory and thinking abilities but can still perform their daily activities independently.
What was assessed?
The community-based cross-sectional study involved 184 adults aged 55 to 85 years from the city. Cognitive function was assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), while blood samples were analysed for vitamins A, D, B1, B2, B6, B9 and B12. Researchers also measured neuronal biomarkers, including beta-amyloid, total tau, neurofilament light chain and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
Anthropometric measurements, blood pressure, blood glucose levels and other biochemical parameters were also evaluated to identify factors associated with early cognitive impairment. It was found that 36.4% of participants had mild cognitive impairment. The affected individuals had lower blood levels of several micronutrients, including vitamins D, B1, B2, B6, B9 and B12. Deficiencies in vitamins D, B2 and B9 were particularly more prevalent among the MCI group.
Better cognitive performance
Participants with MCI also had significantly higher blood glucose levels and elevated systolic blood pressure. In contrast, higher levels of vitamins, especially vitamins D and B6, were associated with better cognitive performance.
“While further studies and trials are needed to establish causality and assess the impact of nutrient supplementation, these findings underscore the value of early nutritional assessment and timely interventions as part of healthy ageing strategies,” said Scientist & Head of the biochemistry division at ICMR-NIN, G. Bhanuprakash Reddy, who led the research.
“Healthy ageing requires attention not only to disease management but also to nutritional well-being. Our findings highlight the importance of maintaining adequate micronutrient status and strengthening early nutritional assessment among older adults to support cognitive health and promote healthy ageing,” said ICMR-NIN Director Bharati Kulkarni, in a press release.

Item surprises big two for Juddmonte International glory
We were treated to another epic renewal of the Juddmonte International on Wednesday but it was far from the match-race that it was built up to be, with Item delivered late to deny Almaqam in a thrilling finish to the York feature.
Wednesday 19 August 2026 16:30, UK
Item delivered for Andrew Balding and the sponsors to land a 10-1 surprise in the Juddmonte International at York – with the big two of Constitution River and Ombudsman only third and fourth respectively.
Hawk Mountain rather unexpectedly set the early pace, with stablemate Constitution River tucked in keenly behind him and odds-on favourite Ombudsman at the rear under William Buick, kept company by another Aidan O'Brien runner, Action.
Hawk Mountain was still in front as they moved to the top of the long Knavesmire straight, with Buick beginning to make headway on the inside rail, as Ryan Moore and Constitution River kicked for home over two furlongs out.

The story so far: Junior doctors across Andhra Pradesh, under the banner of the Andhra Pradesh Junior Doctors’ Association (APJUDA), began a phased strike on August 11, 2026, demanding a stipend revision that has been due since January 1, 2026. What began as a time-bound withdrawal of non-emergency services has since escalated, through repeated rounds of failed talks with the State government, into a withdrawal of emergency services as well from August 17, affecting Intensive Care Units, casualty wards, and labour rooms in government medical colleges and teaching hospitals across the State.
How did the protest begin?
The dispute traces back to Government Order No. 287, issued by the Health, Medical and Family Welfare Department on December 17, 2009, which provides for a biennial revision of junior doctors’ stipends by about 15%, linked to inflation. Revisions followed in 2019 and 2024. The one due from January 1, 2026, did not come through even after seven months, prompting APJUDA to send its first formal communication to the department in July and threaten a strike from August 4. The government sought a week’s time through the Director of Medical Education to negotiate with the Finance Department and the Health Secretary, and the strike was put on hold.
How did talks break down?
With no written assurance forthcoming, APJUDA issued a fresh notice for August 11. A day’s postponement was sought again, this time to hold a two-day meeting at the APIIC Building in Mangalagiri, with representatives from every government medical college asked to attend. At the meeting, the government offered an annual hike of 3% for postgraduate junior doctors and 5% for house surgeons and interns, against APJUDA’s demand for 30%, a figure corroborated independently by both a senior health official and the Indian Medical Association, Andhra Pradesh State (IMA AP State). The official told The Hindu that the department had, since receiving APJUDA’s first communication in July, been studying stipend revision models followed in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. While acknowledging the demand was “justified,” the official described the 30% figure as “abnormal,” and said the government was “exploring all options.”
Doctors have cited two broad justifications for 30%. Andhra Pradesh’s inflation rate of around 5% a year works out to roughly 10% over the two years since the last revision, they say, and the 2026 revision is meant to be a catch-up for that period rather than a purely forward-looking hike. They have also pointed to a sharp rise in workload, including a three-hour increase in outpatient department timings over the past year and the added burden of digitising health records.
What are the other two demands?
APJUDA has also sought strict adherence to National Medical Commission norms in recruiting MSc and PhD holders to clinical faculty posts, saying recent recruitment has exceeded the NMC’s prescribed cap of under 15% for such appointments, and it opposes a proposed increase in the retirement age of doctors from 62 to 65 years, which it says would shrink recruitment opportunities for younger doctors entering government service.
How widespread is the strike?
All 19 government medical colleges in the State are participating, APJUDA said, including six established in the past two years and older institutions such as Andhra Medical College in Visakhapatnam, Guntur Medical College, Siddhartha Medical College in Vijayawada, Kurnool Medical College, and the medical college in Kadapa. The association estimates around 9,000 junior doctors are involved statewide.
How has the strike progressed?
Phase I (August 11): Withdrawal of non-emergency services from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., with emergency and ICU services maintained.
Phase II (August 12 onwards): Complete withdrawal of non-emergency services, extended to 9 a.m.-4 p.m., alongside a voluntary relay hunger strike. Emergency and ICU services continued to be maintained through this phase.
Revised deadline: APJUDA’s original deadline of August 15, 5 p.m., for a written government response was extended to August 16, 5 p.m., as negotiations continued.
Phase III (from August 17, 8 a.m.): With no satisfactory written response received by the revised deadline, APJUDA began withdrawing emergency services as well, including in Intensive Care Units, casualty and labour rooms, while non-emergency services remain suspended.
Has the medical fraternity weighed in beyond APJUDA?
Yes. IMA A.P. State and the IMA Junior Doctors Network, Andhra Pradesh State, urged the government on August 16 to resolve the 15% stipend revision due under G.O. No. 287 since January 1, 2026, which they said was by then more than seven months overdue. IMA leaders were careful to distinguish this from APJUDA’s separate 30% demand, which they asked the government to “sympathetically consider” as well, citing inflation, workload, and stipend disparities with other States. Dr. S. Balaraju, President, IMA AP State, and Dr. Subhas Chandra Bose Moturi, Hon. General Secretary, IMA A.P. State, jointly appealed to the Health Minister to intervene directly and hold immediate talks with APJUDA, warning that prolonged agitation would serve the interests of neither doctors, the government, nor the public.
What has APJUDA said about patient care?
The association maintained emergency and ICU services through Phases I and II, even as postgraduates, many already working 36 to 48 hours a week and, in some cases, up to 90 hours, joined the protest. Dr. Balagam Dinakar Sai Srinivas, General Secretary, APJUDA, said doctors were sacrificing “valuable time, which we joined this profession to spend caring for patients.” Phase III marks a departure from that position. IMA credited junior doctors for their “responsible approach towards patient care” through the earlier phases and appealed to the public to see the agitation as “not directed against patients.”
What happens next?
APJUDA has said it will not agree to further postponement without a written commitment specifying a firm timeline for a Government Order. “As of now, August 16 is the deadline. From August 17, we will also halt emergency services,” Dr. Dinakar said. With that phase now in effect, and both APJUDA and IMA calling for the Chief Minister, Deputy Chief Minister, and Health Minister to intervene directly, the stand-off’s resolution will depend on whether the government moves beyond verbal assurances to a written order.

A new study published in the European Journal of Ophthalmology has found that a smartphone-based AI system demonstrated high accuracy in detecting major eye diseases including diabetic retinopathy (DR), age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and glaucoma, a press release said.
The study, ‘Smartphone-based offline AI for multi-disease retinal screening: Real-world accuracy’, was conducted by doctors from the NIO Super Specialty Hospital, Pune. In this prospective, cross-sectional study, 193 adults (371 eyes) aged 18 years and above with DR, glaucoma, AMD, or normal fundus (healthy back of the eye) were enrolled between May and December 2024.
The study involved the use of a Remidio Fundus on Phone (FoP) platform integrated with Medios AI multi-disease software, an offline AI system. The Medios AI system has received regulatory approval from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation for clinical use. This platform functions entirely offline.
Dilated fundus imaging was performed using the Remidio Fundus on Phone and Zeiss Clarus 500 cameras. Ungradable images were excluded. The offline MAI algorithm generated disease-specific reports, which were compared to masked grading of the Clarus images by two fellowship-trained ophthalmologists.
The results showed significant diagnostic accuracy: for glaucoma sensitivity was 98.2%, specificity was 99.0%; for AMD, sensitivity was 88.9%, specificity was 97.5% and for DR, sensitivity was 84.6%, specificity was 99.0%.
The study concluded that the results supported scalable, point-of-care retinal screening in resource-limited settings with this system.

Was it meat or glucose that fueled the growth of the human brain? If evolutionary science told us, hitherto, that human brain expansion relied on meat to grow, a new study has an interesting addition to this theory. Published in a recent issue of Science, the study posits a dual fuel strategy - sugar and meat - as having powered brain expansion in humans.
The multi-centre study by Jennie Brand-Miller et al, does not discount the role of meat in brain expansion, but argues that natural sugars and starch found in fruits and honey delivered the required glucose to power a rapidly-expanding human brain. “What foods enabled the evolution of the large human brain? Currently, that diet is usually framed around increasing intake of animal foods: meat, protein, fat, and omega-3 fatty acids,” the authors explain, but go on to model the glucose needs of humans and their ancestors from four million years ago, until recently.
How the brain grew
Over a period of four million years, the size of the human brain is said to have increased from around 300 grams in early hominins (bipeds) to about 1,500 grams in modern humans. As brains grew, so did demand for glucose, which is required by other tissues including red blood cells, kidneys and reproductive organs. “The human brain is unusually large for our body size and requires substantial amounts of energy,” Jennie Brand-Miller, professor of human nutrition at the University of Sydney Charles Perkins Centre and School of Life and Environmental Sciences, said.
The study does not dismiss the importance of hunting or animal protein; rather, it establishes that human brain expansion relied on a balanced, dual-fuel strategy. Meat provided critical amino acids and micronutrients, while natural sugars and starches delivered the essential glucose required to power a metabolically expensive brain.
These findings discover a new glucose pathway to brain development – natural sugars may have supplied the energy needed to support brain metabolism before the advent of cooking which made starch-rich foods easier to digest. The paper is co-authored by archaeologist Karen Hardy, professor of prehistoric archaeology at the School of Humanities, University of Glasgow.
A quarter of dietary energy
Prof. Brand-Miller explained that raw starch will not release glucose, meaning that early humans likely relied on naturally-sweet foods long before cooked grains became a regular part of the diet. The modelling employed by the researchers suggests that sugars provided over 25% of dietary energy, fulfilling the obligatory glucose demand. Pounding and cooking (grains) releases glucose specifically, not merely energy. The evolution of a bigger brain is therefore a story of carbohydrate foods as much as animal foods. “While animal foods were important, the brain’s need for glucose has largely received little attention from anthropologists,” she added.
Explaining the element that the modelling brings to current evolutionary theory, Prof. Hardy, said: “The human evolutionary diet has a strong focus on meat eating and the need for protein. But we also require energy and this is best provided by glucose obtained from plants.”
The earliest hominins such as ‘Lucy’, whose brain was the same size as a chimpanzee, as well as Homo habilis and Homo erectus, were therefore likely highly reliant on carbohydrate-rich foods, particularly fruit, the modelling establishes. It was only later, as the use of fire and cooking became more widespread, that starch from underground food sources such as wild yams, water lily rhizomes and African potato contributed to glucose intake. This might also explain to some extent why humans crave sweet foods.

Chinese robotics giant Unitree soars in stock market debut
- Published
The world's biggest humanoid robot maker Unitree Robotics made its stock market debut in Shanghai on Wednesday, with its shares soaring by more than 600%.
In the highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO), the Chinese firm's shares opened at 1,100 yuan (£120.60; $163.12), well above the 150.8 yuan offer price.
The listing on the technology-focused Star Market - which is widely known as China's Nasdaq - marks a milestone for Beijing's ambitious plans for the country's robotics industry.
It comes as the US and China are battling to dominate the global market for robots and artificial intelligence (AI) models that power them.
While Unitree is not the first Chinese humanoid robot maker to list on the stock market, its debut marks the first in mainland China.
Robots like automated industrial equipment and smart vacuum cleaners are already widely used in factories, warehouses and homes.
Now, the humanoid robotics industry is attracting huge amounts of investment as major companies - including Tesla, BYD and Amazon - are developing two-legged machines capable of performing tasks usually carried out by people.
What is Unitree?
Unitree, officially known as Yushu Technology Co Ltd, was founded in 2016 and now plays a key role in Beijing's ambitions to develop advanced technology.
It has become a robotics industry leader, selling devices from sensors and automated arms to four-legged and human-like machines.
The firm shipped more than 5,500 humanoid robots last year as demand for the technology grows.
Unitree is one of the few companies in the sector to make money, delivering a net profit of 278 million yuan in 2025.
It is a fierce rival to developers in the US as it produces robots with similar features but at lower prices.
The company is based in Hangzhou, in eastern China. The region is home to a so-called golden cluster zone of robotics firms, which have benefited from huge government investments.
That support helped drive a more than threefold increase in the number of Chinese robotics firms between 2020 and 2024, according to state-run China Daily.
Robots are also seen as a potential solution to issues posed by China's ageing population, which is expected to lead to a shortage of workers in the country, according to Fei Qin, an associate professor at the University of Bath.
Beijing considers the robotics sector a "strategic priority" in its pursuit of leadership in advanced technology, she said.
"Robots are where AI leaves the screen and enters the economy" in factories, hospitals and, potentially, the home, Qin added.
US robots tend to have more user-friendly software but it is difficult to ignore the lower prices offered by Chinese manufacturers, said Harold Soh, a researcher from the National University of Singapore.
Unitree's robot dogs start at $2,700, a fraction of the roughly $70,000 price tag for Boston Dynamics' four-legged device, Spot.
"They're not exactly comparable because some of Unitree's dogs are much smaller," Soh said. "But the price is a big difference."
Unitree has been selling humanoid robots since 2023, with its $13,500 child-sized G1 model hitting the market the following year.
Meanwhile, major US rivals - including Elon Musk's Tesla - have yet to start delivering rival products.
Unitree robots have been at the centre of a huge marketing push ahead of the firm's IPO.
This week, its machines are competing in the 2026 World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing. The event features hundreds of teams competing in events such as running and football as well as less sporty challenges like box opening and sorting library books.
In February, Unitree's robots caught the eye of the public and researchers when its G1 robots put on a display of martial arts moves during China's Spring Festival Gala.
The live broadcast showed the robots performing a range of moves "in a way we'd never seen before," said robotics researcher David Hsu.
"It was an indication of a rise of an industry," Hsu added.
A bellwether for robotics firms?
Some experts expect Unitree's market debut to be a gauge of investor appetite for the fast-growing humanoid robotics sector.
The listing has given the public a rare chance to invest in a humanoid robotics company and could set a benchmark for other manufacturers, said Jack Pearson from investment firm RoboStrategy.
The listing also marks a "turning point" for China's robotics industry, as Unitree's success comes even as the US is curbing imports of foreign-made robots, Pearson said.
Unitree's IPO comes almost three years after smaller Chinese rival UBTech Robotics listed on the Hong Kong stock market.
In July this year, UBTech drew global attention when it unveiled what Chinese state media described as a "hyper-realistic" robots designed to offer "emotional support and everyday interaction."
More robot makers, including Leju Robotics and AgiBot, are expected to follow UBTech and Unitree with stock market listings in the coming months.
But the optimism around the industry comes as some experts have voiced doubts over demand for robots for uses outside industrial and commercial settings.
Robots are still years away from working effectively in homes, Soh said.
Developers need to address issues like longer battery life, privacy safeguards and reliability, he said.
Initially, the market will be for robots being used in places like factories and hospitals, he added.
China-US tech rivalry
Robots and AI have become the latest flashpoint in the rivalry between the US and China, as both nations view them as strategically important industries.
US President Donald Trump's administration said in July that it would ban new Chinese-made humanoid and quadruped robots over national security concerns and protecting US manufacturing.
Beijing rejected the claim, accusing Washington of "politicising" trade issues.
The US has also set tough restrictions on other Chinese technology - including AI models and electric cars.
China's dominance of the robotics industry highlights a broader issue faced by Washington as Chinese firms become more "deeply embedded" in global manufacturing, said Christine Wan from the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
Other countries may be reluctant to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers at the risk of disrupting domestic manufacturing, Wan said.

So far, Western robots have not made the same impact on factory floors or in the consumer market.
Boston Dynamics, a major US robotics developer, has said it will roll out human-like machines in car maker Hyundai's factories in two years' time. The South Korean firm has a majority stake in Boston Dynamics.
Other US firms, like Amazon and Tesla, have also announced plans to use humanoid robots in their operations.
Earlier this year, Musk's firm announced that it would use its manufacturing plant in California that made Model S and X cars to produce its line of Optimus humanoid robots.
Amazon, which tested the use of humanoid robots in its warehouses in 2023, told the BBC it is continuing its research into next-generation robotics.
The BBC has also contacted Tesla and Boston Dynamics for comment on their humanoid robot plans.
One thing is clear, said Hsu, the US has lost its lead on robotics.
"We no longer hear about American robotics companies in the news. It's the Chinese robot companies that are making news today," he added.
"They have replaced America as the cool kids on the block."

We Americans remember our presidents in all sorts of ways, with monuments and statues, on coins and street signs. Another thing we do is wait—we wait until a president is safely out of office, or dead, before we bestow such honors.
Donald Trump has bent many democratic traditions, but this one, he’s discarded altogether. Trump has been putting his name on buildings since before most Americans were born. He built his political career atop his personal brand, and much of his second term has been defined by an obsession with leaving his mark. The result is something entirely new in the nation’s history. The more you look, the more you see Trump’s face, name, or signature all around you—on a government building, infrastructure project, banknote, taxpayer-funded website, or official document.
COMPLETED
Trump’s face has appeared swiftly, often with little warning—and nowhere more so than in the nation’s capital. To find a comparable leader so fixated on the proliferation of his image, the historians I spoke with reached across oceans and time: The face of Hafez al-Assad, who ruled Syria for nearly three decades, was printed on children’s schoolbook covers; Mussolini covered Rome’s Palazzo Braschi with a display featuring his head. Obviously Mao Zedong comes to mind. This creation of a cult of personality is partly how strongmen have sought to erase memories of their predecessors and “insert themselves into the social fabric,” Ruth Ben-Ghiat, a historian of authoritarianism at NYU, told me. There may not be a perfect comparison, but past regimes offer clues, the scholars said, about how a leader’s ubiquity can help inure citizens to broader shifts in their relationship to their government.
Kevin Carter / Getty
Trump’s face—staring back at federal workers, residents, and tourists from banners draped on agencies such as the Labor Department—sends a message that “he is inseparable from these more impersonal institutions of governance,” says Lisa Wedeen, a political scientist at the University of Chicago.
Kevin Carter / Getty
A banner featuring the president’s face appeared on the Agriculture Department (right) last year, but was taken down soon after. Banners similar to it remain on the Labor, Justice (left), and Interior (center) Departments, despite objections by Democrats over the cost and the message they send—especially at the Justice Department, which, particularly since Watergate, has tried to operate autonomously from the president, for all sorts of obvious reasons.
Anna Moneymaker / Getty
The U.S. Institute of Peace, a government-funded think tank, had Donald J. Trump added to its name in December, even as a battle over the administration’s efforts to take control of the institute continues to play out in court.
Kevin Dietsch / Getty
The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts likewise has become the target of a Trump takeover. The center, initially named the National Cultural Center, was renamed for Kennedy through an act of Congress two months after his assassination.
Kevin Carter / Getty
Less than six months after loyalists Trump installed on the center’s board put his name on the center’s facade, the lettering came down following a judge’s order. But two months later, a tarp continues to cover the spot where the president’s name once was—and the board now wants to inscribe this on the facade: Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump.
Andrew Leyden / Getty
In a rush to “beautify” Washington, D.C., the president has turned stretches of the city into a construction zone—in part by redirecting money once used for national-park repairs. The most notable among these beautification efforts involves the Reflecting Pool and launched a thousand headlines this summer, as fresh sealant flaked off and algae bloomed.
Saul Loeb / AFP / Getty
Although every president brings his own interior-decorating sense to the People’s House, Trump has dramatically altered the building’s appearance. At least three paintings and one statue at the White House illustrate the moments following the July 2024 attempt on Trump’s life in Butler, Pennsylvania.
Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux
Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux
Chip Somodevilla / Getty
Demetrius Freeman / The Washington Post / Getty
Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux
Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux
Andrew Harnik / Getty
Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux
Doug Mills / The New York Times / Redux
Trump has filled the White House with portraits of himself. One painting is positioned between official portraits of former First Ladies Laura Bush and Hillary Clinton. Another, which is hanging in the West Wing, depicts him, Henry Clay, and Abraham Lincoln with the label The Tariff Men. Yet another shows Trump with Lincoln and Ronald Reagan.
Celal Gunes / Anadolu / Getty
Late last year, the White House unveiled a “Presidential Walk of Fame” in the colonnade connecting the West Wing to the White House residence. Gold plaques and framed images of past presidents, including an autopen in place of President Biden, are examples of the administration’s attempts to rewrite history—in Trump’s signature color, no less.
As part of the celebration of America’s 250th birthday this year, the administration released what it calls the “Patriot Passport”—a special commemorative document featuring Trump’s face. The State Department began issuing the passports in July to those applying in person at the Washington, D.C., passport agency.
National Park Service
This year’s $80 annual resident National Parks pass looks quite different from those issued in years past (think: misty redwoods, a camouflaging frog, a snowy mountainside). Now it features Trump’s face beside George Washington’s. An environmental group sued, arguing that the Interior Department had violated a law requiring the passes to display the winner of an annual public-lands photo contest.
Trump has made mass deportation a pillar of his domestic agenda, but the Trump Gold Card offers a special residency permit to foreigners willing to make a $1 million “contribution” to the United States. (Only one person is said to have received the card thus far.) A government website claims that a Trump Platinum Card is coming soon—offering up tax-related benefits in exchange for $5 million. Officials have said the funds collected through the visas will be directed to the Treasury Department.
Brendan Smialowski / AFP / Getty
Trump’s name made its way into the “.gov” URL for the site advertising the administration’s child-savings-account program—as well as to the top of the official IRS form that applicants must fill out.
Two other government websites similarly bear Trump’s name: TrumpRx deals with prescription-drug costs and launched in February; TrumpIRA advertises a federal platform for retirement savings, and is set to roll out in 2027.
Trump celebrated his 80th birthday on June 14 with a UFC fight on the White House’s South Lawn. Other Americans could celebrate the occasion at national parks: The Interior Department deemed it a “resident-only patriotic fee-free” day.
@realDonaldTrump / Truth Social
This spring, the Treasury Department announced that Trump’s signature would appear on future bills—a first for a sitting president. U.S. Treasurer Brandon Beach, the official who oversees the production of coins and paper money, called the move “not only appropriate, but also well deserved.”
Saul Loeb / AFP / Getty
A major promise of Trump’s first presidential campaign, the border wall—which remains under construction—includes plaques featuring his signature.
Elsewhere around the country, local officials have pushed for naming streets and highways after the president. Although the majority of those measures have so far gone nowhere, a few came to fruition. A Trump bridge was unveiled in Tennessee last month, and Palm Beach International Airport was renamed for the president. Trump’s sons were passengers on the first flight to land at the freshly renamed airport.
Helen H. Richardson / MediaNews Group / The Denver Post / Getty
Last March, Trump deemed a portrait of himself that had been hanging in the Colorado state capitol since 2019 “purposefully distorted.” Lawmakers voted to “immediately” remove the unflattering picture.
Thomas Peipert / AP
A few months later, the president celebrated the portrait that took its place. The artist, Vanessa Horabuena, says she drove 33 hours in two days that summer to hand-deliver another one of her paintings to the White House.
IN THE WORKS
The Kennedy Center debacle offered the president a reminder: “Letters can easily be taken off of the surface of buildings,” Lawrence Vale, an MIT urban-planning professor who studies capital-city design and national identity, told me. Come 2029, if a Democrat wins back the White House, it’s difficult to imagine the Trump-faced banners and paintings remaining up for long. Other things—multimillion-dollar monuments, travel documents, money in circulation—would be far more challenging to undo.
CFA (Commission of Fine Arts)
It’s not in the official name, but everyone can plainly see—it’s the Arc de Trump.
Jim Bourg / Redux
Andrew Harnik / Getty
Inspired by Napoleon’s Arc de Triomphe, the prospective arch has faced backlash from locals worried that the 250-foot-tall monument would ruin the city’s skyline and tarnish the sacred stretch that connects the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery. The arch is still in the planning stage, but the president has shared various models with donors.
Salwan Georges / The Washington Post / Getty
Trump has dismissed the idea of the “President Donald J. Trump Ballroom” as “fake news.” But a list of the project’s donors referred to it as such, and top White House officials have reportedly used the name too.
McCreary Architects PLLC 2025 / whitehouse.gov
Regardless of its formal title, a completed ballroom where the East Wing stood a short while ago would represent the fruition of one of the president’s biggest passion projects—and, invariably, remain associated with his name.
AP Graphic / Treasury Department
In the history of empires, dictators spreading their likeness via gold coin is not particularly novel. In the history of the United States, a sitting president last appeared on a coin 100 years ago, when Calvin Coolidge was featured alongside George Washington on a commemorative half-dollar issued for the nation’s 150th birthday. Last month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that the U.S. Mint would soon begin producing a $1 gold-colored coin with Trump’s face on it.
Kent Nishimura / AFP / Getty
The Donald J. Trump $250 Bill Act proposes featuring the president on a new $250 bill. The legislation is unlikely to make it out of committee, as federal law says only portraits of deceased individuals may appear on U.S. currency. (Although living people have appeared on commemorative coins like the one Bessent announced, no living person has been featured on paper money since that statute was enacted 160 years ago.) But Beach, the treasurer, reportedly asked for prototypes of the $250 note, prompting the departure of the Treasury’s printing director. She wrote to her colleagues: “The buck stopped here.”
Andrew Caballero-Reynolds / AFP / Getty
The Navy’s plans for a new fleet of 15 Trump-class battleships were announced in December. But the project is still a long way off. Earlier this month, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the first of the warships would take at least eight years to build—and that the program could cost $275 billion.
US Air Force
The Air Force, meanwhile, in a nod to Trump—the 47th president—awarded a contract to Boeing in March to develop “the world’s first sixth-generation fighter aircraft,” to be called the F-47. “It’s a beautiful number,” Trump said when announcing the plans for the new jets.
ON TRUMP’S WISH LIST
Trump—and those in his orbit looking to flatter him—will almost certainly propose more places for his name and face to appear. The president could grow dissatisfied with having his name on just one airport, especially one that serves fewer than 10 million people a year. Or the new football stadium coming to Washington might grab his attention. And, of course, there is his obsession with being on Mount Rushmore. Many ideas that seemed improbable when they were first introduced have since been carried out.
@realDonaldTrump / Truth Social
The first time Kristi Noem met Trump in the Oval Office, she was a congresswoman from South Dakota, and he told her: “Do you know it’s my dream to have my face on Mount Rushmore?” she recounted in a 2018 interview. She remembered laughing in response; the president wasn’t laughing. On a recent trip to the monument, the president and his guests were served cookies on Air Force One that featured five presidents on the mountain, with Trump sketched in to the right of Lincoln.
Courtesy Washington Commanders
Last fall, ESPN reported, Trump was telling people privately that he wants the planned new Commanders stadium in D.C. to be named after him. White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt wouldn’t confirm the rumor, but she did tell the outlet, “That would be a beautiful name.”
Courtesy Dulles Airport
The airports named after John F. Kennedy (in New York), Ronald Reagan (near D.C.), and George H. W. Bush (in Houston) may be serving as inspiration. (Never mind, of course, that each of those airports was renamed after each president had died or left office.) As Dulles Airport, in Northern Virginia, prepares for a major renovation, Trump has told people that he wants the international hub renamed after him, ABC News reported; there’s a bill ready to be resuscitated that would do just that.
The tenures of previous world leaders obsessed with imparting their images onto history have yielded troves of artifacts—and left successors with the question of what to do with them all.
As Hungary’s Communist era came to an end, the government confronted one such quandary. Budapest’s new government didn’t want to melt statues down or discard them, so in 1993, it deposited dozens of them in a park 20 minutes outside the city center. In one sense, the park became an oversize storage unit for junk the Hungarian public no longer needed; in another, it was a tourist attraction in its own right—a memorial to the way that a past regime had sought to memorialize itself.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.

The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.

The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

When the Indian government announced the resignation of its education minister in late July after weeks of protest, there were widespread celebrations. Students from across the country had joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party amid growing resentment over repeated examination cancellations and question paper leaks.
The pressure of exams in the country has only increased in recent years. The number of student suicides rose from 8,068 in 2014, to 14,488 in 2024 – an increase of roughly 80% – according to the Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India report released by the country’s National Crime Records Bureau. After family problems, failure in examinations has been listed as the leading cause of suicides among students.
For families who say they lost their children to education system mismanagement and examination scandals, watching the protest scenes unfold on television came with mixed feelings. Some were happy that future students may be spared the same fate; others questioned why it had taken so long.
The Guardian spoke to four families about what happened to their children and how they feel today.
Anshika Pandey, 20, Delhi
Anshika Pandey, the eldest of twin sisters and four siblings, was, her father says, the calmest, quietest and most responsible member of the family. Revision books still lie neatly stacked, bags and accreditation cards hang from the nails where they were last placed. Her ambition was to be a doctor in the community where she lived, to be able to help the “poor people in need of medical care” some day.
Pandey studied for more than 12 hours every day, worked part-time at a store for nearly six hours and slept no more than five hours each night.
This year’s national eligibility cum entrance test (Neet) to gain entrance to medical training was her third attempt at becoming a doctor. After sitting the exam on 3 May, she was hopeful. But on 12 May she learned that the exam had been leaked for the second year in a row and there would be a resit.
“Anshika was deeply hurt. She had been hoping to enter college this year and was happy with the exam she had taken. Still, after cancellation, when I tried to console her, all she lamented was how could she hope to give another good exam,” says her father, Indradhar Pandey, a cab driver in Delhi.
Anshika remained calm and performed her household duties and engaged with everyone normally. But two days later, on 14 May, when everyone had left for work and her twin sister and younger brother were napping, she hanged herself.
Anshika’s dream had been to move her family, especially her siblings, from the slum where they lived. Her younger sister, Pragati, hopes to fulfil that dream and reminisces about how the two sisters had talked about it several times.
Anshika’s sketches and positive messages and mantra chants on the walls of their home, which she wrote to motivate herself, are now the memories her family is refusing to let go of.
Sufi Shaheen, 19, Delhi
Before leaving the house on the morning of 25 October 2024, Sufi Shaheen straightened her hair and put on her favourite jeans. As she left, she asked her mother for 10 rupees (8p), unlike other days when she would ask for 100. Then she headed for her joint entrance examination (Jee) lesson.
Her mother, Sultana Khatoon, asked her why she was leaving the house on an empty stomach. Shaheen replied she would be back soon. Twenty minutes later, she jumped from the seventh floor of a tutoring centre, about a mile away from her home.
It has been almost two years since she died, but Khatoon has not recovered from that day. She is being treated for severe depression and bouts of headaches.
“She was my only daughter of the four children and more like a friend. Every time I stepped out of the house, she would help me get ready. Even though she was deeply passionate about studying and becoming an engineer, she also loved dressing up and made everyone in the house do it too,” says Khatoon, as she looks through her daughter’s school photos.
Living with her parents and three brothers on her father’s modest income as a technical engineer, Shaheen had dreamed of becoming a software engineer and “excelling even more than the boys in her community”, says her mother.
A quick learner and highly motivated, Shaheen taught herself to draw and paint, and even learned to speak Japanese and Korean. But she had been stressed for several months and feared not being able to clear her second attempt at the national engineering entrance exam in January 2025.
When India’s National Testing Agency made changes to the Jee exam syllabus, Shaheen couldn’t sleep for days. She remained stressed, cried when talking to her brother and her best friend on the phone, and wrote a note to her parents in which she apologised and asked her younger brother, Masoom, to make their dreams come true.
“Almost two years later, Masoom was ranked 188th in the whole of India in his CUET [common university entrance test]. But we do not have Shaheen to celebrate this with,” says Khatoon.
Pradeep Kumar Mahich, 22, Rajasthan
“Even God will not be able to stop me from becoming a doctor this year,” were 22-year-old Pradeep Mahich’s words to his father right after his Neet exam on 3 May. This was his fourth attempt and, most importantly, he felt confident. But the announcement of the exam paper leak and resit broke his heart.
No one in the family had ever “dreamt so big”, says Pradeep’s father, Rajesh Kumar, a farmer in Rajasthan’s Sikar district. Kumar sold a large part of his farmland and took a loan of 11 lakhs (£8,600) under the farmer’s crop loan schemes.
“Sikar, the main coaching hub for Neet, is only an hour and a half from our village. My eldest daughter, Babita, who was preparing to join the police, and my son were both studying in Sikar, renting an apartment. This was his fourth year of tutoring, and the money from selling the land and the loan was slowly being consumed. I would send monthly expenses of £250 and Pradeep’s annual tutoring fees of £4,000, asking them not to worry about money and focus on his studies,” says Kumar.
“Pradeep had told me, ‘Papa, we will do a big celebration before I go to college. And one day I’ll return to serve the people of the village,’” says Kumar.
On 15 May, as he did every day, Kumar sent milk and curd to his two children on a bus that goes to Sikar; Pradeep came to pick it up at 9.30am then went home and told his sister he would help prepare lunch. But when his sister was showering, he hanged himself. She has taken a break from her studies and returned home.
Seeing students protesting on his television screen, Kumar says he is relieved that the eduction minister has gone but says there should be a proper investigation so that “no family suffers the same fate that we did”.
S Anitha, 17, Tamil Nadu
S Anitha belonged to an underprivileged lower caste, or Dalit, community from Tamil Nadu’s Ariyalur district. Born to a daily wage labourer, her mother died when she was seven, leaving her grandparents to raise her.
As a teenager, she decided she wanted to become a doctor. “At such a tender age, she was so focused that we used to feel proud of her,” says her brother, Manirathinam. “She knew what she wanted and never distracted herself with anything else. She never asked for any clothes, jewellery or food – her focus was clear and she knew the circumstances.”
She scored a perfect 100 in physics and chemistry at school and was offered a place to study aeronautical engineering at the state’s technological institute. But when she could not even meet the cut-off marks in the Neet exam, she realised that she had been studying a different syllabus.
Tamil Nadu had already criticised the national government for imposing an all-India examination – “disrupting the federal structure” – because it had a different education system. As a result, the state was exempted from Neet in 2016, but not in 2017, the year Anitha sat the exam.
When the supreme court ruled on 22 August 2017 that admissions to medical school would be based only on the Neet exam, she lost hope. On 1 September, Anitha hanged herself in her grandparents’ home. Her suicide became the subject of a public debate and led to widespread protests across the state and even in Delhi.
Her brother took part in last month’s protests in the capital and, while happy about the Indian education minister’s resignation in July, argues that all exams should become state-run, rather than by central government, as not everyone can afford the hefty tutoring fees needed to sit the Neet exam.
He now runs a free library and education centre in Anitha’s name.

The Atlantic Announces Ian Bogost and Gabby Deutch as Staff Writers, and Nick Summers and Talya Zax as Senior Editors
Today The Atlantic is announcing four new members of the editorial staff: Gabby Deutch and Ian Bogost as staff writers, and Nick Summers and Talya Zax as senior editors.
Ian is a familiar name to Atlantic readers, having been a contributing writer for the past 15 years; Gabby was an Atlantic editorial fellow in 2018 and 2019, and for the past five years has been a senior correspondent at Jewish Insider; Nick is a senior features editor who has worked at New York magazine, Bloomberg Businessweek, and The New York Times, where he is currently the acting Sunday Business editor; Talya will be a senior editor on the Books desk, and has most recently been the opinion editor at The Forward.
Below is the staff announcement from editor in chief Jeffrey Goldberg and executive editor Adrienne LaFrance:
We’re writing to share excellent news: After nearly 15 years as a contributing writer, Ian Bogost is joining The Atlantic as a staff writer; an alumna of the Atlantic fellowship, Gabby Deutch, is returning to us as a staff writer; and Nick Summers and Talya Zax are coming on board as senior editors.
First, Ian. As all of you know by now, Ian is an original—and he has contributed so much to our magazine over the years, with uncommon creativity and range. Ian has produced serious reporting on the cultural and social power of Big Tech, and helped our readers understand the knock-on effects of DOGE under Trump, the chaotic rise of AI in higher education, and the decline of American populist-industrial ambition. He has also analyzed the ontology of slushies, the merits of cow therapy, the delight of toasters, the glory of the 747, the design of carry-on bins, and the strangeness of the McRib sandwich. And he has played with all kinds of formats. (Remember that time he built an old-timey slang generator?) In addition to his reported features and essays, Ian writes the new Ordinary Extraordinary newsletter, which is growing rapidly. When he isn’t writing for us, Ian also serves as the Barbara and David Thomas Distinguished Professor at Washington University in St. Louis. And he is the author of 11 books—most recently The Small Stuff: How to Lead a More Gratifying Life, which was published last month—and is a founding partner of a game and design studio.
Next, Gabby. A member of the 2018–19 fellowship class (along with the previously announced, happily returning Maddy Carlisle), Gabby went on to NewsGuard, where she covered the 2020 election and the proliferation of conspiracies and falsehoods during the coronavirus pandemic as Washington correspondent. Gabby has spent the past five years as a senior correspondent at Jewish Insider, focusing this election cycle on how disputes over anti-Semitism and Israel are affecting both the Democratic and Republican Parties. Her reporting has appeared in The Washington Post, Politico Magazine, Tablet, and Wired. We can’t wait to welcome her back.
In more good news, Nick Summers will be joining us as a features editor. Nick is a talented and experienced editor who comes to us from, among other publications, New York magazine, Bloomberg Businessweek, and The New York Times, where he is currently the acting Sunday Business editor. He is a skilled director of business and finance coverage—including investigations and deeply reported profiles of industry leaders—and he’s also assigned and edited stories on topics as varied as the scourge of LED lighting (clearly Nick will have much to discuss with Gilad) and a highly unusual copyright fight.
And finally, Talya Zax is joining us as a senior editor on the Books desk. A sharp, stylish, and omnivorous writer and editor, Talya comes to us from The Forward, where she spent more than a decade at the intersection of news and the arts—including as the publication’s deputy culture editor and, most recently, as its opinion editor. Talya has written for The New York Times, The Washington Post, and, of course, The Atlantic, where she has contributed reviews and reported stories about fiction and theater. We are very happy she’s agreed to join us and can’t wait for her to start.
