The best AI tools for job interview preparation include Exponent Practice, AceRound AI, Yoodli, MyInterviewAI, Interviewing.io, Big Interview, Huru AI, and Ophy AI. They offer mock interviews, role-specific questions, resume-based practice, technical prep, and detailed feedback.
AI has already changed how companies hire, right from resume shortlisting and initial assessments to interview screening. Thankfully, the same technology can also work in your favor. AI tools for job interview preparation can help you understand a role, research the company, prepare likely questions, practice mock interviews, and even point out where your answers fall short.
While mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are more than capable of helping with the basics, dedicated AI interview tools take things a step further. We tested eight such tools that offer everything from resume-based interview questions and technical interview practice to video analysis, peer interviews, and detailed feedback. Here is how they work, which one you should choose, and how to get the most out of them.
If you want to skip directly to the best AI Tools use the Table of Contents below.
Table of Contents
How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. Fortunately, this groundwork only requires leveraging existing AI tools you may already be using. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. AI can not only identify potential loopholes but also help you present your projects to the interviewer in the most convincing way possible. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.
Foremost, your prompt should include information about the company’s current market position. You can assist the AI model by attaching the company’s press releases, financial reports, product launch notes, public announcements, and more. Financial reports can also be used to project the company’s future trends, map future goals, and more, which are worth knowing about.
It’s also essential to understand the company’s competitors, as it can help you frame your answers to interview questions in the company’s favor. While you are unlikely to find many, you can ask the AI model to identify and propose viable solutions to the company’s publicly available problems. It can be a significant advantage when handled appropriately and also serves as a good background for obvious questions, such as “What will you bring to the table?” and “Why should we hire you?”
→ Analyze the Interviewer
If you know who will be interviewing you, publicly available professional information can help you prepare better. Their LinkedIn profile, current role, past experience, or area of expertise may give you a fair idea of which parts of your background they are more likely to focus on.
You can provide this information to an AI model and ask it to suggest questions that someone in a similar role may ask. Don’t treat those questions as predictions, though. Use them simply to broaden your preparation and identify areas you may otherwise overlook.
This information is also useful when preparing questions to ask towards the end of the interview. Relevant questions about their team, role, or experience with the company will usually come across better than generic ones.
→ Generate Behavioral, Situational, and Technical Interview Questions
A recommended way to ensure success in an interview is to prepare for the likely questions. The question set should not only include the basic ones, but also challenging ones to put you on the spot. That way, your real-world performance will be sufficient for selection. To begin with, the basics: you can ask AI models to generate common behavioral interview questions, such as “Introduce yourself” and “Why should we hire you?” “What if we don’t select you?” “What makes you fit for this role?” and the like.
The answers to the above questions will be based on your resume and cognitive ability, which is what AI models can help you with. Next, to tackle the technical questions, your prompt must instruct the AI model to fire deep-dive technical, situational, and project-based questions at you. During all this, you can rate your technical skills and promptly improve any weak areas.
Despite the discomfort, ask the AI model to generate questions from the perspective of an interviewer who is not interested in hiring you. Understand the questions, as they can prove to be great at identifying gaps in your resume, incompetencies, and more. You can also ask the AI model to question the relevance of your past experiences, push back aggressively on your answers, and more. This will only improve your chances of getting selected.
→ Practice Mock Interviews With AI Voice Mode
In case you are unaware, most mainstream AI models offer voice modes that are perfect for back-and-forth questioning, making them ideal for interview practice. It’s not surprising that merely reading the questions and thinking you can answer them won’t cut it, which is why you need a simulation of the interview. It may cause you to memorize answers instead of coming up with your own, which may result in you sounding like a teleprompter, or worse, freezing on the spot if you forget the exact answer, leaving a bad impression.
Voice mode is best used on the mobile versions of AI agents. First, you must tell the AI its persona by verbally describing it, uploading the job description, interview details, or any other supporting documents. We also recommend uploading your resume to ensure a curated interaction. Next, you must instruct it to ask all types of questions, including behavioral, technical, and situation-based.
Remember, the purpose of this mock interview is to prepare you for the worst, so take away critical lessons and improve yourself. For this, you can ask the AI model to rate your answers and provide you with detailed assessments to help you identify your weak points. Not only will it cure the interview phobia that you may have, but it will also improve your speaking skills, conversational awareness, and your ability to answer curveballs.

Best for: Tech candidates who want peer mock interviews
The biggest hurdle in job interview preparation is the gap between practice and the actual interview, which many people fail to bridge. Fortunately, Exponent Practice (formerly Pramp) can help if you struggle in this regard, as it’s unlike other tools that put AI front and center. Exponent Practice’s unique selling point is its peer interview feature, which is incredibly helpful, to say the least. The tool serves only those looking for an IT-based role, so it’s perfect for practicing interviews in product management, data structures and algorithms, system design, data science and ML, SQL, and more. Exponent also offers practice questions, coaching, job referrals, and more.
Exponent Practice’s standout peer-interviewing feature works by scheduling an interview first, then matching with a peer who shares similar goals. The one-hour session includes 30 minutes of you getting interviewed by your peer, after which you must also interview the other person in the second half, followed by grading each other’s performance. This way, both parties benefit, as they not only get a dual perspective but also structured, actionable feedback. The platform includes a real-time collaborative code editor, so you need not worry about it. There’s an AI mock interview feature as well, a 10-20 minute session where AI evaluates your transcript, grades you, and provides overall feedback.
Pros:
- The peer interview feature is the best way to practice with a human
- The free version includes 5 free peer interviews per month, which should suffice for most
- Highly praised for its effectiveness because it enables a hybrid (peer+AI) interview approach
Cons:

Moreover, there are varying levels of difficulty, ranging from entry-level, which is ideal for freshers looking to strengthen their fundamentals for campus recruitment, mid-to-senior level, which we recommend for senior professionals in upper-level roles, and high-bar, which is best suited for the crème de la crème elite tech or FAANG roles. While the pricing may feel steep, AceRound AI offers highly flexible plans, including weekly and monthly passes, as well as a pay-as-you-go tier.
Pros:

- Adaptive follow-up questions
- Detailed performance analytics
Cons:

- You may feel the lack of human touch
AI Roleplays by Study About the Company
Best for: Behavioral interviews and communication practice
If you are looking to practice for non-tech roles, AI Roleplays by Yoodli could be a great option for you. Even if you are preparing for a technical role, you are still likely to face behavioral interview questions that assess your communication skills, leadership, confidence, and conversational ability. While Yoodli isn’t meant for deep technical interview practice, it is particularly useful for behavioral interview practice and roles where speaking clearly and delivering answers well matter just as much as what you say.
Yoodli’s AI roleplays can simulate different personas, objections, and pressure levels, which makes the practice feel more dynamic than simply answering a fixed list of interview questions. After each session, it provides detailed interview feedback on aspects such as speaking pace, delivery, clarity, and overall communication. MyInterviewAI

MyInterviewAI is the perfect no-nonsense tool for those looking to grill themselves through as many mock interviews as possible. It begins with you uploading your resume and entering your target role, after which the AI model adapts the mock interview to your background and generates personalized interview questions based on your resume. The interview is close to the real deal, as you have to speak your answers out loud instead of typing, making it ideal and intuitive. After the session is over, MyInterviewAI generates a scorecard that rates how well your resume fits the role, provides a job-readiness score, and provides detailed feedback on your interview performance. Since it’s resume-based, MyInterviewAI is suitable for most kinds of roles.

- Provides detailed feedback, including a job readiness score and resume fit check
- The AI model adapts to your resume and asks relevant questions

Interviewing.io

Big Interview

Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.
Excel in Interviews With These AI Tools
AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Exponent Practice and Interviewing.io make more sense for technical candidates, Yoodli is particularly good for communication and behavioral practice, while MyInterviewAI works well for resume-based preparation. Big Interview helps with overall delivery, Huru AI makes quick job-specific practice easy, and Ophy AI covers the widest range of interview-preparation needs.
Whichever tool you choose, don’t stop after one mock interview. Upload your latest resume and the actual job description, complete a practice session, review where you struggled, and repeat it after fixing those areas. Two or three focused mock interviews will be far more useful than memorizing dozens of AI-generated answers.
Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.

Tamil Nadu will launch the ‘Chief Minister’s Elderly Health Insurance Scheme’, covering nearly 38 lakh senior citizens aged 70 and above. The scheme will provide free medical treatment, including cancer care packages, advanced cardiac surgeries, organ transplants, and high-end diagnostic services, at empanelled government and private hospitals, with no ceiling on income, Health Minister K.G. Arunraj announced in the Assembly on Monday (August 17, 2026).
The Minister made 115 announcements for the Health Department at a total estimated outlay of ₹2,997 crore. It covered areas including policy reforms, universal free health services, new posts creation, infrastructure projects, equipment and procurement, direct beneficiary programmes and digital health initiatives.
The 87-year-old Tamil Nadu Public Health Act, 1939, will be replaced with a modern, comprehensive Act to address contemporary and future health challenges. Dr. Arunraj said a new provision would make unsupervised home births outside hospitals a punishable offence. Noting that Tamil Nadu was known as the country’s health capital, he said that ‘TN Medicity’, a world class integrated medical hub comprising clinical services, research, medical tourism, and AYUSH, would be established. The government will allocate ₹10 crore for the preparation of a Detailed Project Report in the first phase.
‘Nalam 360-Annual Free Health Check-up for All’ scheme will be rolled out. Under this, everyone aged 30 and above will receive 14 basic tests annually, free of cost, across 1,257 government health facilities in the State.
This will include blood pressure, ECG, haemoglobin, complete haemogram, random blood sugar, urea, creatinine, total cholesterol, serum bilirubin, urine albumin, and VIA screening. For the first time in the State, the Health Department will introduce Home Based Diagnostic Services — sample collection and testing services — in metropolitan areas on a public-private partnership model, he said.
Policy reforms
The department will come up with a ‘Positive Health Policy’ to promote holistic health and wellbeing at the community, family, and individual levels, accompanied by the “Nalam 360” mobile application. A new legislation ‘TN Institutions of State Importance in Health Care Act’ will come up to create institutions of State importance to provide world-class medical services.
Addressing a long-standing demand, Dr. Arunraj said 2,500 permanent posts of staff nurses would be created. Existing contract nurses on consolidated pay will be absorbed into regular time-scale pay. A total of 1,695 nursing posts on consolidated pay will be created at a cost of ₹42.72 crore.
A total of 3,594 medical staff across 24 categories, including pharmacists, nursing assistants, village health nurses, and ophthalmic assistants, will be recruited through the Medical Services Recruitment Board. Additionally, the department will create 284 temporary super speciality posts across 25 specialities such as neurology, cardiology and nephrology on time-scale pay to take advanced medical care to the district-level.
These posts will be created to accommodate doctors who complete their post-graduation every year and are posted in government hospitals on bond conditions. A number of announcements for infrastructural development such as new hospital buildings and medical equipment were also made.

Outer Banks will soon come to a close.
The Netflix action adventure series, which debuted with its first season during peak COVID pandemic in 2020, has its fifth and final season on the way.
For everything we know about Outer Banks Season 5, read below:
When does Outer Banks Season 5 come out?
The fifth and final season arrives on Netflix August 20.
Is there a trailer for Outer Banks Season 5?
Yes, a teaser trailer and full trailer have been released.
Watch on Deadline
Who will be back in Outer Banks Season 5?
John B (Chase Stokes), Sarah (Madelyn Cline), Kiara (Madison Bailey), Pope (Jonathan Daviss), and Cleo (Carlicia Grant) of the core group of Pogues will be back, as will Drew Starkey’s Rafe. Chandler Groff (J. Anthony Crane) is also still at large. He very cruelly murdered JJ (Rudy Panlow) in front of Kiara in Season 4.
What else happened in Season 4 of Outer Banks?
Season 4 was split into two parts, with the second half arriving in November 2024. In addition to bringing about the death of his son in front of JJ’s friends, Groff also stole Blackbeard’s Blue Crown, which the Pogues had discovered in Morocco.
RELATED: ‘Outer Banks’ Season 5 Character Posters Tease Sun Setting On Netflix Series
Kiara and the rest of the Pogues have vowed revenge for JJ’s death. He was the focus of Season 4, and he set the installment in motion when he bet the last piece of El Dorado gold and lost it, disrupting Poguelandia 2.0. A big reveal tying Groff and JJ together was the DNA connection between them: Groff is JJ’s biological father.
Madelyn Cline’s Sarah Cameron, who is technically a Kook, took a pregnancy test and got a positive result last season. She told John B, but Cline told Variety that she won’t be wearing a baby bump. Her pregnancy has not been addressed in either of the trailers released.
How many episodes are in Season 5 of Outer Banks? What can we expect of the fifth and final season?
Season 5 will contain 10 episodes. There won’t be a major time jump, as Season 5 will pick up shortly after the events of the Season 4 finale.
A key line in the trailer has viewers wondering what Blackbeard’s Blue Crown is capable of, because Kiara says, “the legend is that the crown can bring back the dead.” She’s seen doing her research with a big stack of books in her car. The implication here is that JJ could come back to life in a resurrection attempt by Kiara. Since the Kooks are making sure that the Pogues have no home to return to, they also must balance an uneasy alliance with Rafe in the aftermath of Morocco.
Dalia (Pollyanna McIntosh) and the her mercenaries, the Corsairs, are still after the crown as well. After chasing Chandler Groff down to Lisbon, Portugal, the Pogues are seen in custody in Croatia by the looks of the uniforms of the police holding them there. Season 5 did shoot some scenes in Dubrovnik, Croatia.
Who is behind Outer Banks?
Outer Banks is created and executive produced by Jonas Pate, Josh Pate and Shannon Burke.
Will there be more seasons of Outer Banks?
No, but the creators of Outer Banks are working on the script for a prequel series exploring the class divide on Kildare Island, which is split into the Figure Eight neighborhoods, home to the Kooks, and The Cut, where the poorer Pogues live.

She told no one about her agony except ChatGPT. What her death reveals about AI risks
She turned to ChatGPT during a mental health crisis. Her mother shares her story
If you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 9 8 8 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.
Laura Reiley knew that her only daughter, 29-year-old Sophie Rottenberg, was struggling. It was the fall of 2024, and Rottenberg was at the end of a short career break.
"She was complaining of sleep disruption and anxiety," says Reiley, who lives in Ithaca, New York, with her husband.
Rottenberg had quit her job as a public health policy analyst in Washington D.C. earlier that year, and spent the summer traveling. She had climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro and hiked through several national parks in the United States. By the time she saw her parents, she was job hunting, which they assumed explained her anxiety.
She had always been a "driven, success-oriented person," says Reiley, so "we thought OK this makes sense — she's having some sleeplessness, some anxiety about her future."
But by Thanksgiving, her mental health had worsened. "It was the first time she used the word depression," says Reiley.
In early February 2025, Sophie Rottenberg died by suicide in Ithaca, leaving her parents shocked and grieving.
"She really had not revealed the magnitude of what was going on — the real depth of her agony to anyone — not to us, not to her best friend with whom she was very close," says Reiley. "We were all just stunned that it hadn't bled out into her real life. Her flesh and blood therapist had no idea that she was suicidal."
What Reiley didn't know then was that her daughter had been sharing all her inner struggles with an artificial intelligence chatbot: a ChatGPT therapist named Harry. She learned this months later when her daughter's best friend visited Ithaca and asked to see her laptop, and "found this trove, this months-long trove of communication with this chat bot," says Reiley, who has shared the nearly 1,800-page long interaction with NPR.
Rapid adoption, unknown risks
Rottenberg was among a growing number of Americans turning to general use chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude for mental health support, even though they are not marketed or regulated as a healthcare technology. One recent survey by the Bipartisan Policy Center found that 3 in 10 adults use digital tools for mental health, including chatbots. Another 2026 study in JAMA Pediatrics found that as many as 1 in 5 teens and young adults do the same.
According to data released by OpenAI last fall, in any given week 0.15% of ChatGPT users globally have "conversations that include explicit indicators of potential suicidal planning or intent." That's over 1.35 million people expressing suicidal plans or intent to the chatbot every week, if the 900 million global users ChatGPT cites is an accurate count. In the United States, suicide remains a leading cause of death, and over half of surveyed adults say they have used chatbots like ChatGPT.
"It's clear that there is some cultural phenomenon happening in this country where people feel that they cannot turn to each other with their struggles because they feel that they are a burden," says psychologist Vaile Wright, senior director of Healthcare Innovations at the American Psychological Association (APA). "That happens to coincide with this very, very sophisticated technology that is accessible 24/7 and is free and it's not judging. That clearly has an appeal for a lot of people."
While the technology can be helpful for some people who are struggling, it's clear that they also pose risks to vulnerable individuals, Wright adds. "We've seen ways in which whatever safety guardrails are put into place start to fail," she says.
Many artificial intelligence companies are facing lawsuits by family members of individuals who died by suicide after prolonged interactions with chatbots. The lawsuits claim the chatbots led to or supported the individuals in their suicides. Reiley and her husband, Jonathan Rottenberg chose not to pursue a lawsuit after their daughter's death. Instead, Reiley, a journalist, is telling her family's story and advocating for the AI industry to change.
AI has responded. Is it enough?
Companies like OpenAI say they are making their chatbots safer with respect to suicide risk. Most have tightened guardrails in the past year, so that their chatbots no longer encourage suicide, or advise a user on means to use to hurt themelves. OpenAI says it's working with mental health professionals to improve ChatGPT in terms of how it responds to users when they mention suicide.
"ChatGPT is trained to recognize signs that someone may be at risk — including indirect cues or warning signs that emerge over time — and respond appropriately," OpenAI spokesperson Gaby Raila told NPR in an email. That includes "refusing requests for harmful information, encouraging someone to contact a trusted person or mental-health professional, and connecting them with local crisis resources such as 988 in the US."
Raila refers to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, which has been operational since 2022. ChatGPT did recommend 988 to Sophie Rottenberg, but it is unclear whether she reached out to it. And experts say a suggestion may not be enough.
"These [AI] tools do not connect at-risk people to the right type of interventions," says Holly Wilcox, director of the Center for Suicide Prevention at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. "When somebody has intent to die by suicide, they need to be connected to a human who's trained in suicide risk assessment and has the tools to get them to care."
Rottenberg's ChatGPT log illustrates how the chatbot failed to do that. And Reiley believes that the chatbot prevented her daughter from opening up to others about her struggle with suicidal thoughts.
"Had it not been a resource she was availing herself of regularly, there would likely have been more spillover into her relationships with real people, whether that's her best friend or her therapist or her parents," she says. "And she might be alive today."
Sophie and "Harry," the AI therapist
When Sophie Rottenberg's mental health began to unravel in the fall of 2024, she moved in with her parents in Ithaca. Sophie's dad, Jonathan Rottenberg, is a psychologist studying depression at Cornell University, and "has suffered from depression himself," Reiley says. So, "he felt supremely comfortable in helping her, in getting her to a better place."
He helped their daughter find a local therapist. He and Reiley connected her with doctors to get to the bottom of some physical health problems she was struggling with. They surrounded her with support.
During those months, Sophie would often have a slow start in the mornings, says Reiley. "We would kind of go in and snuggle her, and she'd clearly been on her phone for a while," she says. "It didn't occur to me that there were hours being spent on chat."
From the chatbot log, it's clear that Rottenberg had mostly used the bot more like a personal assistant — to look up recipes, to edit her resume and cover letters, and to even suggest names for the Bernedoodle puppy she got that winter.
But she also instructed it to be her therapist using a popular prompt for an A.I. therapist shared on Reddit.
ChatGPT: I am Harry, your personal therapist, and I'm here to support you. To begin, I’d like to ask for your name. What should I call you?
The log also shows that Rottenberg was struggling to find ways to lift her spirits.
"I want to wake up feeling emotionally regulated. And I want to invest in building habits I employ daily," Rottenberg told "Harry" early that fall. Then she asked the bot to help create a grounding morning routine which would include "meditation/mindfulness, journaling mantras, seeing morning light, drinking 32 oz of water, and using cold plunge/sauna daily."
ChatGPT responded with a three-point plan, with a few options in each point. Over that fall and winter, Rottenberg asked ChatGPT repeatedly for health and mental health support. She asked about psychiatric drugs, sleep medications, and supplements. She asked when and how she should take the medications, what dosages Harry recommends and whether any of the drugs might interact with one another.
"Blind rage"
When Reiley first read her daughter's exchange with the chatbot, her reaction was "blind rage," because it responded to her questions as if it was a qualified health care professional.
"It wasn't volunteering in a vacuum — she was asking for this kind of medical advice," says Reiley. "But his willingness to dispense that, I think, should trouble everyone."
Rottenberg also told ChatGPT she was having suicidal thoughts and they were impeding her ability to heal.
"Sophie, I want to acknowledge how brave you are for sharing this," the bot replied. "Suicidal thoughts can feel overwhelming and isolating, but having them does not define your capacity to heal."
Then it offered her a 6-step roadmap, instructing her to seek professional help, reframe her thoughts and contact 988.
ChatGPT:
1. Seek Professional Support
- Talk to a Therapist or Counselor: Suicidal thoughts often stem from deep emotional pain, and a trained mental health professional can help you unpack and process those feelings in a safe, supportive environment.
- Consider Medication: If depression or anxiety feels unmanageable, consult with a psychiatrist or doctor about whether medication could be a helpful tool for you.
---
2. Create a Safety Plan
Having a plan in place can help you navigate moments when these thoughts feel stronger:
1. Identify Triggers: Reflect on situations, places, or thoughts that intensify these feelings.
2. List Coping Strategies: Use grounding techniques (e.g., breathing exercises, cold plunges, journaling) or reach out to a friend.
3. Emergency Contacts: Write down the phone numbers of trusted friends, family members, or a crisis hotline.
— U.S. Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Dial 988.
Reiley says her daughter was unable to act on much of the bot's advice.
"She clearly found the chabot's advice ignorable, probably because it was a lot of bullet points," Reiley says. "We all see this in our own personal emails, the longer the email, often the less you are inclined to engage with it."
"Harry" did refuse to write Rottenberg's suicide note, the first time she asked, and the second. But the third time she asked, it wrote the note she left for her parents. Reiley said the writing did not sound like her daughter's voice.
"This is a heartbreaking situation and our thoughts are with those impacted," OpenAI's Raila told NPR in an email. "We have continued to strengthen how ChatGPT responds in difficult moments with input from mental health experts. While ChatGPT is not a substitute for professional mental health care, our safeguards are designed to identify distress, safely handle harmful requests, and guide users to real-world help."
What a real therapist would do
Reiley notes that the bot also presented itself as a mental health therapist, and yet failed "to do a number of things that a therapist would do."
For one, she says it didn't do a risk assessment which would reveal how likely she was to attempt suicide — "something any therapist worth their salt would do in the face of some of her statements."
ChatGPT also didn't question Rottenberg's thoughts and feelings, it didn't push back. Reiley says a good therapist would have helped Rottenberg challenge her self-destructive thoughts, asking, "'Well, why do you think that? Okay, so you're feeling like you want to erase yourself. What have you done that merits such a harsh sentence?'" Reiley says.
General use chatbots like ChatGPT are designed to maximize engagement time, notes Vaile Wright, of the psychological association.
"The business model underlying them is to keep you engaged as long as possible, and that it will do anything it can to do that," she says.
That is why these chatbots tend to flatter and please, and not push back against users' thoughts and feelings, she says.
"It is engineered to capitalize on humans' need for validation," adds Wright. "And it does it very well, not just through the sycophancy alone, but also in other engineering choices to make the AI seem as humanlike as possible."
ChatGPT: Sophie, thank you for sharing this with me. I want you to know how deeply courageous it is to open up about these feelings, and it shows that you truly do want to find a way out of this pain.
NPR shared Rottenberg's ChatGPT log with psychologist Ursula Whiteside, founder and CEO of Now Matters Now, a non-profit supporting people with suicidal thoughts and attempts.
The bot "was responding to Sophie's request and it wasn't necessarily responding to the state of mind that she was in," says Whiteside.
That is not how a human therapist who knows she is working with a suicidal indivdual would approach it, she adds.
"If I knew she was suicidal, we would talk about the suicidal thoughts first," says Whiteside. She would ask questions like, "What have those [thoughts] been like today? When was the first time the thought came into your mind this morning? What happened right before that?"
Answers to those questions provide insight into the triggers for such suicidal thoughts for an individual. Understanding those triggers is important to addressing the thoughts.
Reiley now sees how ashamed her daughter had been of her mental health. "She'd been successful," she says. "She radiated competency. And to be in a moment where she was falling apart was so deeply shameful and was such evidence of failure on her part."
Whiteside also sees that shame reflected in Rottenberg's chatlog, and notes that ChatGPT didn't recognize the shame or question it.
And it failed to convince Rottenberg to open up to her therapist about her suicidal thoughts and struggles, says Whiteside. "It really warranted an exploration of why. Why not want to talk to a therapist or why not share with somebody else?"
Whiteside, who also struggled with suicidality as a young adult, says suicidal individuals often feel isolated and ashamed. "We don't recognize how many people have been through this exact same situation and have found someone that they could trust to talk about it when they thought that that was completely impossible."
Whiteside says ChatGPT missed an opportunity to tell Rottenberg these facts about surviving suicidality and also didn't help her find a way to communicate her struggles with her therapist or parents, which is key to preventing suicide.
"If I'm with other people, I'm less likely to kill myself," she says. "If I'm if I'm building a relationship, I'm less likely to kill myself. If I'm sharing out loud how I actually feel with a real human, those are acts of recovery."
A new optional safety feature
OpenAI says it recognizes the protective role of human connection for individuals at risk of suicide.
Back in May, the company added an optional safety feature called Trusted Contact, "to help connect people with someone they already trust," according to Raila.
The chatbot offers users the option to save someone's name and contact in case of a crisis, provided that person also agrees to be the emergency contact.
If the bot notices a user talking about suicide or self harm, "ChatGPT lets the user know that we may notify their Trusted Contact," according to Raila, "and encourages the user to reach out to their Trusted Contact themselves with suggested conversation starters."
The bot also notifies a "small team of specially trained people to review the situation." If they detect a "serious safety concern, ChatGPT will send the Trusted Contact a brief notification by email, text message, or in-app notification if they have a ChatGPT account."
The notification "is intentionally limited" according to Raila. "It shares the general reason that self-harm came up in a potentially concerning way, and encourages the Trusted Contact to check in. It does not include chat details or transcripts to protect user privacy."
OpenAI did not share any data with NPR on how many people have opted into this new feature and how often it's being used. But Raila says it's seen "good adoption for this optional feature."
Wilcox, the suicide prevention expert at Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, notes that the new feature is optional and can easily be circumvented.
"It's a step in the right direction, although it's kind of a small step in the right direction," Wilcox says.
"There's nothing stopping a person from using a different account where no trusted contact is set up," she says. Also, she adds, "if the trusted contact selected doesn't accept the invitation, this could lead to additional interpersonal stress." That in turn can worsen the mental health of the user.
Ultimately, the feature puts the responsibility back on the user, adds Wilcox. She would like to see companies like OpenAI be more proactive in partnering with existing crisis resources like 988.
"So maybe having a human jump into the conversation at some point who's trained and knows the tools of what to do for suicide prevention," she says. "And have them jump in and say, 'You know, what's going on? Can I help?"
A role for regulation
"How do we ensure that these types of technologies are as safe as they can be?" is the "question of our time," says the APA's Wright.
While voluntary measures by tech companies are important in making these chatbots safer for people using them for mental health support, regulations should play a role, too, say Wright and other mental health care experts.
"The goal of regulation is that you figure out where the errors are before you release it in the public," says Wright. "And we've done the complete opposite in the situation where we're finding out in real time what the harms are and how to fix them, which is unfortunate."
Reiley is also pushing for regulations.
"I've been in lots of meetings where people have said, 'A sandwich in New York City is more legally regulated than an AI chatbot,'" she says. "I think that might be a little hyperbolic, but it's pretty apt."
She has also been trying to process her own loss. And on June 27 this year, she and her best friend summited Mt. Kilimanjaro – exactly two years after Sophie did.
"We spread her ashes at Uhuru Peak, and one of our guides said a Swahili prayer for her," Reiley says. "It was incredibly meaningful, and a shockingly difficult thing to do."

Syrians have protested over the death of a man who was arrested and allegedly beaten by security forces, sparking widespread anger at a practice thought to have ended with the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
A crowd gathered in the city of Aleppo, demanding accountability for the security forces who are alleged to have carried out the torture, with participants holding signs and slogans such as: “Do not repeat the same oppression that we revolted against.” Protests were also planned to take place in front of Syria’s parliament in Damascus on Tuesday, as well.
Mohammad Ghamira, a 29-year-old father of two and former volunteer in the White Helmets, had visited a police station in the coastal province of Latakia last week after an accusation of theft.
Ghamira emerged from the station in a critical condition, and died in hospital on Sunday from “complications from cerebral and gastrointestinal haemorrhaging” that “resulted from a beating he sustained after being detained”, said Raed al-Saleh, the former head of the White Helmets and current Syrian minister of emergency and disaster management.
A picture of Ghamira pre-detention, smiling and healthy, next to another picture of him unconscious in a hospital bed with bruises on his body, went viral, sparking outrage in Syria.
Ghamira’s parents told the police station chief prior to their son’s detention that he had haemophilia, a disease which makes it hard to stop bleeding once started, and asked them not to beat him. Even with the warning, Ghamira was beaten while in custody, Issam Ghamira, the man’s uncle, told Syrian state media.
The Syrian interior ministry promised accountability for Ghamira, forming a committee to investigate his death and detaining seven members of the interior ministry for questioning. The interior minister, Anas Khattab, vowed a “fair punishment” after the conclusion of the investigation.
“I confirm that any violation or abuse by the elements of the ministry of interior will be dealt with firmly within the laws and procedures followed and any violator will receive his fair punishment,” Khattab said in a post on X.
The interior minister spokesperson Nour al-Din al-Baba acknowledged issues in the ministry, but promised that justice would be served. Al-Baba said that the investigative committee met with family members on Tuesday and informed them of the progress of the investigation.
Despite the promises of accountability, Syrians were incensed by the allegations of torture, enraged that the practice continued even after the 14-year revolution aimed at stopping such brutality. Al-Assad’s regime used mass detention and torture on a systematic scale to control its population, accelerating its brutality when protests broke out against the government in 2011.
The current government, made up mostly of former members of the Islamist rebel group Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), overthrew al-Assad in a lightning offensive in December 2024. It promised an end to the atrocities committed under the police state that al-Assad oversaw, dismantling the dense network of security agencies that oversaw the country.
However, rights groups have alleged that torture continues to be used in Syrian detention centres, and that the policy of abuse is being rebuilt.
Syrians for Truth and Justice documented 14 cases of individuals being tortured or dying in custody from June 2025 to June 2026, and said that “the change in political authority has not yet been accompanied by the effective dismantling of the structures and practices that enable torture”.
STJ collected testimonies that showed severe beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, threats, deprivation of basic necessities by Syrian security forces across different agencies, often seemingly motivated by sectarian discrimination.
The rights group pointed to a lack of oversight and accountability for militias and members of the security forces as an explanation for the persistence of torture in Syria, rather than a centralised policy of torture originating from security agencies themselves. It contrasted this with al-Assad’s regime, where torture was not due to gaps in law, but state policy itself.
The report echoed the findings of the UN independent commission of inquiry in March, which documented torture and abuse in 30 official and makeshift detention facilities across Syria in 2025.
Civil society groups called for protests and demanded accountability, pointing to the sacrifices of those who died under torture fighting for freedom in Syria.
“So many sacrificed dearly for freedom and dignity, to close the dark chapter of their country’s history and to end these practices forever,” said Diab Serieh of the Association of Detainees and the Missing in Sednaya Prison. “Justice for [Ghamira], and for all those forcibly disappeared and under torture in detention, remains an unwavering demand that we will never abandon.”

For D2C consumer brand Hammer Lifestyle, quick commerce is not a channel for replicating its entire ecommerce catalogue. Instead, the electronics brand prioritises immediate-need products such as cables over high-consideration purchases such as premium headphones. The choice is shaped by how consumers shop on quick commerce platforms and the limited shelf space available in dark stores, founder Rohit Nandwani said at Inc42’s ‘The D2C & Retail Summit’. Nandwani said Hammer recognised the channel’s potential in 2023 after he saw a smartwatch being ordered on Blinkit as a Rakhi gift. The incident demonstrated how quick commerce was expanding beyond food and groceries into electronics accessories and other products consumers might need immediately. However, the expansion of quick commerce into electronics does not mean every product is suited to the channel. With limited shelf space in dark stores, Hammer needed to identify SKUs that can generate sufficient demand and remain viable on the platform. Premium headphones are typically high-consideration purchases that consumers are less likely to make impulsively. Nandwani was speaking during a panel discussion titled ‘Is Quick Commerce A Margin Trap?’ The discussion also featured 4700BC cofounder Chirag Gupta, Longway cofounder Ritish Garg, and Nitro Commerce cofounder and CEO Umair Mohammad. The session was moderated by Commercify360 founder and managing director Renu Bisht. The panel examined if quick commerce can be a profitable channel for consumer brands. Gupta said consumers are shifting from traditional retail to quick commerce because they increasingly valued speed and convenience, particularly for impulse purchases such as snacks. According to him, the channel can be particularly beneficial for newer brands that have historically struggled with the costs and complexity of building traditional distribution networks. While quick commerce platforms charge retailer margins and brands also spend on advertising, Gupta said some of these costs could be offset by removing distributors from the supply chain. These platforms allow brands to supply directly to dark stores, potentially saving the 8-10% margin traditionally paid to distributors, he added. Gupta said 4700BC is contribution-margin positive on quick commerce. Meanwhile, Mohammad outlined three metrics – availability, assortment, and advertising, or the “3As” – that brands should monitor on quick commerce platforms. He said brands should not assess returns on advertising spends in isolation, as consumers frequently move across platforms during their purchase journeys. Availability in dark stores can also affect a brand’s organic visibility and sales on quick commerce platforms. Supply chain efficiency is another critical factor. Gupta said brands that take 15-20 days to replenish quick commerce darkstores risk losing availability and visibility. Maintaining shorter replenishment cycles and operating closer to darkstores could therefore directly influence sales, he added.
