Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has launched his campaign for a historic fourth term and vowed that as long as he lived he would not allow the “shameless” right to return to power.
Addressing a sea of supporters in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, the 80-year-old politician reminded voters of the chaos and violence that unfolded during the 2018-2022 presidency of his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, whose son, Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula will face in October’s presidential election.
Lula recalled how hundreds of thousands of citizens died during a Covid outbreak Jair Bolsonaro was accused of bungling with his anti-science policies. Gun ownership soared as laws were relaxed, allowing criminal groups to expand their arsenals. “They handed out … more than a million weapons,” Lula said, promising to dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare as well as developing Brazil’s rare earth deposits, the world’s second largest after China’s.
Lula also said he would improve security by targeting the rich organised crime bosses who lived in luxury apartments. “It’s easy to kill a crook in a favela. But the guy running the show lives in a penthouse … and we need to stop this,” Lula said. He also told his far-right rivals to “show some shame”.
Lula was speaking at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his astonishing rise to the presidency began in 1979 when, as 33-year-old union leader, he spearheaded two historic strikes that helped end the military dictatorship. Those strikes made Lula a household name and in 2002, after three failed attempts, he won a landslide victory to become his country’s first working-class president.
During Lula’s first two-terms, from 2002 until 2010, he was credited with fighting hunger, dramatically expanding social welfare programmes and access to higher education and improving Brazil’s global standing, although his administration was blighted by corruption scandals. His successor, Dilma Rousseff, became Brazil’s first female president but led the country into a severe economic recession before being controversially impeached in 2016.
In 2018, Lula was jailed for alleged corruption and he spent 580 days in prison before the supreme court quashed his conviction. Lula’s imprisonment allowed Bolsonaro to win that year’s election, ushering in four years of environmental destruction and international isolation.
In 2022 Lula won his third term, defeating Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin and vowing to rescue the country from “one of the worst periods in Brazilian history”. “This nightmare is over,” Lula declared at his January 2023 inauguration. A week later, far-right radicals rampaged through the capital, Brasília, in a botched attempt to bring Bolsonaro back.
Bolsonaro was jailed in 2025 for 27 years for plotting that failed post-election power grab. Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator, launched his campaign on Sunday with an event on Rio’s Copacabana beach, previously the scene of huge rallies in support of his father. “I am going to be Brazil’s next president because I’m going to fight this system,” Bolsonaro, who wore a bullet-proof vest under a yellow Brazil shirt, told thousands of supporters.
Polls suggest Lula holds a slender advantage over Bolsonaro, with 43% of intended votes to his rival’s 40% in a run-off, which will take place on 25 October if, as expected, no candidate secures 50% of the vote in the 4 October first round.
André Pagliarini, the author of a book about Lula called A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, said the showdown would be “the single most important electoral contest this year in the world”.
Pagliarini said he believed a Bolsonaro victory would be a significant boost for the pro-Trump “reactionary block” that has won elections across Latin America, from Argentina and Chile to Colombia, where the far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella recently took office.
Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly asserted its leadership over the region, launching deadly military operations against alleged “narco-terrorists” in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific, threatening to “take back” the Panama canal and, in January, abducting Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro. Last week, the US state department published an incendiary video declaring that “American dominance in the western hemisphere will never be questioned again”.
In recent months Trump has turned up the heat on Brazil, designating its two biggest organised crime groups, the Red Command and the PCC, as terrorist organisations. That has kindled fears of a US military intervention on Brazilian soil or interference in Brazil’s presidential election.
During a visit to a jungle training camp in Panama on Friday, Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, said Washington planned to use the military to “ruthlessly” pursue Latin American drug traffickers, “just like [they did with] Isis and al-Qaida” during the “war on terror”.
The idea, Hegseth said, was to “do bad things to bad people – because for too long, bad people did bad things to good people inside the United States of America and across Central and South America”.
There was anger at the US outside Lula’s campaign launch on Sunday, where some activists handed out stickers that read: “Fuck Trump.”
Seixas Alves, a 33-year-old Lula supporter, said he worried the decision to classify Brazilian drug factions as terrorist groups could be used as a pretext for a US attack. “Just like they [did with] Saddam Hussein,” Alves added, referring to the Iraqi dictator’s supposed development of weapons of mass destruction.
In Rio, Flávio Bolsonaro praised Trump’s decision to target the Brazilian crime groups and said he was the only politician capable of “sitting down with the US”.
In Vila Euclides, Simone Tebet, a centrist Lula ally, urged voters to do everything they could to stop Brazil falling back into the hands of far-right politicians who wanted “to kill Brazilian democracy” and create “a country of hate”.

In the Henrik Ibsen play The Wild Duck, Dr. Relling dispenses a drug that soothes the most profound self-loathing: livsløgn, a “life-lie,” a form of grandiose self-delusion that lets the pathetic figures who take it believe that they are geniuses and noble romantics. The life-lie, it turns out, is a hell of a drug—perhaps the most potent Scandinavian pharmaceutical invention before Ozempic—and keeps the play’s fragile characters from succumbing to “self-contempt and despair.” Against Relling’s advice, another character, Gregers, decides to free these losers from their life-lies and expose them. The play ends with a suicide.
On Friday, the former Cambridge professor Jason Arday died at the age of 41. British police said his death was “unexpected” but not “suspicious.” This classification, unexpected but not suspicious, includes the possibility that he died accidentally. But reports of Arday’s delicate emotional state at the time have led most to assume that he killed himself after weeks of accumulating revelations that he had lied compulsively for personal and professional gain. One of his last public statements was an interview with The Times of London in which he affirmed that he was “not a liar,” a line itself so blatantly false that any Ibsen fan would have recognized symptoms of a livsløgn overdose. He gave no George Santos–like, impish shrug at having been finally caught. (What took you so long?) He did not prepare to switch careers to pursue reality-TV stardom or write a Catch Me if You Can–style memoir about the dupes he met along the way. Instead, his response suggested—it is painful to notice this now, when nothing can be done—that he felt he had to stick with his story. That way led to a catastrophic end: narcissistic collapse, in which the lies stop working on others and finally on the liar himself. Arday appears to have convinced himself, wrongly, that the last remaining option was suicide, which was, of course, his final self-delusion. His lies won him undeserved praise and status, and they gave (unforgivably) false hope to people whose loved ones have severe developmental delays. But the only lie that ever killed anyone was the last one.
Some are now suggesting that Arday was the victim, and the people who drew attention to his lies, the villains. Ibram X. Kendi suggests that Arday might even be vindicated after a full accounting of the allegations against him. (Keep in mind that in addition to his straightforward acts of fabrication and plagiarism, always of less powerful academics, he claimed to have taken part in a British documentary series that preceded his birth.) And the hapless Good Law Project, which persuaded dozens of Cambridge bigwigs to rally behind Arday and dismiss his critics as racists, has issued an open letter calling for an investigation of “the press.” The media’s alleged crime: writing about this extraordinary case of a habitual liar’s appointment to a distinguished academic post, rather than letting the liar keep embarrassing himself and his institution. “Reasonable public interest” in the case had dissipated, the letter says, yet the press kept digging. Arday’s death was, it says, the “direct, foreseeable and foreseen result of press harassment.”
A Buddhist proverb says that when a wise man points at the moon, the fool stares at his finger. The media were unrelenting, but con-man stories are always popular, and the bigger the victim, the better. The press’s obsession was in proportion with the outlandishness of the lies told by Arday and on his behalf, and with public interest in the failures they revealed. Those failures were intellectual, institutional, and even legal. Arday called the cops on an academic who had asked him hostile questions, and he instructed a law firm to send a threatening letter to a reporter who did the same. The focus on those who pointed out Arday’s shortcomings, rather than on Arday himself and those who abetted his rise, is a clear sign that lessons from this miserable episode remain unlearned. The people responsible for it may repeat their errors and, in some cases, commit appalling new ones. (Kendi compares Arday’s treatment to a “lynching.” This analogy is tenable only if you think lynching means harshly criticizing people for actual transgressions, rather than summarily murdering them for no reason at all.)
Some lies are so preposterous that intelligent people who believe them bear some responsibility for being taken in. And they are outright guilty for repeating the lies and urging others to believe them. This is obviously so in Arday’s case. The lies depended on willful credulity, as well as amplification by other professors, including Cambridge’s Hilary Cremin, who went on the BBC and told Arday that “you are the best in the world, in terms of the research that you do.” Reviewers gushed over his books and pronounced them moving, “brave,” and “insightful.” Defenders did begin to distance themselves when the lies became even more lurid and inexplicable, as with the claims that a masked man invisible to security cameras had menaced Arday with a knife and that someone had sent him the head of a pig, which he disposed of rather than preserved as evidence. The trajectory of his deception seems to have been from tragedy (a man carried away with lies and too compulsive to stop telling them) to farce (once the lies became ridiculous enough that only a complicit person could believe them) and finally back to tragedy on Friday. Arday’s colleagues, his editors, and the people who knew he was a fraud but said nothing have absorbed some ridicule for their role in hiring and publishing him. But to date, I have seen no evidence that they have considered their complicity, let alone repaired the damage to their institutions by explaining their error or, better yet, just resigning.
They elevated Arday, a fragile and disturbed person, into a position where his fragility would be tested and he would be shattered. Even if the Cambridge Faculty of Education’s standards were so low that his inadequacies would remain unremarked there, he was a fellow of a Cambridge college with real scholars who would eventually be indignant upon realizing that their new colleague’s scholarship consisted of copy-paste jobs, semiliterate nonsense, and fan notes on his favorite 1990s Brit-pop. Did Arday’s allies think no one would notice? That those who noticed would be forever intimidated into polite silence? That drinking sherry in the common room of Jesus College would be a pleasant experience for Arday himself as he waited to be found out? Those who placed Arday in that situation were cruel and heartless. They may as well have taken a skin-and-bones Make-A-Wish kid, told him that he could fly, and shot him out of a cannon. The journalists were not the ones who stuffed Arday into the cannon and lit the fuse. They were gravity.
In The Wild Duck, Ibsen’s main villain is Gregers, the crusading moralist who makes it his mission to “rescue” the characters from their sustaining life-lies and help them and those who respect them see their deficiencies. The Gregers in this case is Nathan Cofnas, a philosopher with an abiding interest in race and a particular curiosity about the supposed mental deficiencies of Black people. Cofnas’s views on race science (he believes that very few Black people are cognitively equipped to be employed at a “meritocratic” university) led him to be run out of Cambridge in 2024, just as Arday was being appointed to one of the university’s most prestigious chairs. Cambridge’s failure to vet this appointment left an opening for Cofnas, smarting from his own dismissal, to take on the unsavory task of assembling a dossier on Arday’s work. The results were so galling that morbid curiosity drove others to scrutinize everything else about Arday, including his implausible claims that he secretly raised large sums for charity and was among the world’s greatest long-distance runners.
Dr. Relling calls Gregers’s urge to disabuse and expose “an acute attack of integrity,” and he warns that going cold turkey off livsløgn will not end well for patients or others. (Other Ibsen plays are relevant here too: In some, the collapse of illusions afflicts whole towns, not just a few of their members.) The difference between Gregers and Cofnas seems to be that the latter, perhaps as a result of his being scorned by Cambridge, has no affection for the people whose life-lies he methodically destroyed. Cofnas recently told the podcaster Winston Marshall that “talking about” race “makes people feel bad, and there are a lot of things that are true that make people feel bad that we don’t need to talk about.” But the subversion of academic standards, at what Cofnas perceives as his own expense, demanded action. The result will be good for academia, Cofnas insists, a far better outcome than preserving the good feelings that went along with silence.
In Ibsen, when Gregers forces integrity on a self-deluded character, that character’s daughter decides to kill herself. Gregers sounds most like Cofnas in the final scene. He is confident that her death, however horrible, will “set free all that is noble” in those who partook in the life-lie as they see life for what it is. Life sustained by delusion “is not worth living,” Gregers says. But he knows the cost of being an odious truth teller. “I am glad that my destiny is what it is,” he tells Relling: “to be the thirteenth at table,” the guest who everyone wishes would stop showing up, because he brings misfortune to any dinner he attends.
Arday was hired to teach social science. A terminal irony is that his main contribution to that body of knowledge will be as a case study, about a community that elevated a flawed man to a position exalted beyond his ability, without knowing or caring that they were actually offering him as a human sacrifice.

Over the past nine years, Donald Trump has returned again and again to the concept of steam power. He loves the way that steam propels fighter jets off the decks of aircraft carriers, and he laments that the Navy has pivoted to electromagnetic launchers in its new ships. “That beautiful scene,” he rhapsodized at a rally in 2023: “That steam goes off, and that plane gets thrown the hell off; the power, beautiful. And it’s cheap!”
By The Guardian’s accounting, Trump has spoken publicly about these steam catapults every year since 2017, when he claimed to have told the crew of the USS Gerald Ford that they’d be “going to goddamned steam.” The Gerald Ford is the only one of the Navy’s 11 operational aircraft carriers that’s not currently equipped with steam catapults. Instead, it uses the more modern Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS), which runs on electricity from the vessel’s two nuclear reactors. Trump’s wish for the Gerald Ford to return to steam was never fulfilled; the ship was already the water. Until last week, future ships were set to use electromagnetic propulsion too. But on Thursday, Trump ordered one of the Navy’s planned carriers, the USS Doris Miller, to be outfitted with steam catapults instead.
It’s a potential logistical nightmare. Although the ship isn’t expected to be assembled until later this year, its parts are already under construction. Experts have said that returning to steam power at this stage in the ship’s development could dramatically increase the cost to taxpayers and delay the building process. The Doris Miller won’t be completed until the mid-2030s, and a future administration may backpedal. But the fact that the president remains so dedicated to the idea says something about his commitment to aesthetics over strategy—and to remaking the military according to his personal preferences.
Trump’s order gives officials 60 days to figure out the details, but plans for the Doris Miller are already under way. General Atomics, the contractor responsible for the ship’s EMALS system, released a statement explaining that “nearly 50 percent of production” is complete and warning that “changing course now would introduce significant cost, schedule and integration risks.” Electrical infrastructure can’t be easily swapped for steam once a ship’s layout has been mapped. Areas on the Doris Miller that might have housed pipes have been designated for other things. Bryan Clark, a naval analyst at the Hudson Institute, told me that such an extreme redesign of the ship’s interior could cost the Navy billions of dollars.
EMALS isn’t perfect. Its development was lengthy, even by the Navy’s standards; the Gerald Ford, on which it debuted, cost the U.S. billions of dollars more than expected. But the investment has now been made. EMALS has been successfully launching planes for years. Part of Trump’s somewhat-opaque argument against the new system is that it’s a fancy, unnecessarily complex replacement for the old-fashioned way of doing things. “Digital,” he said in 2017, is “very complicated. You have to be Albert Einstein to figure it out.” Last month, he claimed to have been told that only “geniuses” from MIT could work on it.
Trump is right to suggest that when it comes to military technology, flashier doesn’t always mean better. After all, Iran’s cheap drones have consistently challenged the far richer and better-equipped United States. But steam isn’t as efficient as he thinks. Today, Clark told me, electromagnetism is a more reliable way to get a plane into the air, requiring fewer repairs in the aggregate. This is one reason that, despite the cost of developing EMALS, Trump’s claim that steam is a “cheap” alternative doesn’t necessarily hold up; a ship that requires fewer repairs may require fewer taxpayer dollars in the long run.
The president hasn’t explained why he chose to make such a cumbersome change at this particular moment. Other, more pressing issues could likely use his attention: A shortage of certain kinds of munition, for example, has put the U.S. at a disadvantage in the war with Iran. And the Navy has lately been facing criticism over the conditions aboard another carrier, the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been deployed in the Middle East for almost nine months. Sailors have reported food shortages, degraded living conditions, and mental-health struggles. The president dismissed CNN’s report about conditions on the ship as “fake news,” but Admiral Brad Cooper, who’s overseeing the war in Iran, acknowledged the mental-health concerns on Sunday. The USS George Washington is now set to relieve the carrier.
Trump’s recurring fascination with steam reflects his broad interest in how things should look rather than how things should work. He’s reportedly considering asking the Navy to make another design change: shifting the command center on new aircraft carriers farther forward so that the ships can look more like World War II–era vessels. The current placement of the command center at the back of the ships “was done for efficiency and safety,” three current and former U.S. officials told The Washington Post. In December, Trump announced the development of a new class of battleship, to be built according to his own preferences. He wants it bigger and more attractive, and has even given it his own name—the “Trump class.” (Earlier this month, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the new ships could cost Americans about $275 billion in all.) “I am a very aesthetic person,” Trump said at the time.
That’s one way to put it. Since returning to office, he’s demolished the White House’s East Wing to build a gilded ballroom, paved over the Rose Garden, and planned to put an imperial arch near the Lincoln Memorial. The president is apparently on a mission to align American institutions with his own taste—and to bulldoze what’s already been built to do so. The “beautiful scene” of a steam catapult may please Trump in much the same way that these other forays into design and architecture do. But the U.S. is at war. It’s probably not the best time to delegate the Navy’s resources to a vanity project.

Valve just leaked several new videos showing the Steam Frame’s unboxing, setup process, and various accessories. The videos apparently appeared on the ARM Steam client following an update, but they were “quickly pulled after that,” according to the Steam Hardware Updates account on X.
Watch Valve set up the Steam Frame in its own leaked videos
Leaked demonstrations show how to use the Steam Frame with its wireless dongle and accessories.
The Steam Frame is Valve’s virtual-reality headset that can stream games from a PC or play them locally. Valve first took the wraps off the headset last year, and it offers LCD screens with 2160 x 2160 resolution per eye, a Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 chip, and an up to 110-degree field of view. Manyavar is as much a technology and data company as it is an ethnic wear brand, claimed Vedant Modi, the company’s chief revenue officer. Speaking at a fireside chat at the seventh edition of Inc42’s D2C & Retail Summit in Gurugram, Modi cited several examples of how the brand leveraged advanced data analytics and AI to scale to over ₹1,000 Cr in revenue with margins exceeding 65%. One of the most lucid examples came when moderator Praharsh Chandra, cofounder and CBO of logistics firm Shadowfax, asked him to describe how the company uses data to drive decision-making. “Our taste as founders does not matter. So, that was the biggest learning we had... a lot of people obsess over their own taste. If you ask a designer if they have a great collection, they will say it’s great, and if no one bought the collection, they will say the market hasn’t evolved yet. For us, the biggest insight was: how can we look at a product from a data aspect?” said Modi. He explained that Manyavar doesn’t use traditional colour names like blue or black, instead breaking every garment down into a collection of subcategories such as colour, texture, fabric, design type, and numeric codes designating each option within the subcategory. This, in turn, is used to automate store-level inventory allocation based on data about consumer trends. “South Delhi and Karol Bagh behave very differently because very different sets of customers are walking into our stores. Even within Delhi, only 35% of our inventory from a design angle would be common between these two locations,” said Modi, adding that 70-75% of decisions are taken by algorithms, and the remaining edge cases are taken by AI. He added that Manyavar aims to sell through 90% of the inventory it supplies to any store. Here, too, automation and data-driven algorithms are crucial to achieving this critical performance metric. “Our system automatically starts to understand if a product is doing well somewhere, but not elsewhere, and will automatically send it from one store to another,” he said. While this clears a further 7% of inventory, the remainder is typically donated as dead stock, which enables the brand to maintain its premium pricing without resorting to discounting. Manyavar has also taken two decades’ worth of historical data, almost 85 Cr data points, and uploaded it to a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that connects to its deeper AI systems, Modi noted. Modi said that the brand's overall growth was increasingly being driven by their ability to turn data into decisions — from product design and inventory allocation to store-level performance. By combining granular data, automation and AI, the brand is reducing guesswork, improving sell-through and protecting margins, showing how technology can become a core competitive advantage in traditional retail.

The U.S. debt tops a record-shattering $40 trillion. Yes, with a T.
The federal debt topped $40 trillion Wednesday, a new high-water mark for red ink that shows no sign of receding.
The news, reported by the Treasury Department in its daily financial update, comes just five months after the debt surpassed $39 trillion. The government continues to pile up debt at a rapid clip, as spending outstrips revenue by more than $2 trillion a year.
"Our current fiscal trajectory is plainly unsustainable, and that's the best-case scenario," said Margaret Spellings, president of the Bipartisan Policy Center. "Even in the rosiest scenarios, we're speeding toward a cliff and refusing to turn the wheel."
The deficit widened further after the Supreme Court struck down many of President Trump's tariffs, forcing the Treasury to refund more than $100 billion in import taxes that were collected illegally.
Government spending continues to surge
The administration sought to blame the ballooning deficit on Democrats.
"President Trump pledged to clean up Joe Biden's fiscal mismanagement," White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement. "That's why the Trump administration has been focused on slashing waste, fraud, and abuse in federal spending while accelerating economic growth to get America's debt-to-GDP ratio trending in the right direction again."
Government revenues have grown 3% this fiscal year — but spending has grown even faster. And the debt-to-GDP ratio has worsened since Trump returned to the White House.
The government is spending more than a trillion dollars a year just to pay interest on the mounting debt. Interest is now the government's second biggest expense, trailing only Social Security.
Interest costs in the first ten months of this fiscal year were 15% higher than they were in the same period a year ago. That reflects not only the growing debt but also the higher interest rates that investors are now demanding in order to keep lending the government money.
Bond markets are reacting
The yield on 30-year Treasuries reached a 19-year high this week. That raises borrowing costs for everyone else, since mortgage rates and other interest rates often follow long-term Treasuries.
The average rate on a 30-year mortgage neared 6.7% last week, according to Freddie Mac.
"Federal debt is already raising the cost of living and choking out other spending and investment, threatening our economy and Americans' long-term prosperity," Spellings said.
So far, Congress has shown little appetite for tacking the problem.
"$40 trillion should be a wake up call. But neither Congress nor the president have a credible plan to stop it from growing," said Carolyn Bourdeaux, executive director of Concord Action, a group that advocates for fiscal responsibility. "We owe the next generation better than this crushing debt and another hollow promise that someone else will deal with it later."

Hadjar to miss Dutch Grand Prix with wrist injury
- Published
Red Bull's Isack Hadjar will miss this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix after injuring his wrist during the summer break.
The Frenchman will be replaced by New Zealander Liam Lawson, who normally races for Red Bull's second team Racing Bulls.
Lawson's replacement will be Japan's Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull's reserve driver, who was dropped from the leading team at the end of last season.
Hadjar is understood to have broken his wrist while boxing.
Lawson's promotion, albeit temporary, is an opportunity for him to atone for a disappointing two races for Red Bull at the start of the 2025 season.
Lawson had been due to race alongside Max Verstappen for all of last year, but was demoted to Racing Bulls after the first two grands prix following two lacklustre performances.
Red Bull have had a difficult first half of 2026, with four-time world champion Verstappen yet to win a race.
The Dutchman finished 2025 just two points behind world champion Lando Norris of McLaren after an impressive revival in the second half of the season in which he made up more than 100 points on the championship lead.
Verstappen's best results so far this year are second places in the Austrian and Hungarian Grands Prix.
Verstappen races at his home grand prix for the final time this weekend - the event at seaside town Zandvoort will drop off the calendar after this season because organisers are no longer able to make it financially viable.

Takaya Awata went from a college dropout to a billionaire selling bowls of chewy udon noodles across Japan. Now, he’s betting the humble dish can become a global fast-food category alongside burgers, chicken and pizza, with the U.S. at the center of Toridoll Holdings’ overseas ambitions.
“We want udon to become one of those major global categories,” Awata, 64, said in an interview at Toridoll’s headquarters in Tokyo. The founder and chief executive officer wants Toridoll, with almost ¥280 billion ($1.8 billion) in annual revenue, to join the trillion-yen ranks of the world’s largest fast-food chains, primarily by growing its flagship Marugame Udon brand.
The challenge is scaling up the business and finding a way to win over consumers unfamiliar with a staple of no-frills Japanese cuisine. Unlike the better-known, thinner and yellowish ramen noodles typically served up in a seasoned bouillon, udon are thick, chewy white noodles that swim in a much simpler broth.

Enough new coalmining projects were proposed last year to increase global supplies by 2.5bn tonnes a year, an increase of 11% from the year before, even as demand for coal plateaus, according to a new report.
Global Energy Monitor, an NGO, found that India ignited a rise in new coalmine proposals in 2025 despite a global slowdown in the number of mine openings because of falling demand for the fossil fuel.
The increase was driven almost entirely by the states of Jharkhand and Odisha, which doubled their proposals for new coalmines in line with an ambitious plan from India’s ministry of coal to increase the country’s output.
India plans to increase its coal production by nearly 100m tonnes to 1.15bn tonnes in the 2025-26 fiscal year to help meet the country’s rising demand for electricity to support economic growth and contend with heatwaves, which have become more severe and more frequent because of the climate crisis.
The planned increases come despite signs that the world is beginning to turn its back on coal in favour of renewable electricity, Global Energy Monitor said.
Coalmine proposals slowed in the years after the Covid-19 pandemic but have begun to climb again, raising concerns that mining could increase in the future despite a slowdown in the number of new facilities.
The startup of new coalmining projects has fallen steadily in recent years, according to the Global Energy Monitor’s latest report.
It found that enough new coalmines to produce about 113m tonnes each year began operations last year, down by 40% from 2024, which was already the lowest annual total in a decade.
This was largely owing to a slowdown in new mines in China and Australia, which fell by 44% and 96% respectively.
Global Energy Monitor warned that India’s rise in new mine proposals was at odds with the slowdown in global coal demand predicted by the International Energy Agency for the end of the decade.
Wind and solar power surpassed coal generation in the global electricity mix for the first time last year, according to a separate report from energy thinktank Ember, in a “milestone moment” for climate action.
China and India were largely responsible for the rise in renewables, according to the Ember report, while the US and Europe continued to rely more heavily on fossil fuels.
Tiffany Means, a senior researcher at Global Energy Monitor and co-author of the report said: “The economic rationale for expanding coalmining becomes progressively weaker as low-cost clean energy continues to displace coal.
“Rather than locking in decades of additional coal production, governments have an opportunity to cancel projects that remain in the development pipeline before they advance to construction.”

Social media giant Meta has reportedly begun taking steps to address concerns raised by the Central government over child sexual abuse material (CSAM), deepfakes, unlabelled AI-generated content, among others, hosted on its platform following several rounds of discussions with officials. As per a report by PTI, this comes after discussions between the social media major and the Central government over the former's handling of CSAM, with the government pressing the company to strengthen its identification and removal of unlawful material. Citing sources, the report added that Centre has told Meta that CSAM violates Indian law and that the company could lose safe-harbour protection if it fails to meet its legal obligations. Meta’s global team has also explained how its algorithms and other systems operate and outlined measures it plans to introduce in response to the government’s concerns. Some of the problems, officials acknowledged, require “judgment calls and tweaks”. As per a report by PTI, the Centre has sought to draw a distinction between regulation and censorship. As per government sources, its aim is to ensure that platforms comply with Indian law and limit the harms arising from social media, rather than restrict legitimate coverage. “The message has gone home,” the sources were quoted as saying by PTI. One unresolved issue is the persistence of harmful AI-generated material. The government has questioned why such content can reappear after being flagged, and why AI-generated videos without appropriate labels remain accessible on Meta’s platforms. In an earlier meeting, officials also pressed Meta to increase human oversight of content moderation, particularly for Indian languages and material shaped by local cultural and social contexts. The government is separately examining WhatsApp’s proposed username feature. Officials said the issue is broader than WhatsApp and could have implications for other messaging services. The latest development marks another stage in the Centre’s scrutiny of social media intermediaries. Earlier this month, the company’s global team landed in India after MeitY summoned its global public-policy leadership over Facebook’s temporary removal of a video posted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The video, posted on July 23 amid student protests over alleged paper leaks and irregularities in NEET examinations, was PM Modi’s first address to students during the protests. Facebook restored it several hours later, attributing the removal to an error in its content-moderation systems. The episode triggered a series of discussions between Meta and the Centre, eventually leading to an apology from the company. While Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan met with the Centre over the issue, government sources told PTI that CEO Mark Zuckerberg had also apologised over the broader content-moderation lapses, including CSAM and deepfakes Meanwhile, Elon Musk-owned X will have to comply with Indian law even as it rolls out a new policy to make government requests for content takedowns public, a government official said, as per PTI report. This comes after Musk said X had introduced a new algorithm under which “any censorship required by the governments is now clearly visible”. The Centre, however, has made clear that the policy will not override India’s legal requirements.

Demand for artificially generated smut is surging. But the quality of the visual content being created and shared—like on companion apps, where adult performers are selling their likeness to give fans a 24/7 experience, WIRED reported in March—isn’t exactly movie-level caliber.
Rogue Studio, a cinematic AI-generator platform built around adult visual storytelling, is trying to change that. Launching today, the studio, which bills itself as a “playground for creative ethical mischief,” plans to deliver industry-level video production without creative and sexual restrictions. Its marquee product is Rogue 1.0, an AI video-generation tool for making uncensored adult content that is comparable to other pro-level models Hollywood is using.
“There really isn’t a place for a sophisticated creator to go make content that’s rated R. Either they go to these skeezy NSFW sites that are built on outdated open-source tech, or they try to do high-quality stuff but they’re censored up the gills,” a Rogue Studio cofounder, who goes by Mr. Rogue, tells WIRED. “It’s a very fine line between being a sophisticated platform for adults versus becoming just a porn site. And we do not want the latter. We want to do what HBO did for television.”
Rogue, which has subscription tiers ranging from $29 to $299, offers all the safe-for-work frontier models within its system—similar to Higgsfield, it includes NanoBanana, Seedance, Kling 2.0, and others—in addition to its own proprietary models for generating adult-oriented images and video. Using the platform, you can employ multiple elements from several different AI-generator models when drumming up ideas.
Let’s say you have a concept for a freaky sci-fi horror short. You could potentially start ideating on a zombie character using Midjourney, then use Rogue’s AI tools to add more high-definition uncensored features to the character.
According to its terms of service, Rogue prohibits user-generated images or videos for training, and it strictly forbids the creation or distribution of nonconsensual deepfakes, child sexual abuse material, unauthorized depictions of public figures, and other illegal or abusive imagery.
In an effort to prevent bad actors from using the platform to make these prohibited visuals, Rogue has three layers of human moderation. The first is at the prompt level, which searches for keywords and flags them for possible account suspension if it is determined that there is clear illegal intent. The next layer is inside the system, called the intention layer. Bad actors might try to outsmart moderators by slightly misspelling a real actor’s name to generate a deepfake image, so moderators will reread the prompt to assess the user’s intent. The final layer analyzes the image or video created before it is shared with the user. For example, if a user prompts “famous blonde singer” and the image generated looks like Taylor Swift, the image won’t get delivered.
Mr. Rogue tells WIRED that he and his fellow cofounder, both of whom are movie producers, have decided not to disclose their names because of the “real risk” involved in being associated with creating erotic-themed work. “Because of the climate right now in Hollywood and working in AI, you have got to be very careful,” Mr. Rogue says. (WIRED verified that the pair of founders do, in fact, work in Hollywood; they have produced movies with a combined box office of over $2 billion.)
In the wake of the 2023 Hollywood strikes, where labor unions fought to secure guardrails against the unapproved digital likenesses of actors appearing in films and TV, leading studios have been assessing ways to incorporate AI into productions with the goal of lowering expenses.
The friction has led to AI being seen as unfavorable and has created a stigma around it. Rogue’s cofounders know this but don’t want to shy away from the tech’s creative potential.
The reality is that AI is no longer a distant possibility for Hollywood. Computers are already working behind the scenes to animate preproduction storyboards and create a more efficient editing process, such as polishing VFX effects and audio. Netflix recently revealed that 300 of its shows use generative AI. The integration is happening at a scale bigger than many viewers realize, Matt Belloni, a founding partner at Puck who covers the business of Hollywood, told WIRED earlier this month.
Since 2000, sex scenes in movies have declined by 40 percent, according to a 2023 study conducted by The Economist. But recent releases suggest that the industry may be turning a corner. “Movies are getting horny again,” one film critic who specializes in erotic thrillers told the BBC. According to a recent survey from entertainment research firm Luminate, despite an overall backlash against AI in Hollywood, one-third of consumers now feel indifferent toward the use of AI in production across all areas, except when it comes to writing and acting.
Rogue is making a bet that the continued adoption of AI tools—particularly ones focused on delivering premium visuals—could potentially supercharge that experience for viewers to the point where the quality of a performer’s delivery isn’t determined by whether it is AI or not, the cofounder says.
“We’re so used to uncensored meaning you get a fraction of the quality. Right now too much of the art form is being lost.”

For the fourth time in four years, Peacock has raised its prices.
The Select plan, which has ads and doesn’t include sports, movies, or Peacock originals, went from $8/month to $9/month. The monthly fee for the standard ad plan (Premium) went from $11/month to $13/month, and the ad-free plan (Premium Plus) went from $17/month to $20/month. Annual pricing, as previously, offers 12 months for the price of 10 months.
Peacock’s previous price hike was in July 2025, when the middle tier (with ads) went from $8/month to $11/month, and the ad-free plan increased from $14 to $17. Peacock also raised prices in July 2024 and August 2023. NBCUniversal launched the service in 2020.
The streaming service turned its first quarterly profit in Q2 2026 with $189 million in adjusted EBITDA. During that quarter, Peacock saw revenue from subscriptions increase over 50 percent and advertising revenue rise nearly 70 percent, Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said during a call with investors in July, according to a transcript.
Peacock also gained 2 million subscribers in Q2 and now has 48 million.
But just because Peacock is now profitable, it can’t necessarily expect the same level of success in upcoming quarters.
In the call with investors, Comcast co-CEO Michael Cavanagh said he expects Peacock’s profitability to improve on an annual basis but vary from quarter to quarter, with profits depending on what content, such as sporting events and shows, debuts each quarter.
NBCUniversal must also keep Peacock profitable amid big, ongoing spending on live events, including an 11-year deal under which the company will pay $2.5 billion a year to air about 50 NBA games exclusively on Peacock, along with distribution rights for NBCU’s other distribution platforms, including broadcast channels. The company has made other large investments in sporting events, including Sunday Night Football and the Premier League.
Higher prices could theoretically help fund more programming. But with Peacock only recently becoming profitable, it’s possible that the annual price hikes could continue being the norm.

A video of Prime Minister Narendra Modi moving around a stage greeting people while the national anthem plays in the background is viral on social media, with users claiming that the Prime Minister was being disrespectful to the anthem.
An user on Facebook, Kumar Raj, shared the purported video on August 15, Independance Day, with Modi circled out. The post has garnered 2.3 million views. It was shared around 14,000 times and has received 30,500 reactions.
Activist Piyush Manush shared the same video on Facebook, which was viewed over 76,000 times.
Several X users also amplified the viral video, amplifying the same claim.
Fact Check
A keyframe in the viral video showed a screen placed on the podium which mentioned the location of the event as Jasauli Kharag, located in Bihar’s Siwan city. The date mentioned was June 20, 2025.
A relevant keyword search led us to the original video uploaded from the Prime Minister’s official YouTube channel. In this video dated June 21, 2025, Modi, seen in the same attire as the viral video, walked onto a stage while he was being introduced by the speaker. Amid cheers from the audience, he waved to them and shook hands with other dignitaries present on the stage. At no point can the national anthem be heard playing in the clip.
Thus, the claim that Prime Minister Narendra Modi disrespected the national anthem by walking around the stage while it played is misleading. The original video shows Modi being introduced by the speaker and waving to a cheering audience, with no national anthem playing in the clip. The anthem heard in the viral version was added later to the original video, altering the context of the footage to amplify a false claim.

The federal agency tasked with studying ways to improve America’s outstandingly poor healthcare system is “on the brink,” experts warn. The Trump administration has cut its staff by 75 percent, canceled its grants en masse, and is refusing to spend tens of millions of dollars appropriated by Congress.
Whether the agency “will survive the second Trump administration is an open question,” health policy experts Aaron Carroll and David Atkins wrote in an opinion piece published today in the Annals of Internal Medicine.
The agency in question is the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), which has focused on ways to improve patient safety, healthcare quality, care delivery, and new technologies and practices since the 1990s. In the past, “Republican leaders recognized that health care disparities were fundamental quality problems,” Carroll and Atkins wrote. But recently, disparities in care have become partisan issues.
During Trump’s second term, DOGE cuts led to the firing or retirement of an estimated 75 percent of the AHRQ’s staff. In July, AHRQ abruptly sent grant cancellation letters to around 150 researchers. More than 100 research grants collectively worth over $250 million have been canceled. Although Congress appropriated $345 million for the 2026 fiscal year, much of it has gone unspent, with only $15 million going to grants so far. As such, scientists across over 30 states have halted research, laid off staff, shut down programs, and stopped pursuing new lines of research.
“Profound concern”
In addition to the losses in data and research findings, Carroll and Atkins lament the loss to the scientific community. “This is what it looks like when we stop developing the next generation of health services researchers.” Reversing the damage is doable, but will be difficult, they write, while calling on Congress to act.

In July, an Alt News post about the upcoming Bollywood film ‘Chauhaan’ was removed twice by Instagram. The post survived when we shared it the third time, but only after two references to Burhan Wani were removed. The episode offers a glimpse into the opaque manner in which content restrictions are being enforced on Instagram in India, and raises key questions amid growing concerns over censorship on the platform.
The original post was a carousel based on an Alt News analysis of the teaser of ‘Chauhaan’ starring Ajay Devgn. The 2.24-minute video shows its protagonist dismissing pellet guns as an ineffective crowd-control measure causing only “limited damage”. This stands in stark contrast to the documented reality in Kashmir, where pellet guns have killed scores, and blinded or permanently disabled thousands. The teaser sparked an online backlash for trivialising violence as entertainment, pairing it with upbeat music. The story can be read here.
Alt News first uploaded the carousel on July 1. Instagram restricted the post within minutes. Since the carousel contained visuals of pellet injuries, Alt News initially suspected that these images might have triggered the removal. The carousel was therefore modified, with some of the visuals changed, and uploaded again.
Instagram removed the second version as well.
Alt News then removed two references to Burhan Wani on two slides in the carousel and uploaded it for a third time. This version was allowed to remain online.
The sequence raises the possibility that the use of Burhan Wani’s name itself may be restricted on Instagram in India — an apparent moderation measure that has not been publicly announced by either Meta or the Indian government.
A search for “Burhan Wani” on Instagram currently yields no results.
What makes the episode particularly striking is that Instagram never explicitly told Alt News why the post was being removed. The platform’s notifications stated that the action had been carried out “through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements” and cited India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.
The notification did not identify the specific legal requirement behind the action, the government order on the basis of which the post had been restricted, or the particular element of the post that had triggered the removal — a point that multiple users affected by the government-ordered censorship frenzy has flagged over the past weeks.
An Opaque Moderation System that Leaves Users Guessing
As for us, Alt News had to figure it out through trial and error. This raises the question — Why should a user have to go through this process to find out why their post has been restricted? If a particular name, word or image is prohibited under a legal order, why does the notification not clearly state so? A user should not have to repeatedly alter and repost content, guessing what may have triggered a platform’s moderation system.
The opacity is particularly concerning because the platform appears to know what triggered the restriction. Its automated system identified the content and removed it within minutes, yet the user is given no meaningful explanation for the action. Instead, the notification offers only a generic reference to an automated system and “legal requirements”.
Besides, a blanket restriction on a name such as “Burhan Wani” makes little sense because names can occur in entirely unrelated contexts. Other people may share the same name, while legitimate references, including news reports, historical discussions or fact checks, could be caught by the same restriction.
Alt News emailed Meta spokespersons asking when the apparent moderation rule relating to Burhan Wani was implemented, why it was enforced without public notification, why users were not clearly informed about the reason for the restriction, and what other names or keywords may be subject to similar restrictions. The company has not responded.
Interestingly, we found that a similar restriction may be in place for ‘Monu Manesar’ was well. A search with these terms throws up the same response. Mohit Yadav alias Monu Manesar, a controversial ‘gau rakshak’ associated with the Bajrang Dal, has been accused in several cases linked to vigilantism and communal violence. He was arrested in 2023 in connection with the alleged abduction and murder of Nasir and Junaid, two Muslim men from Haryana. He has denied the allegations against him.
The apparent restriction comes amid a wider and increasingly opaque censorship controversy surrounding Instagram in India. A recent investigation by The Indian Express found that from March to July 2026, the government sent 1.95 lakh blocking orders to Meta, or one every minute on an average. Over 1 lakh of these were for Instagram.
The Burhan Wani episode illustrates another dimension of this opacity. If the name is itself subject to an undisclosed moderation rule, users have no way of knowing this in advance, or of understanding why content that merely mentions him is being restricted.
And even though the sequence strongly suggests that the references to Burhan Wani triggered the removals, this remains an inference. Instagram has not confirmed that this was the reason.
Fact-Check Posts Restricted
Posts related to an Alt News fact check were restricted in July 2026 on both Faecebook and Instagram.
The report looked at false claims about an old video that showed armed Nihangs clashing with police and breaching barricades. It was being circulated as ‘Khalistanis’ joining the Cockroach Janta Party protests at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar. In reality, the video was from June 25, 2026, nearly a month before the CJP protests, and showed Nihangs from Punjab marching toward Uttarakhand during a protest. The story can be read here.
Our social media posts on the fact check were restricted in India by both the platforms. And we do not know why.
Readers should note that a click on the ‘How we made this decision’ tab does not bring about any clarity. The response only states, “We are legally required to restrict access to your post in certain locations. We have taken this action based on a local legal requirement.”

Stomach pain is one of the most common symptoms people experience. It can range from mild discomfort caused by indigestion or gas, to severe pain caused by conditions such as appendicitis, gallstones, pancreatitis or intestinal obstruction.
Doctors say the site, severity, onset, duration and progression of the pain, along with other symptoms, can provide important clues about its cause. However, the intensity of pain alone does not always indicate how serious the underlying problem is.
“Some people with a serious condition may have only mild discomfort, while others with a less serious problem may experience severe pain,” says S. Jennie, professor, department of general Medicine, SRM Medical College Hospital and Research Centre, Chennai.
Where it hurts
The location of abdominal pain can sometimes point to the organ involved. Burning or discomfort in the upper abdomen or lower chest may occur with acid-peptic disorders. Pain in the right upper abdomen, particularly after meals, can occur with gallbladder disease. Severe upper abdominal pain that radiates to the back may be seen in pancreatitis.
Pain that begins around the navel and later moves to the lower right side may occur with appendicitis. Pain in the lower abdomen or side may also occur with kidney stones.
However, these patterns are only clues and should not be used for self-diagnosis, says Arul Prakash, gastroenterologist, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai. “It is difficult to differentiate between a minor and major problem based only on pain,” he says.
Mild, short-lived pain that improves after passing stools or gas, resting or drinking fluids is generally less concerning. In contrast, sudden, severe, localised, persistent or progressively worsening pain should be assessed by a doctor.
Watch for warning signs
The symptoms accompanying abdominal pain often provide a better indication of urgency than the pain alone. Persistent vomiting can cause dehydration and may also occur with intestinal obstruction. Fever may suggest infection or inflammation.
Blood in vomit or stools should never be ignored. Black, tar-like stools or coffee-ground-like vomit can indicate bleeding in the digestive tract. Severe diarrhoea, particularly with high fever, severe pain or blood in stools, also requires medical assessment.
Increasing abdominal swelling, especially when accompanied by vomiting or an inability to pass stools or gas, can indicate bowel obstruction. Yellowing of the eyes or skin may point to a problem involving the liver, gallbladder or bile ducts.
The SHARP warning signs
Dr. Jennie suggests remembering the SHARP warning signs: sudden or severe pain; associated symptoms such as vomiting, fever, bleeding, jaundice or confusion; advanced age, particularly with chronic illnesses; rigidity or marked tenderness of the abdomen; and pain during pregnancy or after surgery.
Chest pain or difficulty breathing along with upper abdominal pain also warrants urgent assessment, as some heart conditions can mimic abdominal discomfort. Dr. Arul Prakash notes that patients have occasionally mistaken heart attack symptoms for acidity and treated themselves with over-the-counter medicines.
Avoid self-treatment
A common mistake is to assume that every episode of abdominal pain is due to ‘gas’ or acidity. Repeatedly taking medicines without establishing the cause can delay diagnosis.
Painkillers such as ibuprofen, diclofenac and aspirin can irritate the stomach and increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding in susceptible people. They should not be taken casually for unexplained abdominal pain.
An antacid may provide temporary relief for occasional, familiar acidity or heartburn. But symptoms that persist for several days, keep returning or become progressively worse need medical evaluation. Antibiotics should also not be started without medical advice, particularly for diarrhoea, as many common gastrointestinal infections are viral and do not require them.
Children, older adults and pregnant women need particular caution. Children may have difficulty describing their symptoms, while older adults can have serious abdominal conditions with relatively mild or atypical pain. During pregnancy, abdominal pain may have benign causes but can also indicate pregnancy-related or surgical emergencies.
People with previous abdominal surgery, gallstones, inflammatory bowel disease or chronic liver, kidney or other major illnesses should also seek medical advice sooner when they develop new or unusual pain.
Doctors say, is not to judge abdominal pain only by how much it hurts. A new, persistent or worsening pain, particularly when accompanied by warning signs, should not be dismissed as acidity or gas.

China censors public mourning as it holds former premier's funeral
- Published
Flags at government sites are flying at half-mast and security vehicles are parked in the heart of Beijing, as China mourns former Premier Zhu Rongji.
Zhu died of an illness last week at 97, and will be cremated at a funeral in Beijing on Tuesday. There has not been footage from the ceremony, which is being kept low-key.
Zhu, who served as China's premier from 1998 to 2003, is remembered as one of the country's most important economic reformers.
While hailing the late premier as a "loyal" party member, the Chinese state is also wary that public mourning for his era of reform can easily turn into veiled criticisms of the current government, under Xi Jinping.
After his death, state media has described Zhu as an "outstanding member of the Chinese Communist Party" and "time-tested and loyal Communist fighter".
But on the internet, posts about Zhu have been contained and censored - like an essay written by economist Zhao Jian, which remembered Zhu's era as a time when people were "properly poor" but saw a clear future ahead.
"There were no smartphones then, no short-form videos and no screens filled by the purveyors of anxiety," he wrote.
"The sky was blue, life moved slowly and people could say what they really thought."
His comments were removed from WeChat the day after publication.
The party has long been fearful of public reaction to deaths of senior officials and public figures.
The deaths of former premier Zhou Enlai in 1976 and Hu Yaobang, a former CCP general secretary, in 1989, prompted widespread outpourings of grief that morphed into protests.
Zhu died just days before the Communist Party leadership gathered to commemorate the birth centenary of President Jiang Zemin, who died in 2022.
The death of Zhu and Jiang, two such prominent leaders from the same era, has prompted a wave of nostalgia among many Chinese people for a time when the country looked as if it was going in a different direction - when it appeared that it may open to the world and allow more freedom for its people.
Candour of a bygone era
Previously purged under Mao Zedong's regime, Zhu was brought back into the fold after Mao's death in 1976.
Zhu served as premier alongside Jiang Zemin, who became Communist Party chief in 1989 and president in 1993.
The two men served alongside each other at the top of China's leadership from 1998 to 2003, leading China through an era of rapid economic growth and entry into global trade.
During that time, China pushed through painful changes: shuttering chronically unprofitable state firms, dismantling the old housing system in favour of a commercial property market, weathering the Asian financial crisis of the late 1990s and joining the World Trade Organization in 2001.
But what appears to captivate Chinese people from that era was that both had a certain style - a common touch.
A Chinese state media documentary about Jiang Zemin's life shows him banging on tables one minute and erupting in laughter the next.
Zhu, meanwhile, once labelled rogue bankers as "half-wits" and described the flood dykes lining the Yangtze River as "flimsy and porous as tofu dregs".
He was also known for his deadpan humour, like at a news conference in 1999, when he was asked about allegations that China had donated to US President Bill Clinton's Democratic Party.
"If the political contribution were to be really that effective, and I have $146 billion of foreign exchange reserve, I can put out at least $10 billion for that purpose. Why just $300,000? That would be too foolish," he said, drawing laughter from the crowd.
The day he died, the Jiang Zemin documentary featured Zhu explaining how he persuaded his comrades to implement tough reforms.
"I'm not here to talk about pros and cons. I am here to talk about how to get things done," he is heard saying.
Circulating on social media is a picture of Jiang laughing together with Zhu and praised their candid communication.
"They told the truth, shouldered the responsibility and spared no effort in serving the people," the post read.
It's a style that has captivated Chinese audiences and stands in contrast with the current carefully choreographed leadership style.
Xi's narrative
The passing of the two leaders into China's history books marks a definitive end to the breakneck reforms of the 1990s and early 2000s, with an emphasis on private entrepreneurship and wealth creation.
That stands in contrast to President Xi, who has exerted greater central control and pressed a state-driven economic policy focused on technological autonomy and strategic industries.
In a 40-minute speech on Monday, Xi called on the Communist Party to carry forward Jiang's legacy, presenting the current leadership as the continuation of his political and ideological project.
"On the new journey ahead, we must heighten our sense of vigilance against potential dangers," he said during Monday's event.
"With an indomitable fighting spirit and superb skill in struggle," we must "proactively meet the major tests posed by high winds and rushing waters, or even by raging storms," he added.
He also praised Jiang's crackdown on a reformist Shanghai newspaper in 1989 after it voiced support for the pro-democracy demonstrations that culminated in the bloody Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing.
"Xi is committed to the great renaissance of the Chinese nation," says Kerry Brown, Professor of Chinese Studies and Director of the Law China Institute at King's College London.
"He's trying to put forward a unified historic narrative - any idea that their leadership offered or suggested a different future path will not be allowed a public airing," he adds.
"Instead, their lives will be knitted into the narrative that everything they did transformed China into what it is now, rather than dwell on any other 'What If's'."
But Xi now faces considerable challenges as China is facing slower economic growth and demographic decline.
House prices have plummeted, youth unemployment is high and factory output is becoming more sluggish.
The days of double-digit economic growth have gone.
This mourning for a bygone era is a mourning for a time when Chinese families felt that if they worked hard, their lives would improve.
For many, that certainty has gone.
As Zhao Jian wrote in his essay: "life was hard, but it was hardship sustained by hope."
He admits now many in China have "material abundance" and "skylines bristling with high-rises and streets teeming with traffic."
But why then, he asks, "do we feel so empty inside?"

A main theme of the nine-book sci-fi series The Expanse is that sometimes you may never know the consequences of a choice you made. The universe, utterly indifferent black box that it is, “never tells us if we did right or wrong,” as the character Naomi Nagata puts it in The Expanse TV show.
That’s the line the developer of the upcoming Expanse video game has adopted as its own slogan. The Expanse: Osiris Reborn is set to release in spring 2027. It’s being developed by Owlcat Games, the Cyprus-based developer known for dense role-playing games like Pathfinder: Kingmaker and Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader.
Osiris Reborn is a third-person shooter and role-playing game where the player slips into the boots of a spaceship captain leading a found-family crew of misfits across the far-future solar system. You fight bad guys and float around in zero-gravity environments in the hard-science setting of The Expanse books and show. Dialog options and choice trees baked into cutscenes let you shape the narrative and change the outcomes. As many people have pointed out, it sounds very much like the Mass Effect video game series.
This will be the studio’s first third-person shooter, a departure for a company known for its top-down role-playing games. Owlcat Games beefed up its staff to build Osiris Reborn, and has faced criticism after releasing a beta version of the game in April. Players lauded the combat and visuals, but many found the story and voice acting lacking. (Apparently the game does not yet incorporate “Belter creole,” a language construct used by characters in The Expanse that has become a beloved part of the series.) It’s important to note that this was indeed a beta test, and the company has said it is aiming to fix some issues players have called attention to, even recasting a voice actor.
The Expanse is a complicated property to adapt, given that Osiris Reborn takes place around the same time as the first and second books of a nine-book series. Owlcat shared some details with WIRED about how it plans to implement choices in the story—moments where the player is faced with the opportunity to make a decision that affects the world and story that plays out.
You can choose a backstory and appearance for your character, but there are no skill classes. Your character is meant to develop based on the decisions you make. There are also choices for how you interact with your spaceship’s crew, and the ability to mentor them to advance their skills in different areas.
There are three competing factions (Earth, Mars, and the outer-space dwellers in the asteroid belt called Belters) you can work with and try to befriend. Owlcat Games says, “Keeping good relations with everyone won’t be easy—you’ll only get one chance to stay on everyone’s good side.”
It all sounds very much like decision-tier systems in games like Mass Effect. Will it compare to the truly transformative choices you can make in a game like Baldur’s Gate 3? Maybe not. Owlcat declined to speak with WIRED directly, but Leonid Rastorguev, the game's design director, replied to questions via email.
“This isn't our first game where the sheer number of choices and consequences is a core part of the experience,” Rastorguev wrote.
For Osiris Reborn, Owlcat is using an internal development system it calls Etudes to build a system of flags and triggers in the narrative that can help track player decisions, even small ones, and carry them forward in the game. Rastorguev says those choices can range from cosmetic changes, to ones that block off or unlock additional content, lead to a character dying, or change the ending.
According to critics who have reviewed the beta, the outcome of the choices isn’t immediately noticeable. One choice—where you have to pick between fighting and standing down from a battle—plays out nearly the same way in the moment no matter which option the player chooses. Owlcat says what beta players haven’t seen yet is “how far that decision ripples.”
“[Players] want to feel that they've left a mark on the universe itself,” Rastorguev wrote. “But The Expanse also has an established canon and major characters whose stories have already been told in the books and the TV series. It would feel strange for us to rewrite their fates, especially by introducing branching outcomes into events that are already firmly established.”
Rastorguev says the key to a successful choice system is to give players enough information to know that they’ve set something in motion, without necessarily giving them the entire chain of consequences. The events may be referenced again in conversations, in-game news reports, or changes in the world, and “can suggest that the consequences of your decision will continue long after you've moved on.”
If that holds, it will be very neat. For a game so influenced by Mass Effect, I do worry that Osiris Reborn might inadvertently recreate Mass Effect 3’s worst mistake, botching the ending of its series by limiting all the choices people had made across the games into three basic options to wrap everything up. Choice systems in games are great, but they often boil down into two or three big options at the end. (The game will have multiple endings, but Owlcat is not ready to say how many there will be or how different they are from one another.)
“We've put a lot of thought into this,” Rastorguev wrote, “and found ways for some of the player's choices to feel meaningful on the scale of the wider universe and potentially shape consequences that extend years beyond the immediate events of our story.”
Sounds like a real moonshot.
