On an early fall afternoon in 2023, midway through a shift in Pawtucket’s District Five, Rhode Island police officer Noel Pichardo noticed a strange camera perched on a utility pole over West Avenue.
Pichardo was 28, five years into the job, and alone in his cruiser during one of the brief lulls between responding to the typical churn of radio calls for domestic disputes, petty disturbances, and welfare checks. The camera was compact and solar-powered, angled down toward passing traffic. Pichardo made a U-turn and drove beneath it again, more slowly this time, to get a better look.
He then began searching for the cameras on roads near highway ramps, at major intersections, along the routes into and out of the city. He found them again and again. By the time Pichardo finished circling the district, he knew exactly where he had seen them before.
Two years earlier, officers had gathered on the second floor of a small police substation in Pawtucket for a presentation about a surveillance system made by Flock Safety. A high-ranking police official stood in front of a PowerPoint and explained that the company’s automatic license plate readers could identify passing vehicles not only by their license plates but by bumper stickers, roof racks, and other distinguishing features. Investigators could search for a particular car across jurisdictions and, camera by camera, reconstruct where it had been.
The system was presented as another tool of routine police work, a way to recover stolen cars, locate suspects, and find missing people. But as Pichardo listened, he found himself thinking less about the vehicles police wanted than about all the others. In a medium-size city like Pawtucket, where a handful of roads carried people nearly everywhere they needed to go, a record of a car’s movements amounted to a record of a person’s life—the places they visited, the people they saw, the routines they followed.
As Pichardo understood it, the Flock proposal had gone nowhere because the city could not afford a permanent installation. So he let it slip from his mind.
But now, on that afternoon on West Avenue, the cameras were all over his district.
Pawtucket’s cameras are one small piece of a sprawling vehicle-surveillance system that touches nearly every state in the country. Flock markets its platform as the nation’s largest fixed license-plate-reader network, processing billions of sightings each month. Because departments can open their records to agencies elsewhere, a camera installed by one municipality can become searchable by investigators hundreds or thousands of miles away.
In 2021, around the time of Pichardo’s training, Flock offered Pawtucket police a free 60-day pilot. Seventeen cameras went up around the city as part of a regional test that also included Cranston and Woonsocket, according to records reviewed by WIRED. The rollout quickly drew criticism. The ACLU of Rhode Island accused the department of installing the cameras surreptitiously, after the pilot began without prior public input or notice to the city council. Pawtucket chief of police Tina Goncalves later apologized, saying that the department would “work better in the future” to communicate with the city council.
The pilot ended later that year, and in May 2023 the local TV news reported that Pawtucket was not moving forward with the installation. Pichardo believed the idea was a dead letter.
It was not. In September 2023, records show, Pawtucket moved forward with a two-year deployment worth $128,000. Records show that the city planned to install 20 cameras along many of its busiest roads, including Newport Avenue, Main Street, Broadway, Smithfield Avenue, and West Avenue—where Pichardo first noticed one hanging over the road.
“Wait a minute,” Pichardo recalled thinking. “When did we make this decision to put these up?”
Within months, Pichardo’s questions would set off a chain of events that, he says, ended his career in law enforcement. They would also eventually place him, somewhat improbably, at the center of a backlash against Flock that unites large factions of the American left and right.
For a policeman, Pichardo contains more than his share of contradictions. He speaks with a thick Rhode Island accent that sounds like something lifted from a cop movie, but he peppers his conversation with occasional references to Nietzsche or obscure films. He describes himself as private by temperament but seems driven to stand out.
Having spent some of his childhood in a poor neighborhood where drugs and gangs were part of the landscape, Pichardo says he learned that it was safest to keep his opinions to himself and stay out of other people’s business. When he was 12 or 13, he learned that his father, who had returned to the Dominican Republic several years earlier, had done so because he had a criminal record and was told it would be best if he left the country. Becoming a police officer offered a way of drawing a line between his father’s path and his own. After studying in the criminal justice program at Salve Regina University in Newport, Pichardo entered the police academy and joined the Pawtucket department in 2018. To hear him describe it, he’s always been something of an outlier on the force. “I’m possibly the only cop who would voluntarily go to musicals,” he once told me.
In the weeks following that fall shift when he first noticed Flock cameras all over town, Pichardo kept picking at the question of how the cameras had returned. Detectives, he says he learned after asking around the department, were already using the system, though many patrol officers like himself appeared to know little about it.
Pichardo contacted his work district’s local city council rep and asked how the cameras had been approved—his first time speaking to a politician, he says—but didn’t emerge with a clear answer. (Records show that the department had notified the purchasing board that it planned to move forward, but there was no public vote before the cameras were installed. The question of approval surfaced only afterward, when a council member asked whether the deployment should have come before the council. Officials said no. Installing the cameras was, they explained, an “administrative prerogative.”)
Police officers swear oaths to uphold the law and report wrongdoing. Inside the department, Pichardo said, the unwritten rule was simpler: Don’t rat. He understood that speaking publicly could end his career. But he says he was inspired by whistleblowers like Frank Serpico and Edward Snowden, men of conviction who broke with powerful institutions and spent years living with the consequences. Pichardo has a pronounced sense of right and wrong and a tendency to treat compromise as betrayal. “You should never sell your integrity,” he says.
License plate readers are a routine investigative tool, useful for locating stolen cars or identifying suspect vehicles without stopping large numbers of motorists. Experts broadly agree that reducing unnecessary police encounters and high-speed pursuits is a good thing. But to Pichardo, that usefulness was beside the larger point. Pawtucket had created a new form of surveillance over public movement with no debate, helping to build a world in which the government could quietly record where ordinary people went. It was not a world he found acceptable. If the officers who understood the system would not raise that question, he wondered, who would?
Pichardo was still wrestling with whether to speak out about Flock when he brought it up with his wife, Emily. “Do what you believe is right,” she said; they would deal with whatever followed. After that, without notifying anyone in the department, Pichardo called a reporter at Pawtucket’s local newspaper.
The article in the Valley Breeze was published on October 11, 2023. Its headline was blunt: “Pawtucket Officer Has a Big Problem With New Cameras.”
In the article, Pichardo called Flock a “grave threat” to privacy and warned that the system was ripe for abuse. He said he had learned of the full deployment from the newspaper itself, not from his own department. If a patrol officer knew so little about the cameras going up around the city, he asked, how much could the public possibly know? The whole thing gave him, he said, “1984 vibes.”
This was not whistleblowing in the conventional sense. Pichardo did not reveal a secret program, leak internal documents, or expose a specific abuse. In some respects, the newspaper knew more about the deployment than he did. What he offered instead was the rare perspective of an active-duty police officer breaking ranks to publicly argue that his own department had adopted a powerful surveillance system without enough scrutiny.
When the article appeared, the first text Pichardo received came from another officer.
“I want to congratulate you on your testicular fortitude,” it read. The officer added that he was proud of Pichardo for doing what he believed was right. Then he warned him: The brass was furious.
Pichardo says many officers supported what he had said to the Valley Breeze. Others, mostly older officers, viewed him as a traitor. One officer asked how he still had a job. Around the station, he was told that officers were calling him “Valley Breeze” behind his back. One sergeant, he says, told him he should quit.
Within weeks, the warnings began to look prescient.
Police internal investigations are not criminal cases. Their purpose is generally narrower—to determine whether an officer has violated a policy, code of conduct, or general order. Investigators interview witnesses, review body-camera or surveillance footage, collect reports and emails, and question the officer at the center of the complaint. The interview is typically recorded, and the officer is often accompanied by a union representative.
The process generates paper. A complaint. A notice of investigation. Lists of possible policy violations. Interview recordings and investigators’ notes. Findings, disciplinary recommendations, and notices of punishment.
Before the Valley Breeze article appeared, Pichardo’s disciplinary record appears to have consisted of a single incident: In 2021, while working a police detail at a production of the musical Annie, he refused a vendor’s request that he wear a face mask, and he received a written reprimand and a two-week suspension. After Pichardo spoke out against Flock, he received notice of an internal investigation into his conduct on October 25, 2023. It would be the first of many.
The department’s complaint, which originated from Chief Tina Goncalves, stated flatly that Pichardo had spoken to a newspaper without prior authorization, had undermined the authority of the police department and its chief, and had suggested that information collected by Flock cameras could be used improperly. His comments, the notice said, were “liable to cause harm to the reputation of the department and affect the impact on the community.”
The potential violations included the department’s mission statement, code of ethics, media-relations policy, and a rule labeled “Criticism & Malicious Gossip.”
Pichardo was ordered to appear at the Office of Professional Standards, a basement-level room in the Pawtucket police headquarters. Across from him, he says, were a lieutenant and a sergeant. A union representative sat beside him but said little.
The interview lasted somewhere between 30 and 45 minutes, Pichardo recalls. The questions were straightforward at first. Had he spoken to the reporter? He had. Had he done so without authorization from the department? He had. Why?
Pichardo gave much the same answer he had given the newspaper: The cameras were tracking people across the city, and the public had a right to know how they were being used. Pichardo says the lieutenant disagreed. Not every police tactic, he told Pichardo, was the public’s business. Departments did not disclose every method they used or every form of surveillance available to them.
The investigators accused Pichardo of violating the public’s trust by speaking to the press.
“I think this department violated the public trust,” he says he retorted. Then they asked who, in his view, should be held responsible. “The chief,” Pichardo said.
WIRED could not review the underlying investigative file, including the recording that might confirm or contradict Pichardo’s account. The city declined to provide the file even when Pichardo requested records concerning his own case. Pawtucket officials did not respond to WIRED’s questions about the denial.
A disciplinary agreement signed in early 2024 does, however, state that Pichardo made “critical statements to the media” about Flock and the department’s leadership. Pichardo maintained that his comments were constitutionally protected speech. The department expressly denied that position in the agreement.
After consulting an attorney, the Pawtucket police union came to the conclusion that Pichardo’s comments were constitutionally protected and sent the city a letter warning that if it disciplined him, it would likely violate his rights. According to union lodge president Michael Cioe, the department initially sought a six-month suspension but reduced the proposed punishment after the union threatened litigation.
Rather than fight the case through disciplinary hearings and possible state or federal litigation, the two sides reached an agreement. Pichardo would serve a 30-day unpaid suspension for speaking to the paper.
Pichardo said he accepted the deal because he didn’t want his coworkers to see him as their enemy. “I wanted the war to end,” he says.
By then, the department had already opened another investigation into his conduct.
A month after investigators questioned Pichardo about speaking to the Valley Breeze, another internal investigation notice arrived. In December, the department opened an inquiry over Pichardo’s failure to appear for a municipal court hearing about a traffic citation, which resulted in an additional two-day suspension. Chief Goncalves was again listed as the complainant.
Then, in March, about a week after he returned to work from the suspension, yet another notice landed—this one concerning an encounter that had allegedly taken place nearly 15 months earlier.
The incident involved a man who was being taken to a hospital for a mental health evaluation. The complaint alleged that Pichardo grabbed the man’s arm, refused to let him retrieve a jacket, and would not allow him to feed his cat. When the man pointed out that the cat could not open a can of food on its own, Pichardo allegedly replied that “cats can take care of themselves” and laughed.
During his interview, Pichardo says he told investigators that the cat already had food and that other officers and mental health clinicians present could confirm that he had handled the encounter appropriately. Pichardo says the inquiry didn’t sustain the allegations, and he received no discipline.
By the spring, Pichardo felt sure that the department was trying to send a message with these three investigations. Inside the department, Pichardo says, there was an unspoken expectation that his disciplinary agreement with his superiors would end his public criticism. Nevertheless, in April he accepted an invitation to testify at a public hearing before the Rhode Island House Judiciary Committee, where lawmakers were considering legislation regulating automated license plate readers.
The hearing was carried live on the legislature’s Capitol Television network. Pichardo spoke off the cuff. He told lawmakers that the proposed legislation did not go far enough. Flock, he argued, was tracking people’s movements, and although he was “not a lawyer,” he believed the system raised serious Fourth Amendment concerns. He said the cameras had captured his own plate five times in a single day, cited an out-of-state officer who used Flock to track his ex-wife, and questioned whether police should possess technology with that kind of cross-jurisdictional reach.
At times, Pichardo’s confidence outran his precision. He asserted that officers’ use of Flock could not be monitored, although the system does in fact maintain user logs and performs regular audits. In interviews with WIRED, he acknowledged the distinction but argued that logs were only as meaningful as the people responsible for reviewing them. He pointed to cases in other jurisdictions where officers had used Flock to track romantic partners or conduct improper searches, sometimes without the misuse being caught until much later. His broader point, he said, was that “anybody’s capable of anything” when given a powerful tool without sufficient guardrails.
About a week later, in response to his testimony, the Rhode Island Police Chiefs’ Association sent a letter to the committee singling Pichardo out by name. It called his testimony “inaccurate at best” and, at worst, “inflammatory and patently false.” The association accused him of misunderstanding Flock’s capabilities, disputed his description of the system’s auditing, and suggested that he either lacked familiarity with the technology or had “an agenda where, in his mind, the truth is irrelevant.”
Back at work, Pichardo says, his union representatives were annoyed that he’d spoken up again. (The union disputes this characterization.) Other officers, even those who largely agreed with him about Flock, or at least respected what he was doing, started to express concerns. One sat Pichardo down and said that if he wasn’t careful, he might lose his job and never work as a police officer in Rhode Island again. “You’ve got to think about your family, dude,” Pichardo recalls him saying.
On May 10, 2024, a new incident set yet another internal investigation of Pichardo in motion: A delivery driver came to Pawtucket police headquarters to report that someone had thrown a bottle of soda at her vehicle during what she described as a road-rage encounter. Pichardo spoke with her, concluded that no crime had occurred, and declined to prepare a report.
The woman later spoke with a sergeant, asking for the incident to be documented, and Pichardo was directed to write a report. According to the department's records, the delivery driver was not initially asking to file a formal complaint against Pichardo, but she did return to the station later that day, recording portions of her exchanges with Pichardo on her cell phone.
Pichardo told her that Pawtucket is an urban environment where people argue and throw things, accused her of acting like a child and having a tantrum, and complained that she had “won” by persuading a supervisor to overrule him.
Several days later, the woman filed a formal complaint with the Office of Professional Standards.
Investigators reviewed the recordings and interviewed another officer on duty. The videos, investigators later wrote, showed the woman remaining largely calm as Pichardo became increasingly dismissive. They sustained more than a dozen allegations, including neglect of duty, insubordination, incivility, and conduct unbecoming.
Pichardo acknowledged to WIRED that his conduct was indefensible. “I should still be the bigger person,” he said.
What he disputed was the punishment: a 40-day unpaid suspension and removal from the detective eligibility list. He also says the union told him he was barred from taking the sergeant’s exam for two years. He was notified of the suspension on the day his second son was born, just as he was about to start paternity leave, meaning that his first 40 days at home with his baby were unpaid—a coincidence he alleges was deliberate.
By early 2025, Pichardo had come to believe the department was finished with him. He no longer trusted that, if a traffic stop, arrest, or routine encounter generated another complaint, anyone in command would give him the benefit of the doubt. He more or less began to avoid active patrolling, he says. Between calls, he often waited at the Fraternal Order of Police building, which he helped maintain, or remained inside his patrol car rather than looking for the next stop. “I was trying to stay off the radar,” he later recalled telling investigators.
Then two more investigations arrived.
The first grew out of a dispute over a snowbound Volkswagen. On February 10, Pichardo responded to what appeared to be an unregistered vehicle stranded in the snow, concluded it was already disabled and had been ticketed, and gave the owner until the following day to move it. A supervisor ordered him to return and have the car towed instead. Pichardo questioned the instruction over the radio before complying. The department concluded that he had essentially been insubordinate.
The second began less than two weeks later. Pichardo responded to a mother who wanted police to document her 13-year-old son as a wayward child after she suspected he had been burning paper inside their home. Pichardo declined to take a report, concluding that she lacked evidence and appeared more interested in having the state remove the boy than documenting a crime. Before leaving, he told her to go inside and “be a mother.”
The department combined the investigations. Rather than focus only on the underlying incidents, investigators reconstructed nearly an entire workday of Pichardo’s life in excruciating detail. Using dispatch records, time sheets, cruiser GPS, and location data transmitted by Pichardo's body camera, they mapped his movements throughout the day of the family call. (They didn’t use Flock data; they didn’t need to.) Their reconstruction concluded that he had spent approximately four hours and 57 minutes at police facilities or the Fraternal Order of Police building rather than on patrol.
Pichardo did not dispute where he had been. He explained that he helped maintain the union office and that officers routinely waited there between calls. From the department's perspective, the location data showed an officer spending much of his shift inside police or union buildings instead of policing the city. The department was recommending termination. The resulting complaint explaining the decision ran 25 pages. It contained 32 administrative charges—10 stemming from the tow dispute and 22 from the family call—and assembled nearly every disciplinary matter from Pichardo's career.
On the morning of July 16, 2025, after roll call, a major asked Pichardo to stay behind.
He knew what was coming.
Chief Goncalves had signed a complaint the day before recommending his termination. The major handed it to him and explained that he was being suspended with pay while he decided whether to request a hearing in accordance with Rhode Island's Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. He had five days.
Pichardo took the complaint home. But the more he thought about it, the less sense it made to fight. Even if he won, he believed, he would return to a department whose leadership had already decided it no longer wanted him.
Two days later, after seven years as a Pawtucket police officer, Pichardo resigned.
His letter was brief. Policing, he wrote, had meant a great deal to him and his family, but over the previous three years the department had made clear that he was no longer welcome because of his “philosophical convictions.” Remaining, he wrote, would only bring more grief to him and his family.
He did not apologize for speaking out.
"My only regret," he wrote, "is that I was not articulate and/or diplomatic enough in my attempts to explain my position." On the 18th, he walked the letter to the Office of Professional Standards, shook hands with his coworkers, turned in his badge, firearm, radio, and keys, and left police headquarters for the last time.
Pichardo alleges that the investigations and escalating discipline he was faced with were retaliation for speaking out about Flock. The reality may be more complicated. His union, which had backed him when the department sought to punish him for his comments to the Valley Breeze, says it saw no evidence that the later investigations were retaliatory. They believed another Pawtucket officer who engaged in comparable conduct would have faced similar discipline.
Whether that is true is difficult to establish. Pichardo does not deny that he broke department rules in several of the incidents. His argument is that the rules were enforced differently against him—that conduct that might have earned another officer a warning became an internal inquiry, and misconduct that might otherwise have brought lesser discipline resulted in lengthy unpaid suspensions. He claims he had seen other officers do worse and face less. There is no way to know what would have happened to the version of Pichardo who never called the Valley Breeze.
After resigning, Pichardo spent months trying to remain in law enforcement. He applied to other police departments, private-security jobs, and campus police positions, including one at his alma mater, Salve Regina University. Some never responded. Others interviewed him before deciding not to move forward. An acquaintance who works in campus security at a local college eventually asked around and offered an explanation: "You're blackballed."
He found work instead as a caregiver for a person with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
Pichardo tried to tell himself that he had done enough. But he couldn’t shake the feeling that he had left something unfinished. “My conscience was still haunting me,” he told me. “I just wanted to be able to say I tried.”
So he sat down with a friend who started a YouTube account for Pichardo, and they recorded a video.
Since I started speaking with Pichardo in April, the debate over Flock has spread far beyond Pawtucket. Across the country, cities have fought over whether to keep the cameras, some jurisdictions have canceled contracts or imposed new restrictions, and lawmakers in both Republican- and Democratic-led states have pushed for new limits on how the systems can be used. For Pichardo, there is something distinctly American about the backlash. The country has long attached dreams of freedom and self-determination to the car, a mythology reflected in advertising and even in the names of the vehicles themselves: Explorer, Expedition, Escape, Maverick, Liberty. Americans who agreed on little else could still recognize the promise of the open road—that, for a little while, a person might simply leave and be left alone. To Pichardo, Flock threatened that promise.
“That’s freedom,” Pichardo told me. “The ability to drive somewhere and no one knows where you’re going.”
The video opens with Pichardo sitting alone in a plain room, dressed in a crisp cream-colored shirt, daylight spilling through a nearby window. Looking directly into the camera, he tells viewers that speaking publicly is "one of the strangest things" he has ever done. But, he says, he feels obligated to warn them about a technology that has quietly spread into communities across the country.
"To put it bluntly," he says, "if you own a car, you are now being tracked."
He expected a few hundred people to watch. Hundreds of thousands did.
Within weeks, an email arrived from one of Tucker Carlson's bookers. Pichardo assumed it was a prank; he had never really sought a political audience. He had deleted his social media accounts years ago and had little interest in becoming a pundit. But in mid-July, there he was, spending nearly 20 minutes discussing license plate readers, surveillance, and the meaning of privacy with the former Fox News host. He was explaining Flock to one of the largest audiences in American media, in a video bombastically titled “Whistleblower Reveals the Largest Mass Surveillance Operation in History and the Coming Slave State.”
Podcasters started reaching out, followed by local reporters and The Washington Post. Strangers urged him to run for office. Others told him to build up his YouTube channel, lean into the moment, and turn the audience into a career.
The prospect was not without appeal. Pichardo was still rebuilding his life after losing his job; a large audience might offer money, security, even a new profession. But something about it felt dishonest. “The only reason people know who I am,” he told me, “is because I criticized something.”
He had watched enough people online to recognize what he thought of as a trap. You begin with sincere convictions about serving the public, then you begin tracking an audience, and in time, he says, “you become a parody of what you were before.”
His mind returned, he says, to a passage from the Gospel of Matthew. “What profit is it to a man,” the verse goes, “if he gains the whole world, but loses his own soul?”

Landslide in South Korea kills one as record rain lashes south
- Published
Torrential rains have pummelled South Korea's Gyeongsang province, triggering a landslide that killed one person and wounded two others.
The landslide buried the first floor of an apartment building in the south-eastern city of Geoje on Monday morning. Rescuers pulled out three people, one of whom was later declared dead, local media report.
This comes as record rainfall triggered by back-to-back storms caused widespread flooding and landslides in parts of China, Japan and the Philippines.
Geoje city saw 124.5mm of rain in a one-hour period, the highest since South Korea's meteorological agency started keeping records for the city in 1972.
Between Sunday and Monday, Geoje received more than 400mm of rain overnight.
Videos on social media show cars submerged in Geoje as strong currents swept the streets.
City authorities announced that some tourist attractions will be closed on Monday due to the heavy rain.
Bus operations and household waste collection have also been suspended due to flooded or damaged roads, authorities said.
On Sunday, authorities urged residents to avoid driving, stay away from places like riverbanks and evacuate to safe areas if needed.
Multiple storms swept through large swathes of East and South East Asia this month, causing widespread flooding and damage to infrastructure.
Forecasters said this year's typhoon season was shaping up to be more intense than usual, due to a strong El Niño that began in June. El Niño pushes up global temperatures and increases the strength of typhoons.
Late last week, "unprecedented" rainfall battered Japan's Chiba prefecture near Tokyo, leaving 10 people dead and stranding thousands at Narita Airport.
The deluge also cut power to more than 20,000 households.
On Sunday, Japanese authorities said the 10th fatality was a man in his 30s who was found dead at his home from carbon monoxide poisoning. He had been using a generator due to the power outage, public broadcaster NHK reported.

England has experienced its driest July since records began in 1836, receiving only 6.5mm of rainfall – 10% of the country’s long-term meteorological average for the month. Wales also experienced its driest-ever July, while Northern Ireland recorded its eighth driest. Scotland was the only country in the UK not to set new records but still received only 69% of its average rainfall for July compared with the long-term average. Southern England faced the worst of the dry conditions with some areas, including the Sussex coast, receiving less than 0.2mm of rain in July. This resulted in widespread low moisture content within the soil, enabling temperatures to reach the high 30s celsius.
Looking ahead, despite notable spells of rain in the north, parts of southern England may receive only the odd shower for the rest of August. Throughout the summer, forecast models have hinted at more unsettled weather reaching the south-east of England at a 10-day range. However, as time edged closer the rain was largely confined to north-western parts of Britain, failing to reach the south-east with any significance. With much uncertainty within forecast models, the risk of this dry period persisting is not out of the question.
There is a disturbance in the Atlantic, approximately 1,000 miles east of the Lesser Antilles. The National Hurricane Centre has predicted an 80% chance of the cyclone forming in the next 48 hours as a short-lived tropical depression. If such a system does strengthen, it will become the fourth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and would be named Dolly. Regardless of any development, there will be a risk of gusty winds and heavy rainfall in Lesser Antilles on Friday night and into Saturday. This year’s strong El Niño is expected to play a significant role in lessening hurricane activity within the Atlantic.
In India, the monsoon continues to cause devastation, particularly in eastern regions where flooding in Assam has caused 100 deaths as of 10 August. Flooding caused by rivers overflowing has resulted in 700,000 people being displaced over the last month. This includes 300,000 displaced near the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia. The monsoon also brought significant lightning, which resulted in the deaths of 14 people in eastern India on the 4 August, including 10 in the district of Giridih. Many of the dead were farm workers, caught in open agricultural fields where there is a lack of shelter to provide safety when such storms arrive.

Why Uganda is winning the battle against Ebola as virus spreads in DR Congo
- Published
The Ebola outbreak in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo has become the second-worst on record, with the official death toll passing a grim milestone of 1,500.
Experts believe the true number of fatalities during this outbreak, which was declared in May, is much higher. And in another alarming update, authorities in DR Congo confirmed on Thursday that the virus was spreading much faster than in previous outbreaks.
Next door in Uganda, a country that also reported infections in May, the picture is entirely different.
The country's health minister described a "moment of joy" as the last Ebola patient was released from hospital two weeks ago.
Uganda only ever recorded 20 cases and two deaths from the virus.
According to Dr Kasonde Mwinga, the World Health Organization's Uganda chief, the relatively low number of casualties was not "by luck or chance".
"It's because people invested in preparedness," she told the BBC.
This outbreak is the 17th to have emerged in DR Congo since Ebola was discovered 50 years ago. By comparison Uganda has had nine since 2000, with officials there saying lessons learnt from past tragedies have allowed them to stop the disease ripping through the country on various occasions.
One example is the case of a 12-year-old girl who arrived at a hospital in the central district of Luwero in 2011.
Her symptoms sparked caution: she was isolated, medics wore personal protective equipment when treating her and when she died three hours later her body was carefully sealed in a coffin. These precautions were able to halt the spread of what a blood sample later confirmed to be Ebola.
"We know Ebola. It's been here a few times, we know how to deal with it," government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told the BBC's Newsday programme.
Uganda's first known case this time was a man from DR Congo who crossed the border for treatment.
Once health authorities confirmed multiple cases had been imported from DR Congo, they activated a specialist Ebola treatment centre at Mulago hospital, in the capital city, Kampala.
The facility, which was used during an outbreak of Ebola last year, held leftover medical supplies and had an "emergency medical team" on standby, Dr David Kaggwa, head of the facility, said.
"It was a matter of sorting and ordering a few more supplies, and then actually in one day we were ready to receive the patients. So, it is easy, it's not that we're starting from scratch," he said.
Out of the 20 people who tested positive in Uganda, 15 came from DR Congo.
The first two cases, it is thought, might not have known what condition they had. But after Uganda and DR Congo jointly declared the Ebola outbreak on 15 May, people with symptoms - which include headaches, fever and vomiting - "came direct to the treatment unit," Dr Kaggwa said.
He suspects that because these patients did not pass through general hospitals, and come into contact with those patients and medics, there was little opportunity for community transmission.
In a bid to stop the disease spreading, the authorities also closed the border between Uganda and DR Congo, despite the financial impact this would have on Ugandans who travel between the two countries to trade.
Uganda acted fast, but it also had an advantage over DR Congo when it came to responding to the virus.
Before the first cases were reported in DR Congo, Ebola had been spreading undetected for weeks. This was because health officials poised to pick up outbreaks had been testing for common species of Ebola, and not the rare species behind the current outbreak, named Bundibugyo.
Uganda only detected its first case after DR Congo had identified and publicised multiple infections - knowledge of the outbreak was out in the open and Uganda could therefore act quickly to contain the virus.
"Surveillance mechanisms were put in place then it was easy to identify all the patients quickly," Dr Kaggwa said.
Comparatively, DR Congo has had a harder time with surveillance and contact tracing.
One field investigator tasked with tracking the virus across Bunia, a city at the epicentre of the outbreak, told Reuters that surveillance had been hampered by poor planning, logistical bottlenecks and the recruitment of inexperienced staff.
"We discover the disease only after it has already spread," Dr Moubarack Kano said. "We're just chasing it."
This is not helped by the insecurity that plagues eastern DR Congo. Ituri, the province at the centre of the outbreak, has been under military rule for several years as the army tries to crack down on dozens of armed groups there.
Further south of Ituri there are large areas held by the M23 rebels, a powerful militia that says it has managed to contain the outbreak.
Its Ebola response co-ordinator Dr Fred Kaniki attributed the achievement to early detection and contact tracing, telling the BBC: "In the course of a month we registered two more cases originating from those index cases and successfully followed up 400 people."
But the M23 conflict and other pockets of violence have displaced millions of people in the region - and that makes surveillance difficult in DR Congo. Artisanal mining and cross-border trade also means Ebola has more chances to spread as people are constantly on the move.
In contrast, Uganda managed to quarantine more than 6,000 contacts of people known to have Ebola during the outbreak. These contacts were isolated for an incubation period of 21 days.
"That is very, very important because usually cases come from those contacts," said Dr Kaggwa.
Kasujja concurs. "I would say that our success is mainly due to our promptness and completeness of follow-up," he said.
This is not the first time Uganda has impressed with its response to a health crisis.
In the 1990s and 2000s, the country was widely praised for its successful campaign against HIV and Aids, which saw the prevalence of HIV drop from more than 10% to 6% in roughly a decade.
A huge government programme had preached the "ABCs": abstinence, being faithful and condom use.
The co-operation of the community is also critical in preventing infections during an outbreak, Kasujja adds.
"To this day, despite the fact that there are announcements that Uganda has no Ebola patients [members of the public] are still being careful, still taking the necessary precautions," he says.
This co-operation is illustrated by one of its first cases of Ebola, a nurse who contracted the virus while working in an intensive care unit in Kampala.
It was shortly before the outbreak was officially declared, and she had treated a patient who later died - unbeknownst to her - of Ebola. She told the BBC how she started feeling ill two weeks later, battling headaches, joint and muscle pains. Painkillers were not working and a hospital ran various tests including for malaria.
She sought a second opinion and that is when she heard that two colleagues had been diagnosed with Ebola - and she immediately chose to go into isolation.
Like many other patients, she co-operated fully with the guidelines even during the frightening time when her 11-month-old baby, whom she was still breastfeeding, was taken away from her and quarantined for 21 days.
Uganda has since announced it is totally Ebola-free, going against the protocol of waiting 42 days from when the last patient recovers to declare an outbreak over.
The health ministry said it was able to make this announcement because the first case of the virus was imported and there was never any "unexplained community transmission".
But there is also the reality that a long, porous border with Ituri, the Congolese area with most infections, means that the virus could easily reach Uganda again.
Thus, Uganda has sent dozens of healthcare workers to DR Congo to help their "brothers and sisters" tackle Ebola, Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi said on X.
"We are going to where the problem is," Kasujja explained. "Uganda cannot win against Ebola if the Democratic Republic of Congo fails."
Uganda has also increased screening at the border and continues to educate the public about measures for prevent or deal with the disease.
"We're always very prepared," Dr Kaggwa said.

Several States are recording a spike in H1N1 cases, among other influenza-like illnesses, viral fevers, and respiratory tract infections. Experts say there is no cause for alarm, but advise that children with asthma and other chronic conditions might require special intervention.
The H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A, and can cause respiratory illness, with symptoms including fever or chills, cough, sore throat, a runny or blocked nose, headache, tiredness, and muscle or body aches. In some cases, patients may also experience vomiting and diarrhoea.
Six times more cases
Delhi has recorded a sharp rise in H1N1 cases, with over 1,300 infections reported this monsoon season — nearly six times higher than the same period last year.
The national capital had recorded 1,344 H1N1 cases by early August, compared with 229 cases during the corresponding period last year. Government hospitals have set up separate isolation wards, and health officials have urged vulnerable groups, including children and older adults, to take extra precautions. Special wards have been set up at hospitals to manage the surge in cases.
A Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) official also said cases had gone up compared to last year, with Mumbai recording 309 cases between June 1 and August 15 this year, compared to 72 cases during the same period in 2025.
Limited testing
Bengaluru doctors say they are seeing a noticeable rise in influenza-like illness, viral fever, and respiratory tract infections among children. Doctors have also confirmed H1N1 cases, though testing is restricted to children with severe or persistent symptoms and those with severe acute respiratory illness.
At the State-run Vani Vilas Women and Children Hospital, paediatrics head Chikkanarasa Reddy P.S. said respiratory complaints and fever account for nearly 80% of the daily paediatric out-patient load, so only children with more aggressive symptoms are being tested. In Bengaluru’s Clarence High School alone, over 500 cases of influenza-like illness have been reported, with two confirmed cases of H1N1 among students, sparking concerns about transmission in classrooms and other crowded indoor settings.
At the Indira Gandhi Institute of Child Health, director Narendra Babu said the hospital was seeing a steady flow of viral fever cases and confirming around two to three H1N1 cases a day among those tested.
Private sector paediatricians are reporting a sharper rise. Vikas Satwik, senior paediatrician and neonatologistat Motherhood Hospitals, said school-going children account for a substantial share. Sujatha Thyagarajan, lead and head of paediatric intensive care and paediatric emergency at Aster Women and Children Hospital, said H1N1 and other influenza A infections were rising earlier than the usual seasonal pattern.
‘Early testing needed’
In Chennai, J.K. Reddy, a senior paediatrics consultant at Apollo Children’s Hospital, said they have been seeing cases of H1N1 among children for the past two weeks, with a slight rise in cases this week. He advised that children suspected of having influenza should be tested within 24 to 48 hours of developing symptoms. Anti-flu drugs are more effective if started in the first few days of fever. Government doctors also confirmed they are seeing patients with symptoms of flu-like illness, but since routine testing for H1N1 is not conducted at government hospitals, it is difficult to classify them.
Janani Sankar, medical director at the Kanchi Kamakoti CHILDS Trust Hospital in Chennai, said: “Most of the children are managed as outpatients. Some of them with extreme fatigue, severe body pain, and lack of oral intake needed hospitalisation. We are yet to see children with H1N1.”
Ravinder Nayak, Telangana’s Director of Public Health and Family Welfare, said the number of H1N1 cases in the State was lower than in the corresponding period last year. Vijay Kumar, superintendent of Niloufer Hospital, Telangana’s premier State-run tertiary care centre specialising in maternal, neonatal, and paediatric medicine, said the hospital had seen an increase in outpatient consultations for viral fevers from June to August, but there has not been any significant rise in H1N1 or influenza cases so far.
Annual flu vaccines for elderly
Influenza A has been rampant in Kerala for the last three months. Cases began to spike in May, with 526 cases and six deaths, and increased through June (2,050 cases, 26 deaths) and July (2,899 cases, 31 deaths). There have been 1,476 cases and 21 deaths reported so far this month, till August 17.
Cumulatively, there have been 7,421 cases and 88 deaths caused by influenza in Kerala this year, with almost all the fatalities seen in people over 50 years of age.
Public health experts in the State have been urging the government to invest in annual flu vaccinations for the elderly so that, apart from reducing mortality, senior citizens are saved from frequent hospitalisations and high out-of-pocket expenditure on health.

Mysterious elephant deaths in Kenya raise questions around pesticides
- Published
News that the recent deaths of 15 elephants may have been caused by pesticides sprayed on tomato crops surrounding Amboseli National Park has raised concerns and questions in Kenya.
Last week, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said that some of the elephants that had died between 24 June and 24 July had shown signs of "partial paralysis" that pointed to poisoning from cyanide used in pesticides.
But conservationists have told the BBC that, perhaps, is not the full story. Farmers we have spoken to in the area were also sceptical.
"We have stayed with this wildlife for decades and have never experienced this," Daniel Nina, who represents some of the landowners in the area, told the BBC.
"So that's why we are wondering why it is happening today."
The tomato farms are found in the Kimana area, which is part of a corridor between Amboseli National Park and the Tsavo National Park in the south of Kenya.
It is a vast area known as the Amboseli ecosystem, which straddles the border near Tanzania where more than 2,000 elephants move along in search of food and water.
These farms thrive thanks to the streams from nearby Mount Kilimanjaro and supply markets in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, and beyond.
The chief vet of Kenya's Wildlife Service, Dr Isaac Lekolool, told us that they had found traces of cyanide in samples taken from the elephants' stomachs.
He says that they are not ruling out deliberate poisoning but it's impossible at this stage to tell what could have killed the elephants.
"It's difficult to tell because we've not seen these kind of cases before. It is almost like a one-off, and it was within a period of about a month," Lekolool said.
Their working theory is that the elephants were exposed to the toxin through pesticides sprayed on nearby tomato farms.
"It could be unintentional. Maybe people are trying to do some controls of pests on their crops, and that could have been maybe a source."
A 2024 report by Kenyan food safety initiative Route to Food found a farmer in Kimana area using an insecticide that had an "active ingredient" that was "a chemical compound of cyanide".
Wangunyu Njuguna, the author of the report, said that despite being illegal in Kenya, some toxic agrochemicals were smuggled through the border with Tanzania.
"The biggest problem is we're not enforcing similar standards in the region," Njuguna said. "There is no-one checking what I go and buy across the border, so I can just go buy anything and walk through the border and no-one stops me."
Highly hazardous substances are common on Kenyan farms and some have been linked to serious diseases.
While regulations against illegal agrochemicals exist, there is weak enforcement and little attention paid to how they can affect animals.
'It's not adding up'
However, we have spoken to several wildlife conservationists who have questioned the initial findings of Kenya's Wildlife Service.
Paula Kahumbu is a world-renowned conservationist who has worked with elephants for nearly 30 years. "We haven't got enough detailed information to have confidence in this claim that it's due to pesticides in crops," Kahumbu said.
"Some information has been released to the public but it's not adding up. Those elephants have to eat a huge amount to kill them."
Other experts who did not want to be named said the pesticide theory was inconsistent with elephant behaviour.
They said that males are more likely to raid farms as they usually take more risks than females and calves. However, only one of the 15 elephants affected was an adult male.
Nina, the landowners' representative, added that unlike the latest incident, previous cases of poisoning in farms had affected zebras and antelopes, which raid the same areas.
"How does cyanide kill the elephants and leave behind the zebras, antelopes and wildebeests, which are eating the grass together?" Nina asked.
Human-wildlife conflict has persisted for decades in communities near conservation areas across Kenya.
Stephen Michael, a tomato farmer in Kimana, says elephants and giraffes occasionally raid farms in the area.
"Elephants come from time to time from Tsavo and Amboseli. They destroy many farms, not just mine," Michael said.
"The last time elephants came, they destroyed cabbages and tomatoes. I lost cabbages worth almost $1,535 [£1,140]. That doesn't include tomatoes. I might start crying if I count that."
Frank Pope, CEO of conservation organisation Save the Elephants, told the BBC the pressure on Amboseli's elephants was not ivory anymore.
"It's land use," he said.
Farms and lodges are increasingly taking up land around the park which was previously used by elephants. It is such activities that Pope says worsen the conflict with wildlife.
"People are moving into areas where there's enough water to grow crops, and fertile soils, and those are the very areas that the elephants tend to use as well."
Nobody knows for sure what's causing the elephant deaths now.
The fear is that the remaining elephants and the people who live near them could still be at risk.

As enterprises increasingly turn to AI to get work done, three new weapons are emerging in their fight to control spiralling AI adoption costs: agent harness, model selection and inference economics. Simply put, AI adoption is no longer being judged solely on model capabilities, benchmarks or impressive agent demos, but on whether these systems can deliver measurable productivity gains without pushing project costs higher. As AI moves from pilots into everyday enterprise workflows, the cost of every model call, token, inference and computing resource begins to add up. The bigger question, then, is not simply which model an enterprise uses, but how the entire AI system is designed around it. Companies are increasingly looking at ways to reduce unnecessary model calls, route simpler tasks to cheaper models and remove AI from workflows where conventional software can do the job just as well. This prompted us to ask a sharper question: what actually goes into cutting the cost of an AI project, and which engineering decisions can keep the bill from rising as deployments scale? Making AI Do More With Less The first lever is the agent harness, the software layer that manages how an AI agent uses a model. It decides what information the model receives, how a task is broken down and how often the model needs to be called. This was illustrated in late July when Sarvam AI launched Sarvam Code, a coding agent that divides engineering tasks between planner, worker and verifier agents. Sarvam said the system completed tasks on Terminal-Bench 2.1 at an average cost of about $2, compared with $4.1 to $27.8 for Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. Sarvam also said its system, which routes work between its Sarvam 105B model and a larger open model, reduced serving costs by about 40%. The point is not that the harness makes the model itself cheaper. Instead, it helps prevent the model from doing unnecessary work. Kausal Malladi, chief technology officer (investments) at INDmoney, says much of an AI agent’s cost comes from the amount of information it sends to the model. As an agent takes more steps, it can repeatedly send parts of the earlier conversation, instructions and other context back to the model. A task that takes 40 steps can therefore consume millions of tokens, even if the original request contained only a few thousand. The job of the harness is to limit this repetition. It can ensure that the model receives only the information it needs for the next step and can store information that is likely to be needed again. This is where caching comes in. Instead of sending the same information to the model and paying for it to process that information again, the system can reuse what it has already processed. Malladi estimates that this kind of caching can reduce the effective cost by roughly 80%. In other words, one of the easiest ways to lower an AI bill is to avoid sending unnecessary information to the model in the first place. This makes the harness an important cost lever. Rather than simply using the model more efficiently, enterprises can use the same model budget to complete more work. Frontier Intelligence Needs A Filter The next lever is model selection. Enterprises do not need their most powerful and expensive model for every task. By routing routine requests to smaller models and reserving frontier models for complex work, they can bring down the cost of each AI-powered transaction without compromising the quality of the outcome. According to Krupesh Bhat, the founder and CEO of Melento, a document automation company formerly known as SignDesk, the goal is to use expensive AI only where it is needed. Melento’s systems route routine requests to smaller, faster models and send only genuinely complex cases to frontier models. “The idea is not to replace capable models indiscriminately, but to match the cost of the model to the difficulty of the task,” said Bhat. To determine whether this approach is lowering project costs, he suggested that enterprises should track: Requests Handled By Smaller Models: A rising share indicates that frontier models are being reserved for genuinely complex work. Average Cost Per Transaction: This shows whether the overall cost of completing a task is falling. Task Success Rate: This confirms that lower costs are not coming at the expense of quality or increased human intervention. If cheaper models handle more of the workload while the success rate remains stable, the enterprise can reduce project costs without compromising outcomes. This is also where the distinction between productivity and savings becomes important. An AI system may complete more work, but that does not automatically mean a project is cheaper. The savings appears only when higher throughput translates into lower spending on models, people, or rework. Using Inference Economics To Cut The Bill Even after removing unnecessary AI calls and limiting the use of expensive models, enterprises still need to reduce the cost of running the AI that remains. This is where inference economics comes into picture. Arjun Nagulapally, CTO at AIONOS, an agentic AI startup, said hefty savings can come by removing AI from parts of a workflow where it is not needed. A customer account lookup, eligibility check or field validation can often be handled by a database or a simple business rule instead of a model. In one project for a telecom operator processing more than a million interactions a month, AIONOS moved roughly 30% of routine steps to ordinary software. It also used an open-weight model trained on resolved customer queries, reused information where possible, and shifted some work to more cost-effective computing capacity. The company said the total cost of resolving each interaction fell by 35%. The largest saving came from the first step, the work that stopped being an AI problem altogether. Other measures help reduce the cost of the AI that remains. Smaller models can handle repetitive tasks, while training them on a company’s own past cases can reduce mistakes and the human effort needed to correct them. Reusing previous answers can also prevent the same question from being sent to the model repeatedly. Enterprises can lower costs further by processing several requests together instead of handling each one separately. This keeps their computing capacity working steadily, rather than paying for expensive equipment that sits idle between requests. They can also use more efficient versions of models that require less computing power while still handling routine tasks effectively. The broader lesson is that lowering AI costs depends on how enterprises design, run and scale their AI systems. It is an engineering discipline that begins before the first production bill arrives. China fund managers stick with AI, chips in August despite July sell-off, survey finds
Investor interest in defensive shares also surges across Asia as more try to hedge against the downside risks of AI investments
Despite July’s sharp sell-off in global semiconductor shares, driven by concerns over AI-linked profitability, artificial intelligence and chips remained China’s most preferred investment themes in August, while more investors moved to hedge tech exposure, according to a survey by BofA Global Research.
The findings come from the August edition of the Asia Fund Manager Survey, for which Bank of America’s researchers polled 98 participants across the region from August 7 to 13. The respondents represented US$272 billion worth of assets under management.
In China, 73 per cent of surveyed fund managers picked AI and chips as one of their two favourite themes, even higher than July’s 60 per cent and June’s 50 per cent.
Stocks featuring share buy-backs or dividend payments ranked as the second most popular theme, with 27 per cent of China-based fund managers selecting them – a sharp rise from 16 per cent in July.
It came after global semiconductor shares tumbled in July on market concerns about potential disappointment in AI monetisation. In the US, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 21 per cent in July – its worst monthly performance since October 2008. In Hong Kong, GigaDevice Semiconductor’s stock fell from HK$1,188 (US$151) to HK$459 in July.
The growing preference for defensive stocks in China appears in line with a broader shift across Asia, where 59 per cent of surveyed fund managers said they were hedging against the risk of a decline in AI-related stocks, more than double the level reported a month prior, according to the survey findings.

The Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences (IMHANS) in Kozhikode, a premier mental healthcare centre under the Health department in Kerala, is yet to get a full-time director after the demise of the incumbent P. Krishnakumar in 2025.
The IMHANS is an autonomous institution that has been functioning in areas of mental healthcare delivery, training, research, and policy development. According to sources, though the previous Left Democratic Front government had initiated a process to fill the vacancy, it could not be completed due to various reasons. Applications were invited from qualified persons under the Directorate of Medical Education and the Directorate of Health Services for the post. Even after a change of guard occurred in the State government, the recruitment is in limbo, it is learnt.
Higher officials in the department were not available for comments.
Dr. Krishnakumar, a long-time director of the institute, passed away in January 2025. For around five months, K.G. Sajeeth Kumar, Principal, Government Medical College, Kozhikode, was given the charge. V.P. Jithu, Head of the Department of Psychiatry, has been holding the responsibility thereafter.
Sources said on Thursday that the staff association at the IMHANS has suggested that T.M. Shibu Kumar, Associate Professor, Department of Psychiatry, Government Medical College Hospital, Kozhikode, be appointed to the post. They pointed out that this could benefit the institution as Dr. Shibu Kumar was familiar with its functioning.
The sources said a full-time director was essential to formulate new schemes in the mental healthcare sector and spearhead research initiatives. Patients from nearly all districts in north Kerala rely on the institute for their mental healthcare needs. The IMHANS provides outpatient services and runs an autism clinic, besides implementing community mental health programmes, child development services, and rehabilitation projects.
Other than this, the institute offers MPhil programmes in Psychiatric Social Work and Clinical Psychology and post-basic diploma in psychiatric nursing. MPhil (Psychiatric Social Work) was launched in 2014 and M.Phil (Clinical Psychology) in 2017, and a post-basic diploma course in psychiatric nursing is being run since 2014. All these courses were launched for the first time in the government sector in Kerala.
The institute got its own building when Dr. Krishnakumar was at its helm. Recognising the community projects taken up by it, the IMHANS was selected by the Union government to be elevated as a centre of excellence in mental health in its 11th plan.

Robinson & Tongue give Root an ideal start to England's new era
- Published
First Rothesay Test, Headingley (day one of five)
Pakistan 171 all out: Shafique 61; Tongue 5-46, Robinson 5-51
England 112-2: Root 37*, Gay 33; Abbas 1-34
England are 59 runs behind
Ollie Robinson and Josh Tongue each took five wickets to give Joe Root the ideal start to his second spell as England captain as Pakistan were skittled for 171 on the opening day of the series at Headingley.
Returning four years after his first stint as skipper left him and his team broken, Root's leadership was barely tested thanks to the excellence of his bowlers and fragility of the Pakistan batting.
Root won the toss, pounced on the opportunity to bowl first and Robinson set the tone by pinning Azan Awais leg before with the first ball of the match.
Robinson expertly exploited the movement on offer, relentlessly hitting a full length for his 5-51.
Tongue took longer to warm to his task but when he also found the correct length, he was also too much for Pakistan to handle. Tongue's 5-46 ended with a final devastating burst of 4-5 from 11 balls.
England needed only 48.1 overs to dismiss the tourists and would have been done more quickly had it not been for 61 from Abdullah Shafique, 42 by Imam-ul-Haq and a near-two-hour rain delay.
It was not all plain sailing for the home side, who lost openers Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay to find themselves 48-2 in the reply.
Captain or not, Root is so often the man to steady England's batting, and he has said his team will not be wedded to a style of play.
In the company of Jordan Cox, who is at number three in place of the injured Jacob Bethell, Root calmly took the hosts to 112-2, 59 behind.
New-ish era, old captain
After the chaos of Ben Stokes' retirement and the sacking of Brendon McCullum, England are in a strange holding pattern. The new era does not begin in earnest until Stephen Fleming takes up his post as coach in the winter.
Root has the immediate task of improving the results of a team that has won only two of its previous 10 matches. This was a strong step in the right direction.
Pakistan have not won a series in this country for 30 years. There is a suspicion that little can be learned about England's fresh start because of the quality of this Pakistan team, especially a batting line-up without injured captain Babar Azam. Wednesday did little to quell that suspicion.
How different was this to the Bazball era? Root, like Stokes, posted himself at mid-off, but did not march around and marshall the field like his predecessor. Much like Stokes, Root was happy to post plenty of fielders in catching positions, though that can be attributed to the match situation.
Perhaps there was a time when the atmosphere felt flat, particularly when Imam and Shafique were adding 91 for the third wicket. Headingley gradually came to life after Tongue removed Imam, and the crowd gave home favourite Root a warm welcome before revelling in his late-evening progress.
Rain is forecast for much of Thursday and much of Friday, though England's first-day efforts have already given them ample time to begin Root's second reign with victory.
Robinson and Tongue inspire England
Robinson and Tongue have different stories from the Bazball era. Tongue was identified as an England bowler partly because of his speed, while Robinson was ignored for a long period for his lack of pace and questions over his fitness.
On this occasion, Tongue was England's fastest bowler, averaging 87.1mph, while Robinson was England's slowest at 78.4mph. As Gus Atkinson and Jofra Archer struggled, Tongue and Robinson because the first pair of England bowlers to claim five wickets in the same Test innings for 20 years.
For Robinson, this was a second five-for in as many matches since he made his Test comeback against New Zealand in June, and came days after he and wife Mia celebrated the birth of their first child.
His control was magnificent, often with wicketkeeper Jamie Smith up to the stumps. The first-ball dismissal of Awais was the first of Robinson's three lbws, all against left-handers. He got the crucial wicket of Shafique, bowled by a nip-backer, and completed his five when Khurram Shahzad hoiked to mid-on.
Like Atkinson and Archer, Tongue began like a bowler who had been playing in The Hundred for the past month. When he finally went full to draw Imam into an edge to second slip, Tongue did not look back.
Tongue was the architect of Pakistan losing their last five wickets for 21 runs. Stand-in captain Salman Ali Agha was cleaned up, Ali Usman and Mohammed Rizwan were lbw – the latter on a marginal DRS – and Mohammed Abbas lost his off stump.
The only question was which of Tongue or Robinson got to keep the ball, a problem solved by the groundsman being asked to cut it in half so each bowler could take a piece.
Chastening day for Pakistan
This was confirmation Pakistan's batting is vulnerable and their bowlers have the skills to challenge England's shaky top order.
The tourists are hampered by Babar's hand injury, and stand-in captain Salman said he would have batted had he won the toss. Saud Shakeel was too late calling for a review when given lbw to Robinson, only for replays to show the ball would have gone over the stumps – one of several marginal decisions that went England's way.
Pakistan were at risk of being overwhelmed when Duckett and Gay made a Bazball-style start to England's reply.
Still, Abbas is a superb operator in the Robinson mould. He was unlucky not to have Duckett lbw in the first over, then was not denied when he pinned the England opener on the shin.
Gay needs to establish himself at the top of the England order and played handsome drives in his 33 before poking Mohammad Ali to second slip. The left-hander looks susceptible to the ball angled across him.
England could have wobbled, only for Cox to show good temperament for his unbeaten 23, while Root was typically assured for his 37. They both have an opportunity to make a significant score.

An image of Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national president Nitin Nabin is being shared on social media (here, here, and here), mocking him for allegedly holding the Tricolour upside down. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The image shows BJP national president Nitin Nabin holding the Tricolour upside down.
Fact: The image is digitally manipulated. The original image shows BJP national president Nitin Nabin hoisting the Tricolour correctly at his residence as part of the ‘Har Ghar Tiranga’ campaign on 13 August 2026. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A Google Lens search of the screenshot of the viral image led us to a post shared by the BJP on its official X handle (archived)on 13 August 2026. The image in the BJP’s post showed several similarities with the viral image. However, the original image showed Nitin Nabin holding the Tricolour correctly, unlike the digitally altered version circulating on social media. The BJP’s post stated that the image showed Nitin Nabin hoisting the national flag at his residence as part of the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign ahead of Independence Day. This confirms that the viral image has been digitally manipulated.
We then reviewed Nitin Nabin’s social media accounts to find out whether he had shared any photograph or video of himself hoisting the national flag at his residence as part of the Har Ghar Tiranga campaign. This led us to a video posted by Nitin Nabin on his official X handle (archived) on 13 August 2026. The video clearly showed him holding the national flag correctly, further confirming that the image circulating on social media had been digitally altered.
